father_raw: Father, a joiner, died when author still an infant.
residences: Edinburgh for 5 years before returning to native village
career_raw: Went to sea on leaving school, but soon returned home to become apprenticed to a draper, eventually setting up a shop on own account.
affiliations_raw: Poet; member of dissenting church; rambler; spare time was spent reading, attending evening classes and meetings at Mutual Improvement Societies and in general mental improvement: ‘...the best antidote for immoral and pernicious influence is to create and foster a love of reading and mental culture...’; lay preacher; engaged in Mission School work; regular contributor to the Juteport Express.
content_tone: A narrative set firmly in the style of a typical Victorian ‘respectable artisan’, discussing childhood reading, self-improvement, schooling and mental advancement. Fond memories of incidents and anecdotes of his childhood years combine with some comment on work life and local politics and village politicians, centred on the evening gatherings at the shoemaker’s shop. A useful document of mid-Victorian ‘respectability’ and of social and political life in a small Scottish village. The volume also contains a fragment of the autobiography of his uncle (pp.187-204) which is a rather literary and rambling piece with comments on dress and the home, but which says more about his parents than of himself.
title: The History of a Village Shopkeeper: An Autobiography

father_raw: Son of a plasterer and Chartist.
residences: Cheltenham (1832-54); Yewdale Bridge, Lake District (1854-5); London (1855-9); Manchester (1859-63); London (1863); Newcastle upon Tyne (1863-1900); Madeira (1900-7); London (?-1906)
career_raw: Errand-boy (1844); apprentice printer (1846-53); compositor (for 1 year on Linton’s English Republic, 1854-5); regular contributor (’Caractacus’) to National Reformer and to Newcastle Chronicle (’Ironside’); journalist (1863-); editor of Newcastle Weekly Chronicle (1864-1900).
affiliations_raw: Active Chartist (from age 16) and Republican, involved in radical struggles of 1850s and 1860s for national and international causes; member of the Fraternal Democrats; founded a Republican Association in Cheltenham (1851); committee member of the Union and Emancipation Society (pro-Northern States in American Civil War); secretary of Central Committee of Friends of Poland; founder of children’s Dicky Bird Society (1876). Publications include An Argument for Complete Suffrage (1860); The Shareholder’s War: an Argument for the North and the Negro (1863); Our American Cousins: being personal impressions of the people and institutions of the United States (London and Newcastle, 1883).
content_tone: Written when aged nearly 70, while in Madeira, Adams provides a highly interesting documentation of social and political life in the years of mid-century radicalism. Among the many themes discussed are social life and change; evolution of transport; fashions; demise of customs (May Day, Royal Oak Day, Whitsuntide, ‘beating the bounds’); disease; conjurors; crimes and trials; children’s street games; apprenticeship; old election practices; travelling theatre; ‘tramping’ and common lodging-houses; ‘penny dreadfuls’ and cheap literature; international politics. The narrative is especially valuable for its study of radical and labour politics with an excellent account of the principles, divisions, demonstrations and leaders of the Chartist movement. A major part of the text was serialised in the Newcastle Weekly Chronicle (1901-2).
title: Memoirs of a Social Atom

father_raw: One of 6 children of a joiner.
residences: Glasgow for most of his life, except for a short period in Edinburgh
career_raw: Employed in a Glasgow printshop (aged 9-12); messenger-boy (aged 12); apprentice compositor, becoming a journeyman in 1839; foreman of print shop (for 7 years), then a manager.
affiliations_raw: Joined the Southern Sabbath Morning Fellowship Meeting at age 16; Sunday School teacher (1838-); ordained a church elder when aged 22; commenced a Christian Institute for young men; chairman of the Southern District Sabbath School Union for 11 years.
content_tone: A brief life history composed chiefly of notes on ancestry and family, with some account of his work life and religious activities.
title: Autobiography

father_raw: Father (dramatic writer) deserted family and author was raised by mother and maternal grandparents (bookbinders).
residences: London and Glasgow
career_raw: Office-boy in an insurance doctor’s office (1901); office-sweeper in the National Press Agency, rising to become a ‘penny-a-liner’ for the London Letter column and, eventually, assistant sub-editor (for 5 years); joined Editorial Intelligence Department of Daily Chronicle (to 1906); contributed articles to numerous journals and newspapers, including Islington Gazette, Agnostic Journal, Freedom, Justice, The Social Democrat; established the Bakunin Press (1907), publishing many of his own writings.
affiliations_raw: Boy preacher; active in Christian Social Mission (1902); converted to theism; voluntary Theistic missioner (1904); established Clerkenwell Freethought Mission; became an atheist; lecturer and propagandist for Freethought and Socialist movements, aligning himself at various times to the Social Democratic movement, socialism, communism and anarchism. Worked increasingly for the cause of socialism with no thought of personal advancement, and strong in his condemnation of careerists and parliamentarians. Imprisoned when aged 22 for defending the cause of Indian freedom. Stood trial in 1922 for publishing birth control pamphlet.
content_tone: More than simply an autobiography, Aldred gives a full account of the theory and activities of the Freethought and Socialist movements in Britain over half a century, providing thorough studies of theism, the Social Democratic Federation, the Socialist Party of Great Britain, atheism, communism and anarchism. Full sketches are provided of many of the activists and theorists of these movements. Further comments are made on sex equality and free love. Fragments of an autobiography appeared in 1908 and 1940 under the title Dogmas Discarded, and these are incorporated in the text.
title: No Traitor's Gait!. Published as serialised pamphlets by the Strickland Press, Glasgow, 1955-63. Bound in one volume in the British Library.

father_raw: Son of a cutler and tool-maker.
residences: various areas of London all his life
career_raw: Employed in a bottle factory at age 11, subsequently working at various jobs to age 14; telegraph messenger (1887-92); sorter (1892-?); spent most of his working life with the Post Office until forced to resign in 1916 because of political activities; held various trade union appointments, including general and organising secretary of Port of London Docks and Wharves Staff Association (1918-20); organising secretary of Union of Post Office Workers (1920-8); MP (Lab) for North Camberwell (1922-31; 1935-44).
affiliations_raw: Joined Independent Labour Party in 1893; secretary of South Eastern branch of Fawcett Association, the sorters’ trade union; editor of trade journal, The Post, and served on union’s executive committee; founder-member of Bermondsey branch of ILP (1908); chairman of West Bermondsey Labour Party (1910); Methodist lay preacher and Sunday School teacher; pacifist, and member of Union of Democratic Control and parliamentary secretary of No-Conscription Fellowship; member of 1917 Club; elected to LCC (1919-25; 1934-46); member of National Executive of LP (1921-6); alderman (1934-53); mayor of Camberwell (1951); London Whip for Parliamentary Labour Party (1923); Parliamentary Secretary to Admiralty (1924; 1929-31); accepted peerage in 1944; member of various parliamentary committees and delegations; chairman of National Dock Labour Board (1944); Privy Councillor (1945); president of UK Band of Hope Union; active in the Brotherhood movement; vice-president of Metropolitan Association of Building Societies; director of Municipal Mutual Assurance and Atlas Building Society; governor of LSE and Dulwich College; JP. Published large number of articles, pamphlets and books, including Christianity and Socialism (1909); Christ and Labour (1912); Newfoundland, the Forgotten Island (1944).
content_tone: Written towards the end of his life, Lord Ammon recalls childhood struggles following the death of his father and mentions briefly early employments before moving on to detail his work for the Post Office; trade union activities; married life; the early days of the ILP; foreign visits (USA, Soviet Union; West Africa; China); public life and activities atlocaland national levels; early 20th century industrial unrest; inter-war Labour politics (first and second Labour governments; General Strike). The text includes manuscript amendments and transcripts of correspondence to the author.
title: ‘A Long Road: An Autobiography’, TS, pp.152

father_raw: 3rd of 11 children of a miner.
residences: Hirwaun (1882-4); Mardy (1884); Hirwaun (1885-1905); Llanwrtyd Wells (1905-8); Ystrad Rhondda (1908-)
career_raw: Assisted at home in raising young family (aged 13-17); dress-maker (from age 17), with own workroom by 1901, employing 2 apprentices; in charge of workroom from 1905; Labour Party Woman Organiser for Wales (1919-48); appointed to the Glamorgan Health Executive Council (1948-).
affiliations_raw: Helped to form the first Co-operative Women’s Guilds in the Rhondda (1910-19); the first woman to be elected to the executive ofthe Rhondda Borough Labour Party (1916); served on the War Pensions Committee and Disablement Training Committees (1914-18); member of the Ministry of Health Welsh Consultative Council; gave evidence before the Regional Survey Committee for Wales on housing and the Sankey Commission on pit-head baths and miners’ housing; attended International Socialist Congress (1931); Liaison Officer for women’s section of the LP in Wales on wartime committees of the Ministry of Information, Board of Trade, Ministry of Fuel and Power, and Ministry of Food (1939-45); member of Pontypridd and Rhondda Hospital Management Committee; JP; OBE; active in Church and Sunday School work; member of Suffragette movement (non-militant); published several articles in the short-lived Welsh Labour paper Y Dinesydd (The Citizen).
content_tone: The author provides a good account of her childhood, schooling and home life and duties but the major part of the narrative is concerned with her political activities and tells of the struggles of women for a place in society and their changing status as wives, mothers and workers. Other topics discussed include the campaigns for pit-head baths and for maternity and child welfare; Labour Party work and struggles in Wales; the strength of North Wales Nonconformity and Liberalism; the miners’ lock-out following the General Strike; Nursery School movement; the fight for pensions.
title: A Woman’s Work is Never Done: being the recollections of a childhood and upbringing amongst the South Wales miners and a life time of service to the Labour movement in Wales, with a foreword by the Rt. Hon. James Griffiths

father_raw: Youngest of 7 children of a shoemaker.
career_raw: Put to the trade of shoemaking before the age of 10; local correspondent to various newspapers, supplementing the earnings of his craft; school attendance officer (1874-5); sanitary inspector (1875-90).
affiliations_raw: A lover of music, poetry and nature; wrote and published own poetry; founder-member, hall-keeper and librarian of Wellingborough Literary Institute; member of Wellingborough School Board (1871-4); member of trade benefit club at Waxton; member of the Society of United Warblers as a youth; author of Sonnets on the Months: And other Poems, Descriptive, Domestic and National (Northampton, 1863); Poems and Sonnets, Descriptive, Miscellaneous, and Special (London and Northampton, 1875).
content_tone: Most of the biographical information appears in an introductory sketch, supplemented by the autobiographical content of some ofthe poems and sketches. Otherwise, the value of the verses and text lies in the graphic portrayal of early 19th century rural life and customs, with particularly interesting comments on trade club meetings; elections and feasts; dame schools; married life; leisure and changing customs; celebrations to mark the passing of the 1832 Reform Bill; Christmas; St. Valentine’s Day; St. Luke’s Fair; gleaning; Plough Mondays; Punch and Judy shows.
title: Sketches in Prose and Verse, with portrait and biographical sketch of the author

residences: Lancashire for most of his life, in and around Middleton, Manchester and Prestwich
career_raw: Worked the bobbin-wheel as a child, soon becoming a hand-loom weaver. Hand-loom weaving remained his chief employment but also worked for spells (notably during trade depressions) as a warehouseman, farm labourer and sailor. Eventually became a putter-out to weavers. In later life worked as a journalist; doorkeeper/messenger at Somerset House (1852); and obtained a livelihood in old age by public poetry reading.
affiliations_raw: Poet; Volunteer; active in the Radical and Reform movements of the early 19th century, being twice arrested for treasonable offences, but after release from prison becoming politically moderate and later joined the Special Constables to put down Chartist demonstrations. Secretary to the local Hampden Club; member of Committee of Parliamentary Reformers. Publications include An Account of the Arrest and Imprisonment of Samuel Bamford, Middleton, on suspicion of High Treason. Written by Himself (Manchester, 1817); Homely Rhymes, Poems, and Reminiscences (1864); The Weaver Boy; or, Miscellaneous Poetry (Manchester, 1819); Walks in South Lancashire and on its Borders (Blackley, 1844).
content_tone: A deservedly ‘classic’ autobiography by one of the leading figures of the early 19th century reform agitation. This first volume deals with the years up to c.1813 and provides a fine account of Lancashire life and manners at the turn of the century, with an especially valuable section on leisure and traditional customs. Topics covered include feasts and festivities; celebrations of Christmas and Easter (’peace-egging’); ‘elections’ for ‘lord mayor’; ‘Riding the Black Lad’; ‘White Apron Fair’; May 1st (mischief-neet”); rushbearing and the Wakes; November 5th; ancestry and family; domestic life; workhouse life (lunatic inmates; diet); schooling; diet and dress; courtship; superstitions; machine-breaking and clashes with the militia. The narrative includes sections of dialogue written in dialect. The 1893 edition omits sections of ‘trivial or passing interest’, compresses the narrative by leaving out formal documents and lists of names, and puts together a number of shorter chapters dealing with the same themes. Apart from omitting a few personal ‘animadversions’ no other change to the text was made, ‘nor hardly a sentence altered’.
title: Early Days, published in parts, then bound

father_raw: Father a rag- and bone-collector.
career_raw: At age 8 he worked turning the wheel at a rope factory, winding yarn for jacket weavers, peeling osier-rods, helping a rotary-hand and asa boot-finisher’s sweater. Apart from a brief period distributing tradesmen’s leaflets he worked as an unskilled labourer in many different factories in Leicester.
affiliations_raw: Through self-education Barclay came to renounce his Catholicism in favour of active work for socialism; belonged at various times to the Social Democratic Federation, Socialist League, Anarchist-Communist Group, and the Independent Labour Party; lectured at Labour Clubs and on reform platforms, and contributed to the secularist The Countryman; wrote series of articles on Leicester slums for The Wyvern; member of Irish National Club, and of Leicester branch of the Gaelic League.
content_tone: Barclay describes in fine detail the life and domestic situation of an immigrant Irish family, forced to England by the 1846 potato blight, with comments on the home, work and diet. The memoirs then turn from personal detail to an account of literature and religion, leading towards the author’s involvement with the socialist cause, with general criticism of the inactivity and short-sightedness of the working class. Descriptions are provided of meetings and correspondence with ‘fellow travellers’, such as Ruskin, Carpenter and Shaw.
title: Memoirs and Medleys. The Autobiography of a Bottle- Washer edited by James K. Kelly, with a foreword by Sydney A. Gimson

father_raw: Youngest of 4 children of a boat-builder.
residences: Suffolk, London, Cornwall and Devon
career_raw: Apprentice shipwright, for 7 weeks only (1901); teacher (1907-?); freelance journalist; novelist and children’s author.
affiliations_raw: Poet; published large number of novels, short stories and children’s books under his own name and under the pseudonyms of ‘Neil Bell’ and ‘Paul Martens’.
content_tone: Bell (i.e. Southwold) deliberately refused to write of his private life and concentrated instead on his job as an author. The narrative tells in full and honest detail of his writing life with personal matters intruding only when relevant to his career.
title: London, of Stephen SOUTHWOLD], My Writing Life

father_raw: One of 6 children of a stonemason and a cotton- and silk-spinner.
residences: Glasgow for most of his life, but with spells in London, Liverpool and Manchester
career_raw: Carried milk for dairy farmer (aged 8 or 9), becoming full-time assistant on leaving school (1894); van-boy to a mineral water manufacturer (for 18 months), then bottle-washer and labeller in same factory; apprentice iron-moulder, remaining a foundry worker for rest of working life.
affiliations_raw: Atheist; member of Independent Labour Party (1900), Social Democratic Federation (1903), then founder-member of Glasgow Socialist Society (later, the Socialist Labour Party), which merged with the Communist Party of Great Britain in 1920; member of the Associated Iron-Moulders of Scotland (from 1904), eventually sitting on its executive committee; member of the West of Scotland Astronomical Society and of the Advocates of Industrial Unionism (1905); editor of The Socialist (1919); author of The British Communist Party. A Short History (1937); John MacLean, a Fighter for Freedom (Glasgow, 1944); Nikolai Lenin. A Brief Biographical Sketch (1925); and of various articles in the Scottish Iron Moulders’ Journal.
content_tone: The narrative begins with a most interesting account of slum life in Glasgow and of mutual aid among the working class at the end of the 19th century. Apart from descriptions of apprenticeship and employments (notably of his work in a foundry), the bulk of the text provides a full account of socialist politics in the opening decades of the 20th century. Among the themes and organisations discussed are the ILP; SDF; Socialist Labour Party; industrial unionism; workers’ education movement (Ruskin College; Plebs League); opposition to World War I; the Clydeside Shop Stewards’ Movement; the Clyde Workers’ Committee; the Russian Revolution; 40-hour strike, 1918; and impressions of the Soviet Union. The autobiography ends with the author leaving prison in 1926 to resume propaganda work for the CPGB. An extremely useful document.
title: Pioneering Days

career_raw: Bookseller’s apprentice (1837), becoming head clerk/manager by the age of 21; actor/strolling player/’mummer’ (c.1846-9); bookseller and newsagent (1849); contributor to various periodicals, including Chambers’s Journaland Hogg's Instructor; editor, and later proprietor, of the North Briton (1855-73); proprietor of the short-run Bawbee (1856) and the slightly more successful Scottish Thistle (to 1859); assistant editor of the Glasgow News (1873-4); journalist and author, contributing to the provincial weekly press and miscellaneous periodicals (1874-92).
affiliations_raw: Member of Mechanics’ Library; author of novels, plays and reports on the Fisheries, published variously under the pseudonyms of ‘Peter Paterson’, ‘William M. Cooper’, ‘Louis Henry Curzon’, ‘Ellangowan’. Publications include The Blue Ribbon of the Turf (1890); Flagellation and the Flagellants [1910]; The Story of a Stolen Heir (1858); The Unappreciated Fisher Folk: their round of life and labour (1883).
content_tone: Most of the biographical details of this pioneer of cheap and popular journalism are contained in a prefatory memoir. This commences with a description of the author’s entry into work asa bookseller’s apprentice (in 1837), and is followed by comments on diet; leisure (theatre; public houses); the pursuit of knowledge; the bookselling trade (1837-8); circulating libraries; cheap periodicals; recollections of his first employer, Mr. W. Tait and his friends, and of contributors to Tait’s Edinburgh Magazine, including Thomas de Quincey, Sir Walter Scott, William and Robert Chambers.
title: Some Memories of Books, Authors and Events

father_raw: Both his parents were servants.
career_raw: Day-labourer from age 14; worked briefly as a weaver (1825) and a turnkey. Was seriously injured in explosion at a quarry where he was working (1829).
affiliations_raw: Self-taught by writing regularly, becoming a respected author and poet. Published various works with his brother, John Bethune, and also on his own account, including Tales of the Scottish Peasantry (1884); The Scottish Peasant's Fire-side (Edinburgh, 1843); Tales and Sketches of the Scottish Peasantry (Edinburgh, 1838).
content_tone: Compiled and edited by William McCombie, the autobiographical extracts appear in the form of correspondence, verse, and a short biography of his brother. Interesting accounts are provided of early home life, work and his literary progress.
title: Autobiographical extracts in William McCombie, Memoirs of Alexander Bethune, embracing selections from his Correspondence and Literary Remains

father_raw: One of 3 children of an ironmonger and proprietor of home-furnishing business.
career_raw: Apprentice soap-boiler (1786-94); assistant to brother in plumbing business (1794-8); imprisoned (1798-1801); proprietor of the Republican Argus when living in Pennsylvania (1801-7); editor of the Democratic Press, when in Philadelphia (1807-).
affiliations_raw: Chairman of the General Ward Committee of the London Corresponding Society; experienced frequent arrests and confinements on various charges because of his political activities, though was acquitted on each occasion until 1798, when convicted of high treason and imprisoned. Alderman of the City of Philadelphia (1822-44).
content_tone: The most interesting section of this volume deals with the author’s political activities and involvement with the LCS, providing an extremely useful assessment of the political climate of the 1790s. The text also has comments on the ‘Church and King Riots’ in Birmingham (1790-1); sketches of Thomas Hardy, John Thelwall, Arthur C. O’Connor, and others; his arrests, confinements and eventual imprisonment.
title: Recollections of the Life of John Binns: Twenty-nine Years in Europe and Fifty-three in the United States. Written by Himself, with Anecdotes, Political, Historical, and Miscellaneous

father_raw: 2nd son of a provincial strolling comedian and actress wife.
residences: Maidstone (1851); Halifax (1862-71); London (1871); Northwich, Cheshire (1877-85); Barnes, S
career_raw: First employment was as odd-job boy in lithographic printing works; apprentice brushmaker (c.1864/5-71?); enlisted in army, achieving rank of sergeant (1871-7); clerk/storekeeper (1877-85); began writing career in 1882 when article published in The Yorkshireman, subsequently working as a weekly columnist and news reporter; resigned from Manchester Sunday Chronicle (1891), to start, with 4 others, the Clarion; freelance journalist (from 1927).
affiliations_raw: Actively involved in Labour movement, helping to found Manchester Fabian Society (1890); drafted constitution of newly-formed Manchester Independent Labour Party (1892); president of Manchester ILP (to 1893); established Cinderella Clubs (social and educational clubs for slum children) in 1889, and the Clarion Scouts in 1894 (young propagandists for socialism); joint convener and financer of Federal Labour Parliament in Manchester (1898); left the Socialist movement in 1914; ardent critic of Labour Party, first from a socialist then a conservative perspective. Published extensively, with his best-known and influential work being Merrie England (1894).
content_tone: A large part of the narrative deals with the author’s boyhood and adolescence, with comments on his early life, schooling, courtship and army life. Although stating that ‘... This is the story of a man’s life, not a history of the Labour movement or the Clarion...’, some (brief) comments are made on socialism and the Socialist movement. A disappointing work from a central figure in the early struggles of Labour.
title: My Eighty Years, with a preface by Alexander M. Thompson

residences: London; Hemel Hempstead; Bexley and Liverpool before emigrating to Australia in 1840
career_raw: ‘Qualified’ teacher at age 15; organised and conducted new school at Hemel Hempstead (1834), then moved to large boarding school at Bexley, and on to British School at Liverpool (1837). Taught briefly at Lancasterian school in Stoke Newington before emigrating to Australia (1840), where he taught, wrote text books, inspected schools and dug for gold. Made fortune from gold discoveries, land speculation and private boarding schools.
affiliations_raw: Member of Mechanics’ Institute; teetotaller; helped to establish Christian Young Men’s Association; contributed articles on education and temperance to various magazines; published tracts and author of various books.
content_tone: Although the author’s ancestors were of ‘high’ birth the Napoleonic Wars had ruined his father and ensured that the family experienced hardship and poverty. Bonwick struggled against the early disadvantages to follow a career in education, becoming very wealthy after emigrating. The narrative provides an excellent account of schools and schooling, in both personal and historical aspects. Comments are also made on his connections with Owenism and on the major political events of the day, including Chartism (more social than political’). The text is divided into 5 parts (Schools and Schooling; Life in Australia; Later Life in England; World Wanderings; Family Records and Poetry).
title: An Octogenarian's Reminiscences

father_raw: Son of an ironmonger.
career_raw: Boy clerk with General Post Office (1904-9), then assistant clerk; keeper in the Department of Ceramics, Victoria and Albert Museum (1938-50).
affiliations_raw: Keenly interested in the theatre, music, painting and literature; active in village life; published extensively, including Old English Porcelain (1928); Dresden China (1934); Gardening Heresies and Devotions (1939).
content_tone: An unusual volume which commences with the author’s opinions of the ‘essential truth about human existence’ and continues to mix personal detail with strong self-analysis and opinions on a wide variety of subjects. Among the topics discussed are working-class life in Battersea in the 1890s; ancestry; home life; childhood recollections; street games; schooling and punishment; sexual knowledge; courtship; a very large section on the theatre and the Arts. Bowyer (i.e. Honey) also makes highly personal observations on religion; socialism; the corporate state; ‘women’s failings’; women’s place in society; population; health; education.
title: Brought Out in Evidence: an autobiographical summing-up

residences: Risca; Abercarn; Newbridge; Newport
career_raw: Started work in the mines at age 12, and remained in the pits until elected miners’ agent for the Western Valleys District (aged 24); vice-president and president of the South Wales Miners’ Federation (until 1920). Elected MP for South Glamorgan in 1906, remaining in Parliament until his resignation in 1920 and acceptance of the post of labour adviser to the Ministry of Labour. Retired in 1927, though still acted as a consultant to government departments and continued to contribute articles to the Western Mail.
affiliations_raw: Teetotaller; Baptist lay preacher; member of the Miners’ Federation of Great Britain executive (1892-3); member of Monmouthshire County Council; vice-president of the Welsh National Liberal Association; vice-chairman of Labour Party (1911); Under- Secretary for Home Affairs (1915).
content_tone: A brief career outline with comments on self-education and the character of miners.
title: ‘How I Got On’, Pearson’s Weekly, 19 April 1906.

father_raw: 8th child of a steel-maker.
residences: or near Sheffield for most of his life
career_raw: Employed for short periods in a shop, a stove-grate factory and in a doctor’s house; cellarlad in a steel-making furnace; bottle-washer in a chemical laboratory (aged 12-20); laboratory assistant. Established reputation as ‘a solver of analytical problems and deviser of simplified methods of analysing steel’, and was employed in this capacity. Conducted own small business manufacturing a composite material.
affiliations_raw: Learned skills as a painter, joiner, stainer, French polisher, upholsterer, and sandal-maker; major official in the Independent Labour Party, and ‘tried his hand’ at soap-box oratory; contributed articles to technical papers on the analysis of steelworks materials. Publications include The Case-Hardening of Steel (1914); The Heat Treatment of Tool Steel (1911); Steel-Makers(1933).
content_tone: Although Brearley makes some comment on his poor childhood, child labour and domestic handicrafts (cutting file blanks), the text concentrates on his involvement in the steel-making process, as an analyst and manufacturer. The narrative also includes observations on life in Russia during the 1905 Revolution; diet; dress; and schooling. The text includes some use of dialogue and dialect, but is generally written in a rather tortuous and pedantic style.
title: Knotted String. Autobiography of a Steel-Maker

residences: Failsworth (1825-c
career_raw: At age 5 had to assist in bread-winning by door-to-door hawking; was later ‘put to the bobbin wheel’ at home, followed by a brief spell in a factory as a piecer, eventually becoming a domestic hand-loom weaver. During period of trade depression he found employment dragging coals from the coal pits. Moved to Manchester to work in various silk manufacturers’ warehouses (up to 1860s); sub-editor on Oldham Times; adopted literature as his profession, contributing articles, poems and short stories to a variety of newspapers and journals; editor of own journal, Country Words (1869-75), which was successful until death of daughter caused him to lose interest. Visited America and then returned to literary profession running his own Ben Brierley’s Journal (1869-91).
affiliations_raw: Literature; founder-member of local Mutual Improvement Society; attended theatre; amateur dramatics; member of Manchester City Council for 6 years (c.1876-82); founder-member of Manchester Literary Club (c.1864). Published widely, with poems and stories appearing in a variety of journals. Author of more than 49 books, including Tales and Sketches of Lancashire Life (Manchester, 1862, 1883); The Lancashire Weaver Lad: a domestic drama in three acts (Manchester, 1870); The Cotters of Mossbury (Manchester, 1871).
content_tone: The first part of the narrative provides an entertaining and informative account of all aspects of life in a northern weaving community in the second quarter of the 19th century. Among the topics covered are breeching; traditional recreations (rushbearing; 5th November; pig- washing); coronation celebrations; childhood games; diet; dréss; cotton mill work and conditions; domestic weaving; Chartism; ‘plug-drawing’ and the strike of 1842. The second part of the narrative is of less interest, and is concerned with describing his literary endeavours and friendships (with an interesting anecdote on Samuel Bamford). Many passages of dialogue are included, written in dialect.
title: Home Memories, and Recollections of a Life

career_raw: Assisted mother in making bread and working on the farm (1784-7); apprenticed to a wine merchant (1887-93); cellarman; clerk in an attorney’s office; recited and sang in a theatre (1799); adopted writing as a profession, c.1799/1800, with his first book being published in 1799. Also served as surveyor and clerk to the local Board of Commissioners. Was granted a civil list pension of $75 in 1852.
affiliations_raw: Wrote and issued popular ballads and street song books when in his twenties; active member of Royal Literary Fund; instrumental in founding Wiltshire Topographical Society; honorary member of large number of archaeological and historical societies; author of The Beauties of Wiltshire (1801-25), 3 vols.; The Architectural Antiquities of Great Britain (1805-14), 4 vols.; Cathedral Antiquities of England (1814-35), 14 vols.
content_tone: Published in 2 volumes in 3 parts, comprising ‘Personal and Literary Memoir of the Author’ (vol. 1); ‘Descriptive Account of his Literary Works’, by his secretary T. E. Jones, and ‘Appendix: biographical, topographical, critical and miscellaneous essays’ (vol. 2). Britton provides a chiefly topographical description of the village of his youth, but includes some interesting comments on travellers (’quack’ doctors) and rural superstitions. He then describes the ‘monotonous and dreary routine’ of his apprenticeship and the ‘vices and illiteracy’ of his fellow servants before moving on to his literary life, with profiles of acquaintances and observations on debating societies. Interesting but brief observations are made on the ‘quackery and imposture’ of William Huntington (see entries 363 and 364) and on the notorious transvestite Chevalier D’Eon.
title: The Autobiography of John Britton, FSA, Honorary Member of Numerous English and Foreign Societies

residences: various places in Lancashire as a child, including Unsworth; Radcliffe; Hunt Hill
career_raw: Started work at local mill as a half-timer at age 10 as an errand-boy, then as a reacher-in and as a cut-looker’s assistant (to age 13); pupil-teacher (1887-92); cashier’s clerk (1892-5); Methodist circuit preacher (1896-1936).
affiliations_raw: Member of Band of Hope; interested in classical music and the theatre; attended socialist meetings in early manhood; started a short-lived magazine with his brother with intention of depicting the struggles of the Radcliffe colliers; contributed articles to local newspapers; published several theological works and others written in Lancashire dialect.
content_tone: The first and more interesting volume deals with the author’s Lancashire childhood, with observations on rural Wakes; ‘flitting’; family history; mendicants and street entertainers; homes and housing; schooling; childhood superstitions; childhood games; local characters; clairvoyancy; chapel festivities; customs and celebrations (Bonfire night; Christmas; Easter; ‘pace-egging”); dress; child labour and factory life. The second volume is concerned mostly with his work as a Methodist preacher, though also contains some comment on the Suffragette movement.
title: Lancashire Bred. An Autobiography, subtitled: Life in a Cotton Town from ‘75 to ‘95; From Ranmoor College to Oxford’s ‘dreaming spires‘

father_raw: Father worked as a miller.
residences: Blackburn (1851-6); Newcastle upon Tyne (1856-80); London (1880-7); Theale, Berks
career_raw: Worked in father’s business on leaving school, then became a poultry breeder (1871). The major part of his working life was devoted to promoting the productive side of poultry husbandry and included appointments as editor of the Live Stock Journal, member of a commission to enquire into the Irish poultry industry; lecturer on poultry under the County Council scheme; lecturer at Reading University College (1895-1910); owner of College Poultry Farm at Theale (1910-).
affiliations_raw: Secretary of National Poultry Organisation (1899-1913); first president of the World’s Poultry Science Association (1912-27); founder of the World’s Poultry Congresses, serving as joint-president (1921, 1923) and sole president (1927); travelled extensively throughout Europe and North America; founder of National Poultry Council, and first president (1920-1), secretary (1921-34); contributed articles to numerous newspapers and journals and published extensively on poultry, including British Poultry Husbandry (1930); Poultry Breeding and Production (1929), 2 vols. Knighted, 1930.
content_tone: Only brief comments are made on the author’s early life with the text concentrating on his associations, nationally and world-wide, with poultry husbandry. Brown also makes general observations on national and international affairs and on his extensive travels. Rather dull.
title: Memories at Eventide

residences: London and the South of England for most of his life
career_raw: Sent to live and work in a laundry at age 9; employed in various other jobs between the ages of 9 and 12, including errand-boy; milkboy; ‘boy of all work’ at a ‘lath-renders’ and at a paper-pattern maker’s; chemist’s lad; street urchin; billiard marker; moulder’s assistant. He was then employed as a seaman for about 15 years, serving in almost every capacity except that of a master, having started as a cabin-boy. Came ashore when in his mid/late twenties and got work as a clerk in the Civil Service, later combining this with a business concerned with buying and selling fancy goods and as a carver, gilder and picture-frame maker. Suffered from business difficulties and threatened bankruptcy. Fortunes again took an upward turn when he was appointed to the staff of the Morning Leader when aged 42, followed by a successful life as public speaker engaged on lecture tours at home and abroad. Author.
affiliations_raw: Regularly attended Lock Chapel as a child; chorister; contributor to Chambers’s Miscellany; sole recreation in his early years was attending religious open-air meetings; published many stories, chiefly of the sea.
content_tone: A lively volume that provides good detail of the author’s early work life as a drudge in a laundry and as an errand-boy. A colourful picture is drawn of the life of a London ‘street arab’ around mid-century before the text moves on to describe his attempts to get a berth on a ship and of his later efforts to provide a home for his wife and growing family. Much of the remainder of the narrative tells of his business struggles in the trade of shopkeeping, and of his legal experiences related to approaching bankruptcy.
title: Confessions of a Tradesman

residences: various towns near Failsworth and Oldham before moving to Ashton-under-Lyne (1885-9); Huddersfield (1889-91); London (1891-7); Leeds (1897-9); Glasgow (1899-1906); Bradford (1906-?); London
career_raw: Started work in a card-cutting room at age 6, remaining full-time for 2 years; half-time ‘little piecer’ from age 8-13, then full-time as a ‘big piecer’; worked as a cotton operative until aged 28, but with short spells in a print works and a cardsheet manufactory; correspondent for local newspaper (1881-4); started own (short-lived) paper, the Oldham Operative (1884); sub-editor of the Cotton Factory Times (1885-9); manager of Yorkshire Factory Times (1889-91); editor of Workman's Times (1891-3); continued to work as a journalist, poet and writer; organising secretary for Independent Labour Party (1897-1902); serial writer; socialist propagandist and lecturer (1895-1914); editor of Bradford Pioneer (1914); on editorial staff of the London Evening Standard (1919) and Pall Mall Gazette.
affiliations_raw: Sunday School teacher; member of Mutual Improvement Society; active in the formation of the ILP; unsuccessful parliamentary candidate on several occasions; member of Glasgow City Council (1902-5); member of Socialist National Defence Committee; member of National Administrative Council of ILP; resigned from ILP and chairmanship of Bradford branch in 1915 on the issue ofthe War, but rejoined in 1925. Published widely, with a large number of books on the issue of agriculture and the necessity for the taxation of foreign investments.
content_tone: A lengthy narrative by one of the founding-fathers of the Labour Party. The first part is drawn from secondary and oral sources and deals with a history of radicalism in the Oldham district of Lancashire from 1800, with references to Hampden Clubs; the introduction of power-looms and factory conditions in the 1840s; and Labour agitation. The second section deals with the author’s childhood and early working life, with graphic accounts of domestic misfortunes and the Walmsley strike of 1858; the home; schooling; diet; dress; ‘flitting’; conditions among the operatives during the cotton famine of the 18605; the American Civil War; parish relief; customs (’pancaking’; rushbearing). The final part deals with Burgess’s career in journalism and the formation and consolidation of the ILP. Providing a detailed account of the early efforts for organisation, and of the battle against Fabianism and collaboration, this amounts to an invaluable source for the study of the ‘gestation’ period of the ILP and Labour electioneering. Co-operation and conflict with such personalities as Robert Blatchford, Ben Tillett, Keir Hardie, H. H. Champion, Bernard Shaw, Sidney Webb, Ramsay MacDonald, and others, are recorded in full. A most useful document, though suffering from patchiness. Contains some dialect. The author is not to be confused with Joseph Tom Burgess (1828-1886), also a journalist and author of the anti-union The Life and Experiences of a Warwickshire Labourer, with his own Thoughts and Opinions on the Strike, as told by himself (George Routledge and Sons, London, 1872).
title: ‘Nineteenth Century Lancashire Textile Operatives Tribulations, 1800-95’, TS, pp.408

residences: Poplar before entering the orphanage, and afterwards in various distriets of London
career_raw: Draper’s-boy (aged 14 or 15); boot-cleaner and tap-polisher in an hotel (aged 14 or 15); clerk in a commercial office (aged 15-19); employed in an advertising agency and as a theatre utility man; assistant to second-hand bookseller; spent 7 years in the office of a literary agency; received commissions which enabled him to devote himself to literary work.
affiliations_raw: He ‘awoke from within’ when he discovered Literature; sold his first story when he was 16; published many works, including Nights in Town (1915); The Sun in Splendour (1926); Murder at Elstree (1936).
content_tone: A highly readable and useful volume which commences with a fine and detailed account of daily life and activities during his childhood years spent in the Poplar district of London, with references to Chinese immigrants and shopkeepers; diet; public houses; the activities of middle-class philanthropists (whom he dismisses with contempt); Epsom races; music halls. This is followed by an equally good description of the years spent in an orphanage, including comments on street gangs, homosexuality and sexual discovery. Burke then discusses his work life, expressing a strong dislike for office work, a feeling compounded by related experiences of poverty, apathy and depression. An enjoyable narrative that contains extensive dialogue.
title: 109a BURKE, Thomas, The Wind and the Rain: A Book of Confessions(Thornton Butterworth Limited, London, 1924), pp.288. [A limited edition of 110 copies.]

father_raw: Son of a publican.
residences: Barnsley (1819-46); York (1846-7); Staindrop, Co
career_raw: Employed in the hand-loom weaving industry for several years after leaving school; in later life worked as a teacher at the Oddfellows Sunday School (c.1838); teacher (1844-5); headmaster (1857-68); grocer (1868-76); school warden (1876-). Also contributed many articles to local newspapers and was employed as the local (Barnsley) correspondent.
affiliations_raw: Active in promoting the advancement of education; founder-member of a Mutual Instruction Society and of the Franklin Club for the Advancement of Mutual and Self- Instruction; a Radical and Chartist, active in local meetings and demonstrations; sometimes chairman and member of general committee of Northern Political Union; member of its Committee of Public safety; spent most of his leisure writing poems and articles of local interest, becoming well-known in the Barnsley area as a thorough annalist of the locality. His Annals of Barnsley was first published in the Barnsley Chronicle in 1873, and continued for many years (4 manuscript volumes, 1844-1864, are located in the Local History Library, Barnsley). Also published various books of poems and pamphlets.
content_tone: Written in the third person this short autobiography offers only a brief outline of the author’s life, with very little comment on his early years except for a short reference to the harsh treatment received while at school. Fuller information on his personal experiences and on Barnsley life can be obtained from his Annals of Barnsley.
title: John Hugh Burland. By Himself [reproduced from the original manuscript],

father_raw: Illegitimate son of itinerant beggars.
career_raw: Variously employed in his youth, including bobbin-winder, beggar, hawker, agricultural labourer (from an early age to c.1822), apprentice felt-hat maker (1822-29). Set up business on own account, on more than one occasion, but was unsuccessful (c.1835-6?). Subsequently worked as a publican (1836-9); commercial traveller; warehouseman; salesman; book deliverer; compiler of commercial directories; collector of subscriptions for commercial magazine (c.1853); debt collector of subscriptions for the Ladies Journal; manager of office; hatter (c.1864-5); journalist on Hexham Courant; clerk (to 1871); inspector of stores for Great Eastern Railway Company (1871-81).
affiliations_raw: Active in the radical and trade union movement of the 1830s; member and delegate of Hatters’ Union; member of Glasgow Trades Committee and the Glasgow Reform Committee; Chartist; fell out of sympathy with radical movement, breaking from Chartists following the call, in 1839, for a general strike; played leading role in establishment of Oddfellow movement in S.W. Scotland, and was eventually elected to Board of Guardians (1846), but resigned after one year (financial reasons?). Author of various works, including An Historical Sketch of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester, 1845); The Language of the Walls (Manchester, 1855); Commercial Enterprise and Social Progress (1858).
content_tone: An immensely entertaining account of the life of a beggar and hawker, reform politics, the decline of the felt-hat making trade and of social change by an aspirant to, and firm admirer of, middle-class respectability. Describing an early life of poverty, sorrow, privations and vagrancy, Burns provides a fascinating insight into the subculture of travelling. From the age of 19 he attempted to climb above these initial difficulties, but with fluctuating success. The narrative also contains very good observations on the reform agitation of the 1830s, despite the author’s dismissive treatment of the movement and his own participation in it. The first four editions (published anonymously) were written in the form of letters to his son, combining middle-class language and literary style with Border and Clydeside dialect and thieves’ cant. The revised edition (1882) was rewritten in retirement and contains numerous small changes to content and style, with an account of his later life and a general review of social change in his lifetime. An invaluable document covering many aspects of economic, social and labour history.
title: The Autobiography of a Beggar Boy; in which will be found related the numerous trials, hard struggles, and vicissitudes of a strangely chequered life; with glimpses of social and political history over a period of fifty years

residences: Murton Row (1837-c
career_raw: Commenced work as a pit-lad (aged 10); employed at various tasks underground (trapper; donkey and pony-driver; pony-putting; water-leader), until he became a coal-hewer (aged 17). Left the pit in 1865 to become full-time secretary and agent of the Northumberland Miners’ Mutual Confident Association (to 1913); MP (Lib and Lab) for Morpeth (1874- 1918).
affiliations_raw: Primitive Methodist Sunday School teacher; walking; cycling; active in establishing educational facilities in mining villages; teetotaller; president of the TUC (1891); attended International Miners’ Conferences; Privy Councillor (1906); Parliamentary Secretary to Board of Trade (1892-5); member of Reform Club, National Liberal Club, Eighty Club. Published articles in Nineteenth Century; Contemporary Review; Fortnightly Review.
content_tone: An excellent account of a childhood spent in mining communities in Northumberland and Durham, with particularly good descriptions of all aspects of pit-life and work, from his time as a trapper and hewer to explosions and disasters, disputes and industrial actions (notably the strike of 1844 and the dispute over ‘the separation system’, 1859) and the beginnings of trade unionsm (1862). Following his election as secretary to the Miners’ Union (1865) the narrative focusses inevitably on the activities and history ofthe Union and the duties of the secretary. The autobiography ends just after Burt’s election to Parliament (in 1874) but is followed by supplementary chapters dealing with his later life, by Aaron Watson. An invaluable source for any study of mining history and trade union politics.
title: MP, DCL, Pitman and Privy Councillor. An Autobiography, with supplementary chapters by Aaron Watson, author of ‘A Great Labour Leader’, etc., and a foreword by Wilfrid Burt

father_raw: Only son and edlest of five children of a tenant farmer.
residences: Scotland for most of his life, but also spent many years in Bradford and a short time in South Africa
career_raw: Assisted on father’s farm; jack-of-all-trades (aged 15-20); schoolteacher (1848-60); editor of Bradford Observer (from 1860) and for over 26 years of the Northern Chronicle, Inverness.
affiliations_raw: Regular contributor to local newspapers of local history articles and antiquarian notes; Inspector of the Poor.
content_tone: A lengthy narrative which combines personal details with general observations on a wide variety of subjects, from local history and religious controversy to working-class life and conditions and national politics. Campbell provides very good accounts of his time in the Highlands and in Bradford and among the many themes discussed are childhood recollections; rural superstitions; gypsies and tinkers; travellers as news-carriers; education and the Church of Scotland; tenant farming and crofting; social life and morals; patriotism and politics; poaching; emigration; struggles for education; journalistic life and work; Socialism; industrialisation and change.
title: Reminiscences and Reflections of an Octogenarian Highlander

father_raw: Son of a general labourer.
residences: Leicester and London
career_raw: From age 10-14 he sold newspapers after school, and then was employed in various jobs including errand-boy, delivery-boy, machine operative, doctor’s receptionist, seam-presser and in other factory labour. Apprenticed to be a wood-cutting machinist, but left job to go to London to become a journalist.
affiliations_raw: Flirted briefly with religion and socialism. Published other works including three further autobiographical volumes, Towards the Mountains (1943); Reaching High Heaven ([1944]); Only the Stars Remain (1946).
content_tone: Born into poverty, Campion soon climbed above his origins by a mixture of self-help, ambition and confidence. The bulk of the narrative falls in the 20th century, though with brief opening comments about his childhood. Written in a racy and exaggerated literary style, intended to entertain and amuse, with frequent use of anecdote and dialogue. A rather insubstantial piece.
title: Sunlight on the Foothills

residences: Manchester, but his work as a journalist demanded extensive travelling at home and abroad
career_raw: Earned first money at age 10 as a pavement artist, and then occupied in various odd-jobs after leaving school before becoming a clerk in a marine insurance company (1904-12); assistant cricket coach at Shrewsbury School (1912); secretary to Cyril Alington, headmaster at Shrewsbury School (to 1916); casual labourer (1916); ‘penny-a-line’ writer for the Daily Citizen (1916); agent for Burial Society (1916); unpaid secretary to C. P. Scott (1916); reporter on the Manchester Guardian (1917), eventually becoming its music and dramatic critic and cricket correspondent.
affiliations_raw: Joined the Independent Labour Party when a young man but soon became disillusioned with socialist politics. Published large number of articles and books on cricket and music. See also his volume of autobiographical reminiscences, Second Innings (1950).
content_tone: The narrative begins with a description of home life in a Manchester slum in the 1890s, but soon moves on to describe the author’s growing interest and involvement in books, music, theatre and cricket, and remains with these topics for the remainder of the text.
title: Autobiography

father_raw: Ist child of a gardener.
career_raw: Forced to start work at age 11 owing to decline in father’s business, commencing in the offices of the Cambridge Chronicle; reading-boy; apprentice compositor (5 years) on Lloyd’s Weekly Newspaper, remaining with the same paper all his working life, rising from compositor to sub-editor and, eventually, editor. Retired, 1907.
affiliations_raw: Member of London Society of Compositors; member of the Scribblers Club; contributor to the Morning Post; Liberal; Freemason.
content_tone: Personal detail combines freely with journalistic notes on matters of local, national and international significance, resulting in a lengthy work that extends beyond autobiography to become a history of the British Press, journalism, Fleet Street and, more specifically, of Lloyd’s Newspaper. Catling recalls in fine detail his childhood years, telling of tinder boxes, theatre, schooling, public executions, elections, agricultural mechanisation, recreation and sports. Major events discussed include elections; Hyde Park disturbances (1855 and 1866); Fenian ‘outrages’ in Clerkenwell (1867); news of Royalty; Home Rule Bill; the ‘Ripper’ atrocities. However, the volume is perhaps most interesting for its account of work life, charting the author’s rise from a humble position on a provincial newspaper to editor of an influential London journal. Detail of workshop customs and duties is provided alongside mention of technical developments. The illustrations include cartoons.
title: My Life’s Pilgrimage, with an introduction by the Rt. Hon. Lord Burnham

career_raw: Cowherd (c.1800); engaged at a timber carter’s (1801-3); ploughboy (1804-11?); employed in chemical works (to 1820), but forced to leave through ill-health; took a general shop at Plaistow (1820-56).
affiliations_raw: Regular attender at the ‘peculiar’ Baptist church before joining the Society of Friends; helped to form a Bible Society at West Ham; correspondent to local newspapers, publishing a series of articles on West Ham in the early 19th century in the Stratford Times, attributed to ‘Old Inhabitant’; superintendent of allotments in Plaistow (for 8 or 9 years); founder-member of the Temperance, or Moderation Society, and later of the Plaistow Total Abstinence Society.
content_tone: An outline of the author’s life, with comments on smuggling and escapes from death, but concerned mostly with religious matters. The narrative commences in the third person but soon changes to the usual first person format.
title: A Short Sketch of A Long Life of Samuel Catton once a Suffolk Plough-boy, showing what prayer and perserverance may do(Rees and Gripper, Ipswich; Arpthorpe, London; Caudwell, London, [1863]), pp.24 + 3pp. extracts, Ip. index. Price: 3d. 4th edn., Harpthorpe [sic.], London; Caudwell, London; [1865].

residences: London
career_raw: Apprenticed to a bootmaker (1833); journeyman before 21, but unsuccessful due to ill-health; enlisted in 77th Foot Regiment (1855), but discharged in 1856 due to ill-health. Not stated what he does after this.
affiliations_raw: An active exponent of atheistic and radical causes. Spoke widely on atheism. Participant in Chartist struggles at Clerkenwell, and the Hyde Park Riots. Member of Council of Land and Labour League and the London section of the Birmingham Education League (1870). In 1884 he began publishing Chatterton’s Commune. The atheistic communistic scorcher (1884-95). Author of several ‘atheistical and revolutionary’ pamphlets.
content_tone: A short but interesting account of involvement in reform agitation from 1848 on, in public demonstrations and organising meetings. Written in the third person, with deliberate disregard for the conventions of grammar and punctuation.
title: Daniel), Biography of Dan Chatterton. Atheist and Communist. By CHAT

father_raw: Son of a postman and a schoolteacher.
career_raw: Civil servant (1909-33); editor for publishing company (1933-51); lecturer for the British Council throughout Europe, India and Africa; poet, novelist and literary critic.
affiliations_raw: Fellow of Royal Society of Literature and of Royal Society of Art; president of the English Association; member of the Society of Authors; member of the Society of Bookmen; president of P.E.N. (1958-9); published extensively, including Hurricane (1919); Some Modern British Authors (1943); Small Moments (1956).
content_tone: A full account of the author’s childhood and teenage years with anecdotes of his youth and observations on schooling, home life, family relations and early work life.
title: Over the Bridge. An Essay in Autobiography

career_raw: Employed in casual jobs on leaving school before settling for a longer period in a flour-mill; apprenticed with a firm of electrical contractors; electrical engineer (to 1914); elected the first full-time district secretary of the Electrical Trades Union in 1914; assistant general secretary of the ETU (1920-4); assistant general secretary of the TUC (1924-6), and general secretary (1926-46); member of National Coal Board (1946-7); chairman of the British Electrical Authority (1947-57).
affiliations_raw: Member of Oakdale Mission Band; member of the Independent Labour Party; joined Liverpool branch of Electrical Trades Union in 1911; president of International Federation of Trade Unions (1928-45); director of the Daily Herald(1929-46); trustee of Imperial Relations Trust (1937-49), member of Cinematograph Films Council (1938-48); vice-president of the National Safety First Association; member of Economic Advisory Council (1930-3); member of Royal Commission on the West Indies (1938-9); member of Consultative Council for the Treasury (1940-6); chairman of Committee of Regional Boards, Munitions Production (1942); president of the World Federation of Trade Unions (1945-6); chairman of Miners’ Welfare Committee (1946-7); part-time member of the Electricity Council (1947-57); part-time member of the Atomic Energy Authority (1958-62); created KBE (1935) and CBE (1958); appointed to the Privy Council in 1940, and raised to peerage in 1946. His many publications include Labour and the Community (1928); I Search for truth in Russia (1936); My Finnish Diary (1940); ABC of Chairmanship (1948).
content_tone: The narrative commences with recollections of a childhood spent on the Mersey (home life, schooling and early work life) but soon moves on to detail his early trade union activities and struggles and his eventual long period of service as a full-time trade union official. Citrine offers a most valuable document of 20th century Labour organisation and struggles, with useful and often very lengthy accounts of significant events. Among the subjects discussed are wartime ’unoflicial’ strikes; visit to the Soviet Union; the General Strike; the Labour governments in the inter-war period; international politics and the rise of fascism and Nazism. The volume ends with the approach of World War II. Much of the text was compiled from notes written by Citrine when the events described took place.
title: Men and Work. An Autobiography(Hutchinson, London, 1964), pp.375 + 8pp. index. Illustrated.

forename: (Charles) Allen [published under the pseudonym of ‘Ben Adhem’
father_raw: Eldest of 9 children of two textile workers.
residences: Bolton (1863-2); Mirfield, Yorks
career_raw: Half-timer in a cotton mill (1876); errand-boy (1876); piecer (1876); pupil-teacher/teacher (1877-84); employed by Bolton Evening News, compiling Post Office Directory (1884-90); produced his own papers, the Labour Light (1890), and the Bolton Trader (1891); employed by the Catton Factory Times (1892-6); editor of the Blackpool Echo (1896-1900), and founder of Teddy Ashton’s Journal (1896-1908); editor of the Northern Weekly (1900-6); kept a small shop in Blackpool (1906-?).
affiliations_raw: Member of Social Democratic Federation and later of the Independent Labour Party; unsuccessful parliamentary candidate for Rochdale (1900); member of Blackpool Cycling Club, the Clarion Cycle Fellowship and the Lancashire Author’s Association; spiritualist; active in the Labour Church; wrote and published extensively on social and political themes from a socialist perspective and on Lancashire places, people, folklore and dialect. His first novel, The Knobstick (1893), took the Bolton engineers’ strike of 1887 as the theme; other publications include Effects of the Factory System (1899), which provides a fulland valuable account of life and conditions in the cotton industry.
content_tone: A long series of articles in which the autobiographical element becomes increasingly replaced by general reflections and comments on various issues and events, including opposition to war; sex equality; capital punishment; fascism. The earlier articles are particularly interesting for their full and graphic portrayal of life in a Lancashire manufacturing district in the second half of the 19th century. Among the topics discussed are childhood; diet; dress and ‘breeching’; disease and death; schooling; adolescent sex; leisure (childhood games; Easter celebrations; children’s comics; theatre); ‘Little Ireland’; the cotton industry and the half-time system; transport developments; courtship; unemployment; female labour and ‘pit-brow’ lasses; and much detail on personal and domestic affairs.
title: Autobiographical articles, Liverpool Weekly Post, 24 Feb-29 Dec 1934, 5 Jan-14 Dec 1935.

father_raw: Son of a grocer (James Coombs Griffiths).
career_raw: Worked on father’s farm (aged 14-18); then began 42 years underground, first as a miner’s helper, then a collier and for 15 years as an ambulance man.
affiliations_raw: Without strong political or trade union commitment, but served on several pit committees; on management committee of Miners’ Rest Home in Porthcawl; founder-member of St. John’s Ambulance Brigade in Resolven; secretary and playing member of Resolven Orchestra; member of Society of Authors; published numerous articles in various journals; wrote scripts of several documentary films; regular radio broadcaster; writing career began in 1934 and had won several literary prizes by 1939. For excellent accounts of pit life, work and conditions see, from among his many publications, Miners’ Day (1945) and Those Clouded Hills (1944).
content_tone: A deservedly well-known and highly-praised account of mines and mining in South Wales, including comments on accidents; dress; methods of payment; face-working; trade unionism and victimisation; the introduction of mechanical coal-cutters; the lock-out of 1921; the General Strike. The text begins with brief detail of the author’s agricultural background before he moved to South Wales at the age of 18, and also includes comments on home and married life.
title: These Poor Hands. The Autobiography of a Miner Working in South Wales

residences: or near Manchester (1819-40); Hull (1841); Newcastle upon Tyne; Sunderland; Glasgow (1842); Edinburgh; Dundee; Derby (1843-?); Stockport; Edinburgh; Huddersfield; London (1846-58); Manchester (1858-68)
career_raw: Clerk in office of Manchester house (1831-40); teacher at Co-operative Schools and secular schools (1833-40); ‘Social Missionary’ lecturer (1840-6); part-time lecturer and clerk (1846-54); editor of London Investigator (1854-7); had own accountant’s office in Manchester (?-1866); supported by sons in later life.
affiliations_raw: Honorary secretary of secular school (1833); regularly attended the socialist ‘Social Institution’; member of Manchester Athenaeum; lectured and published on political subjects; member of the London Literary Institution; honorary secretary of the Owen Memorial Committee; member of the executive committee of the Union and Emancipation Society and of the National Reform Union; president of Manchester Working Men’s Parliamentary Reform Association; founder of Social Reform League.
content_tone: A close friend of Robert Owen, Cooper provides a compelling account of 19th century radical politics, describing his lecturing, debating and publishing on the platform of social reform.
title: ‘An Autobiographical Sketch’, The National Reformer, Vol.xi, No.423

father_raw: Father (a dyer) died when author aged 4 years.
residences: Leicester; Exeter; Gainsborough (1809-33); Lincoln (1833-9); London (1839-40); Leicester (1840-3); Stafford gaol (1843-5); London (1845-6)
career_raw: Employed (not apprenticed) by various master shoemakers (1820-3); worked at shoemaking from home (1823-7); opened own school (1828); schoolmaster (1833-6); journalist and contributor to various periodicals from c.1834 on; edited and published various newspapers, including The Midland Counties Illuminator, The Chartist Rushlight, Cooper's Journal and copyist (1856-8); itinerant preacher (1858-72).
affiliations_raw: Childhood activities included drawing, playing the dulcimer, singing in the church choir, collecting flowers and walking. Cooper’s three other main interests were religion, politics and self-education. During his life he joined the Primitive Methodists (1819), the Wesleyan Methodists (c.1820), ‘Straussianism’ (1848) and the Baptists (1859). In between his bouts of religiosity Cooper became actively involved in the mid-century radical agitation and was converted to Chartism by the plight of the Leicester stockingers. He soon became one of the leaders of the Leicester Chartists and was delegate to various national conventions. He was imprisoned for 2 years (1843-5) on a charge of sedition and conspiracy. His political activity decreased after his release, though he did assist in the formation of the People’s International League (1847) and was president of the People’s Charter Union (1848). His adherence to the principles of self-education and self-help led him to form a Mutual Improvement Society and an Adult Sunday School at Gainsborough (1822), but both were short-lived. Was a member of the Lincoln Mechanics’ Institute and secretary of the Choral Society. Published widely on politics, morality, literature, fundamentalist theology. See also Thoughts at Fourscore, and earlier. A Medley (1885), which comprises a commentary on changes in manners and morals noticed during Cooper’s own lifetime.
content_tone: Cooper was set firmly in the mould of the Victorian, self-educated working man, and much of the autobiography is concerned with describing his pursuit of knowledge and his involvement with Christianity. However, coming between these two passions, Cooper also became an active Chartist and the middle chapters of this volume provide a detailed and fascinating account of the radical struggles around mid-century Leicester. His accounts of the clashes between the colliers and the military in the Staffordshire Potteries (1842) and of the Manchester and Birmingham (or Sturge) conventions are especially valuable. Following his release from prison Cooper ‘kept aloof’ from Chartists and Chartism and his memoirs become dominated by a description of his literary career and acquaintances. A well-known classic.
title: The Life of Thomas Cooper. Written by Himself

father_raw: Eldest of 4 children of a journeyman tailor.
residences: Folkestone (1878-83); Brighton (1883-8); London (1888-91); Brighton (1891-1907); Oxford and adjacent villages (1907-19); Shepherd’s Pit, Headington (1919-22)
career_raw: Assistant to paraffin and firewood seller (1887); errand-boy in tailor’s shop (1888-90); messenger-boy for Reuter’s Telegraph Agency (1891); office-boy to an auctioneer (1901); junior clerk to a butter and cheese merchant; clerk with the Sunlight Soap Company (?- 1897); clerk to a carriers company (1897-9); departmental clerk and cashier with engineering firm (1899-1907); confidential clerk at the Eagle Ironworks (1907-19); professional writer (1919-).
affiliations_raw: Football-supporter; enthusiastic athlete; youthful years were spent ‘running, reading, falling in love and trying to write verse’; spent one term on the rural council; author of many works, including Ugly Anna, and other tales (1944); Ring the Bells of Heaven (1933); Dunky Fitlow (1933).
content_tone: A detailed and finely-remembered work, with a graphic portrayal of the author’s poor childhood. Other themes and topics include dress; schooling; extended family details; prostitution; Oxford social life; writing career. The narrative ends in the early 1920s.
title: It’s Me, O Lord! An Abstract and Brief Chronicle of Some of the Life with Some of the Opinions of A. E. Coppard. Written by Himself

residences: Little Whitefield (1821-4); Wolfhill (1824-37); Collace (1837-41); Banchory (1841-3); Wolfhill (1843-4); Paisley 1844-6); Elgin (1847-50); Perth (1850-2); Blairgowrie (1852-3); Glasgow (1853-4); Dundee (1854-5); Edinburgh (1855-6); Leicester (1856-7); Paisley (1857); Glasgow (1858-67); Edinburgh (1867-80); Perth (1886-)
career_raw: Left school (c.1834) to assist mother at home; apprentice millwright (1837-41); journeyman millwright (1841-3); house-joiner (1844-6); tea salesman (1846-7); opened tea shop with borrowed capital (1847-52); ran a temperance hotel (1852-3); insurance agent (1853-8); employed on the staff of the Commonwealth (1858-9); curator of Anderson’s College and Museum (1859-67); joined the Geological Survey unit of the Civil Service (1867-80). Was earning $350 p.a. when forced to retire through disability.
affiliations_raw: Became interested in physical science at early age and read widely on the subject; studied philosophy and theology in spare time; published The Philosophy of Theism (1857), to be followed by numerous papers and works on scientific theory, geology and philosophy (a full list appears in the volume). Received honorary degree of LL.D. from St. Andrews University (1876); elected Fellow of the Royal Society of London (1876) and was a member of various scientific and learned societies.
content_tone: A ‘classic’ account of a struggle through childhood poverty and illness to become a respected geologist. The autobiography sketches the author’s rise with only brief details of the various stages in his life.
title: ‘Autobiographical Sketch’, in Autobiographical Sketch of James Croll, LL.D., F.R.S., Etc., with Memoir of his Life and Work, by James Campbell Irons, M.A.

father_raw: Father a guillotine cutter in printing trade.
residences: London (1894- 1959); Brighton (1959-81)
career_raw: Worked for short time in printing trade on leaving school, before taking employment as a semi-skilled improver; served in the London Rifle Brigade during World War I; returned to the printing trade after the war as a guillotine cutter, and then a department overseer, staying with one firm for 40 years.
affiliations_raw: Member of Independent Labour Party, being included on the speaker’s panel by age 16; taught occasionally at an Anarchists’ Sunday School in Stepney; contributed articles to the anarchist Torch and Freedom; helped to form the Daily Herald League, becoming secretary of the Central London branch; active in Fabian Society and Labour Party; member of executive committee of South Place Ethical Society; member of Linguists’ Club; London Football Association referee; wrote material for entertaining artistes and had some of his songs published.
content_tone: Descriptions of early life in a poor district of London; schooling; street entertainers and the Suffragette movement precede a lengthy section on his experiences in World War I.
title: The Landlord Cometh

father_raw: 4th child of a colliery worker.
residences: Pontycymmer (1889-97); Clydach-on-Tawe (1897-c
career_raw: Errand-boy to a grocer (c.1899); colliery worker as ‘door-boy’, labourer, repairer’s assistant and coal-hewer (1902-12); stoker on merchant tramp steamer (1910); student minister (1906); ordained a minister (1919); minister (to 1928); wrote and published articles on politics, economics and philosophy (1929); employed addressing envelopes (c.1929); freelance lecturer; editor of New Britain Quarterly (1932-8); returned to the ministry (1939), and ordained a deacon (1941).
affiliations_raw: His two main interests and activities were religion and politics. He was converted to Nonconformity during the Welsh Revival, and to Unitarianism (1905). He wrote various books and published magazines on theological issues. Politically a socialist, the author was active in the South Wales Miners’ Federation (member of Lodge executive) and was an active public speaker. Member of Independent Labour Party and the Socialist League. Fought in Spanish Civil War. A socialist town councillor (1926-8).
content_tone: Brought up in an intensely religious family, the narrative describes a poor childhood that witnessed the decline of religion and chapel life and the rise of social reform and Labour politics. The author adopted religion and developed a high level of political consciousness at an early age, and the volume provides a very good account of early 20th century life, labour, politics and religion in S.Wales and of inter-war politics and socialism.
title: In Search of Myself. The Autobiography of D.R. Davies(Geoffrey Bles, London, 1961), pp.216 + 7pp. index.

father_raw: Did not know father, but he was believed to be a moulder.
career_raw: Started work as assistant to an ironmonger; apprentice picture-framer (to age 20); tramp; hawker of small wares.
affiliations_raw: Poet and author of many works.
content_tone: The narrative mostly describes his tramping adventures in America, Canada and England, with comments on common lodging-houses, Salvation Army hostels, and wayfaring life generally. A well-known classic.
title: The Autobiography of a Super-tramp, with a preface by G. Bernard Shaw

career_raw: Errand-boy; employed at a milliner’s; in service at a firm of leading Manchester merchants (for 42 years); held public recitations; actor; vocalist.
affiliations_raw: Contributed articles to local journals.
content_tone: A brief autobiographical sketch prefaces an account, written in Lancashire dialect, of experiences, adventures and travels.
title: Autobiographical preface in The Rambles and Recollections of ‘R’ Dick’

career_raw: Apprentice engineer (1881); unemployed in early 1890s but active in organising relief funds and soup kitchens; full-time president and general organiser of Workers’ Union (1898- 1900); general secretary of WU (1900-29); secretary of WU group within Transport and General Workers’ Union (from 1929). MP for Barrow-in-Furness (1906-18), and for Clay Cross (1922-33).
affiliations_raw: Joined Amalgamated Society of Engineers (c.1888), acting as the district secretary; member of Independent Labour Party; member of Middlesbrough Town Council (1895-1900) and Board of Guardians; member of executive committee of National Democratic League; on executive committee of Labour Party (1920-2); served on Labour Supply Committee, Munitions Advisory Committee and National Industrial Council during World War I; president of Willesden Co-operative Society; JP (1919). Contributed articles to the Record.
content_tone: A brief account of his early life.
title: ‘How I Got On’, Pearson’s Weekly, 15 Feb 1906.

father_raw: One of 3 children of a station master.
residences: Derby; Burton-on-Trent; Swadlincote
career_raw: Ever since leaving school his occupation had been selling newspapers; also, junior reporter to 3 provincial newspapers.
affiliations_raw: Formed stamp-collectors’ society; contributed articles to various philatelic journals and editor of a philatelic periodical; Fellow of Royal Philatelic Society of London (1909); amateur photographer and chemist; Fellow of Chemical Society of London (1909).
content_tone: Edwards describes a happy childhood, with comments on ‘breeching’ and schooling. Rather than providing a full life history the narrative deals with such subjects as cycling, politics, love affairs, spiritualism and religion.
title: Paper Sir? The autobiography of an old news boy

father_raw: One of 4 children of a carpenter by trade, who also kept a public-house and farmed a fruit garden.
residences: Blackwater (1823-c
career_raw: Assisted father in brewing and gardening (1835-c.1842); under-clerk to a lawyer (18 months); agent for the Sentinel (15 months); began over fifty years connection with newspapers and magazines, first as a journalist and then as proprietor of various journals, including The Public Good (from 1850); Building News (from 1862); Mechanics’ Magazine (from 1869); the Echo (from 1876). MP for Salisbury (1880-5).
affiliations_raw: Attended literary society meetings at an early age; helped to run a free evening and Sunday morning school (aged 17); Anti-Corn Law propagandist and lecturer; member of Mechanics’ Institute; adherent of the Manchester School; ‘moral force’ Chartist; active in the promotion and formation of various political and social organisations, including the Political and Financial Reform Association, the Society for the Abolition of the Taxes on Knowledge, the Committee for the Abolition of Flogging in the Army and Navy, and committees for the Promotion of National Education; delegate to International Peace Congresses (1848-50); president of Anti-Gambling League; president of London Reform Union (1894); president of Transvaal Independence Committee (1881) and the Transvaal Committee (1901); later years were devoted to philanthropy, providing many gifts to free libraries and hospitals. Pamphlet publications include The War a Blunder and a Crime [1855]; The Triple Curse: or, the Evils of the Opium Trade on India, China, and England [1858].
content_tone: A full chronicle of the author’s active and varied life, with comments on schooling; religious life; the pursuit of knowledge; Anti-Corn Law agitation; the Peace movement; Chartism; parliamentary life; philanthropy.
title: A Few Footprints

father_raw: Son of a stonemason.
residences: London
career_raw: Errand-boy in a newspaper office (1899), becoming editor’s secretary and then a journalist; career interrupted by military service (1914-19); resumed former job on discharge but from 1920 started as an independent and freelance writer publishing short stories, articles and sketches under various pseudonyms.
affiliations_raw: No details of interests other than his love of the countryside.
