content_tone: The narrative begins with childhood recollections and memories of a home life spent in tenement dwellings and jerry-built housing. Comments are made on domestic economy, chooling, books, visits to the country, but the greater part of the volume is devoted to anecdotes and incidents which occured during his time as a journalist.
title: I Love the Brooks

father_raw: Son of a battery sergeant-major in the Royal Artillery.
residences: St
career_raw: First employment was in a rope and twine factory; apprenticed to printing firm in Colchester for 6 years (c.1900-6); journeyman compositor (1906-). Engaged in odd-jobs after the war before becoming an assistant reader, and eventually a reader for the Law Times, and then for the Financial Times (1928-40).
affiliations_raw: Active trade unionist, being a member of the Typographical Association (for 44 years), the London Society of Compositors (for 32 years) and of the Association of Correctors of the Press (for 31 years).
content_tone: Written in 1951, the narrative deals only with the author’s working life, but nevertheless provides a good account of the printing trade in the early 20th century. Among the subjects touched on are seasonal and temporary work; ‘tramping’; and the strike in Newport, Monmouthshire (1911) over the employment of a female monotype-operator. There is also an interesting description of his labours in a rope and twine factory.
title: ‘My Life In and Out of Print.

father_raw: One of 5(?) children of a hand-loom weaver.
career_raw: Was put to the bobbin-wheel at age 8, and to the loom before age 10; then employed at calico print works (1833) and a ‘beetling’ works (1834?); ‘on the tramp'; teacher at evening school (1842) and at a township school at Blackwell, Carlisle (1842-5); warper (1845-6); outside clerk and timekeeper on railway construction work (1846-7); commercial traveller, or ‘bagman’ (1847); ‘putter out’ to gingham weavers at Blackburn, and warper in same works (c.1847-8); clerk and timekeeper (1848); clerk and superintendent on railway construction work (1850-3); agent for Temperance and General Provident Institution (1853-4); editor of (radical) Cheshire Observer (1854); agent for a large N.Wales colliery company (1856-7); arranged with company for business to be transferred to self (1857), and henceforward the coal trade formed the staple of his commercial life.
affiliations_raw: Signed the pledge (1840) and became very active in the temperance movement as a lecturer, officiating in various committees, and running a temperance hotel with his wife; member of Working Men’s Reading Rooms and of Mechanics’ Institute; founder-member and secretary Improvement Society; ‘moral force’ Chartist; contributor to local publications; active in local politics, as member of Board of Guardians (1858); first elected to city council in 1860; sheriff and mayor of Chester; JP (1881).
content_tone: Farish describes in fine detail the hardships and poverty of his childhood and the ‘waywardness’ of his life until signing the pledge in 1840 (family history; cholera; dressing children at Easter; gambling; drink). This is followed by an excellent account of the decline of hand-loom weaving, of ‘tramping’, and of the author’s and the weavers’ involvement in radical politics (election disturbances; rick-burning; celebrations to mark the passing of Reform Bill; trade depression, 1837; public meetings, 1838; common lodging-houses). The remainder of the narrative is concerned mostly with his endeavours for the temperance cause and with his involvement in local politics. An extremely worthy and useful volume.
title: The Autobiography of William Farish. The Struggles of a Hand Loom Weaver. With Some of his Writings

father_raw: Daughter of a postmaster.
residences: Farningham; Bristol (1 year); Gravesend (1857); Northampton (1859-c
career_raw: Teaching assistant (1852); Sunday School teacher; teacher (1857); headmistress (1859); contributor to religious journals; poet; author.
affiliations_raw: The author was awakened to religion at an early age and her life was guided by religious zeal and missionary endeavours. Was accepted into the Baptist Church when only 14 and from then her social life remained centred on the chapel. Sat for 6 years on the Northampton School Board (?1885-91); lectured on religious subjects; editor of Sunday School Times (1889-1906); author of many works under pen-name of Farningham, including Girlhood (1869), Harvest Gleanings (1903), and Women and Their Work (1906).
content_tone: Farningham’s happy childhood is presented in an affectionate and almost romanticmanner, though her commitment to the Baptist faith from the age of 14 dominates the remainder of her writing. Factors external to her religion and self are rarely mentioned, except for a brief comment on the strike and lock-out of the Northampton shoemakers.
title: A Working Woman’s Life. An Autobiography

father_raw: Son of a skilled mechanic.
residences: London (to 1919); Oxford (1919-c
career_raw: Factory labourer in works manufacturing motor-cycle engines, parts for lorries and armaments (from age 14 to 1916). In later life made a living from journalism and freelance writing.
affiliations_raw: Member of the British Socialist Party, and was an active propagandist and speaker for the socialist cause and the rights of trade unionists; member of Oxford University Labour Club; served on editorial committee of The New Oxford; contributed sketches, stories and articles to socialist, labour and co-operative journals; imprisoned (1916-19) as a conscientious objector; published several books, including Factory Echoes, and other sketches [1919]; Green Banners. The Story of the Irish Struggle (1938); The History of the Irish Citizen Army (1943); Rebel Irishwomen (1935), and Jim Larkin: the rise of the underman (1957).
content_tone: The narrative begins with the author leaving elementary school at the age of 14 and ends in the mid 1920s. Although rather literary, with much use of dialogue, Fox provides a graphic description of factory life and labour, a highly useful account of socialist politics and of political activity in the pre-war years (strike wave, 1911-13; suffragettes; anti-militarism; Dublin lock-out, 1913; International Workers of the World; dilution; the Shop Stewards’ Movement). Other topics covered include his period of imprisonment, and his visits to the Soviet Union and Ireland.
title: Smoky Crusade

father_raw: 3rd child of 9 of a printer and teetotaller.
residences: Hackney (1848-52); Rochford (1852-65); London (1865-c
career_raw: Left school to assist in printing business managed by father (1861-5); worked in various print shops in London until he was ‘stood off’ when trade was slack; returned to work with father, before accepting offer of a share in the business (1871); opened an office in Southend in 1872.
affiliations_raw: Sunday School teacher and superintendent; secretary of Rochford Literary Institute; member of Cliff Town Congregational Church; church deacon (for 2 years); member of Good Templar Lodge; superintendent of Band of Hope.
content_tone: The narrative commences with details of his family and of a happy childhood. Although much attention is devoted to his religious and temperance activities, Francis also makes some interesting observations on schooling; childhood games; dress; street hawkers; search for employment; Reform demonstrations of 1867 (Hyde Park); work and conditions of employment in print shops; holidays; body-snatching; business life.
title: Reminiscences,

father_raw: Son of a tailor.
residences: Croydon, Norwood and London for much of his life, moving to Sheffield, Liverpool and Barnsley in later life
career_raw: Apprentice in printing office of a cousin on leaving school, but moved to London to work as a ’turn-over’ before apprenticeship completed; started own printing business at age of 22; contributed articles to various periodicals; wrote fiction and serial stories; lecturer; reader and general literary assistant (1853-4); editor, leader-writer and correspondent for various periodicals and provincial newspapers. Journalistic career began when he revived the Communist Chronicle in 1846.
affiliations_raw: Utopian socialist; attempted, unsuccessfully, to organise Co-operative communities; Chartist, serving as a member of the General Council (late 1840s); member of Association of Fraternal Democrats (1847); local office-holder in the National Land Company; member of the radical section of the Reform Association; published extensively. Active, also, in missionary work.
content_tone: Although lacking in personal details this well-known work provides an excellent account of the history ofradicalism and reform agitation throughout the 19th century, and is especially useful for its account of Chartism. Among the topics covered are life in Croydon (1820s- 1830s); electioneering practices; Owenism; Anti-Corn Law League; The 1842 strike movement; the Concordium; popular literature and the spread of knowledge; mission work in Bethnal Green; the Hyde Park demonstrations (1855; 1866-7); provincial journalism and journalists.
title: Forty Years’ Recollections: Literary and Political

career_raw: Worked as a milkboy in the hours before school (1891-3); grocer’s boy (1893-5); employed in a sanitary engineering shop (1895) and in various other factories (1895-1909); ship’s steward of the (1909-10); employed in the Albion Motor Works (1910-12/13; 1914-). Was on the staff Daily Worker for a short period. Elected as the first Communist MP (1935-50), representing West Fife.
affiliations_raw: Joined Temperance Movement as a youth, but only for a short period; joined Paisley branch of Independent Labour Party; founder-member of local branch of Social Democratic Federation; member of British Socialist Party; member of executive committee of United Brassfounders’ Association (later amalgamating to form the Amalgamated Engineering Union); member of Allied Trades Committee; leading figure in the Clydeside Shop Stewards’ Movement, the campaign for the establishment of a Rent Restriction Act and the 1914-18 anti-war campaigns; chairman of the Clyde Workers’ Committee; founder-member of the Communist Party of Great Britain; active in the National Unemployed Workers’ Movement; published several works on Marxism and Communism.
content_tone: An important work by one of the leading figures in the revolutionary struggles of the Clyde workers during World War I, providing a vivid and detailed account of militant activity. Gallacher talks of his family and childhood only when they had some bearing on his development as a working-class agitator. The narrative covers the early years of the SDF, but is most valuable for its portrayal of Clydeside in wartime, with detailed accounts of strikes; jingoism; dilution; his imprisonment; workers’ and soldiers’ councils; the Clyde Workers’ Committee; the Battle of George Square (1919); with profiles of John McLean and John Wheatley.
title: Revolt on the Clyde. An Autobiography

father_raw: 5th of 6 children of a saddler.
residences: and around London for most of his life
career_raw: Errand-boy (1880-2); apprentice engraver (1882-9); journeyman (1889-92); private secretary to Sidney Webb and Beatrice Potter (1892-7); private secretary to Member of Parliament (1897); Labour correspondent for local newspaper (1898); secretary to the London Reform Union (1899-1918); editor of the Municipal Journal (1918-20); secretary of the Fabian Society (1920-39).
affiliations_raw: Member of Communist Club for short period in his early ‘teens’; member of the Socialist League; pioneer of trade unionism in the silver industry; delegate to London Trades Council; volunteer in the London Irish Rifles (1886); joined the Fabian Society in 1890; secretary of Deptford Liberal and Progressive Association; delegate to the International Socialist Congress; election and representation agent; organiser of the movement for railway nationalisation (1905); undertook wide variety of odd-jobs of a political and journalistic nature.
content_tone: Revised in 1944 from earlier drafts, the opening sections provide full details of ancestry, the effects of unemployment and poverty caused by a decline in the saddle-making trade, and of family life. Galton recalls his London childhood, with very good accounts of schooling and childhood games, and some mention of housing and diet. Descriptions of his apprenticeship and work in an engraving shop precede the distinctly political tone of the remainder of this lengthy narrative. Among the topics discussed are the 1880 General Election; the Trafalgar Square Riots of 1886; the dock strike of 1889; Socialism, Fabianism and the Webbs; electioneering experiences; the work of the London Reform Union; LCC politics; war years, 1914-18; Labour Party politics and government in the inter-war years; unemployment and the General Strike.
title: ‘Autobiography’, MS, 14 chapters, paginated separately. Department of Manuscripts, British Library of Political and Economic Science.

father_raw: 3rd of 9 children of a glass-blower.
residences: various houses in Birmingham (1892-1914); London (1919-)
career_raw: Factory worker at a gas meter manufactory (1906-14); commercial traveller (1914); enlisted in the army (1914-19); journalist, on the staff of John Bull and the English Review.
affiliations_raw: Had a passion for reading and studying; interested in contemporary politics, becoming branch secretary of his trade union and a member of the 1917 Club; Sunday School teacher; temperance advocate; author of Labour and the Liquor Traffic [1922]. London;
content_tone: A valuable source for the social historian, with the author providing a full and faithful account of the first 30 years of his life. Excellent descriptions are given of his home and environment; diet; dress; leisure (Nov Sth; picnics; Sunday School outings; gambling; horse- racing); childhood and adolescence; schooling; street life/gangs; traders; rag markets; lodging-houses; attitudes to sex. Periods spent as a factory worker and in active military service are given similarly detailed treatment. Garratt also makes comments on contemporary events and politics.
title: A Man in the Street(J.M. Dent & Sons Ltd., London, 1939), pp.xii,305 + 9pp.index. Illustrated.

residences: Ashburton (1756-69); Brixham (1769); Oxford; London
career_raw: Ship-boy on a coaster (aged 13); apprentice shoemaker (1772-c.1777); lecturer at Exeter College, Oxford; possessed two sinecures as comptroller of the lottery and as paymaster of the band of Gentleman Pensioners; editor of the Quarterly Review; author and translator of Latin and Greek classics, including Juvenal.
affiliations_raw: Poet; author of various works, poetry and translations, including Maeriad (1794); Epistle to Peter Pindar (1800).
content_tone: A tale of self-advancement and influential patronage, with the author rising from humble beginnings to a prosperous and respected position as an author and translator.
title: Memoir of William Gifford. Written by Himself

father_raw: Eldest of 6 children of travelling boot and shoe salesman/commercial traveller.
residences: Leeds (1869-7), Hey (?-1877); Leeds (1877-80); Holbeck Bradford (1890-)
career_raw: Left school at age 12 to assist in housework and nursing; newsboy (to 1883); commenced full-time work for firm of locomotive builders (1883-5); labourer in glass bottlemanufactory (1885-7); succession of jobs, mainly as a small shopkeeper and was at various times in business running a fish and chip shop, then as a tailor’s agent, draper, insurance agent and proprietor of sweet shop. Employed as editor and proprietor of the Tong Pioneer of Social Reform (from 1908, the Bradford Socialist Vanguard). Ill-health caused him to abandon many of his activities in 1920, but he continued to contribute articles to the Labour Pioneer.
affiliations_raw: Teetotaller; member of Salvation Army; member of Bradford Labour Union (1891); member of Bradford Fabian Society (1891); unpaid secretary of Bradford Independent Labour Party (1900); member of Bradford City Council (1904); member of Bradford Corporation’s Distress Committee and of the North Bierley Board of Guardians; president of Tong Socialist Society; published series of pamphlets entitled ‘Pamphlets for the People’; secretary of Bradford branch of National Union of Gasworkers and General Labourers; vice-president of Bradford Trades Council (1908-10); National Union of General and Municipal Workers.
content_tone: The articles begin with an account of Glyde’s early life (Sunday Schooling; participation in Labour agitation), but the political element soon becomes dominant, with a lengthy history of the Socialist movement in Hunslet, Holbeck and Nottingham districts and full details of Labour activity in municipal politics; electioneering; the Social Democratic Federation; the Labour Electoral Association; the history of the ILP, and detailed profiles of various Labour leaders, including Tom Mann, John Burns, Keir Hardie, Ben Turner and Bob Smillie. A valuable record of the early days of provincial socialism and Labour representation. Much of the information from these articles was first published in Glyde’s Bradford Socialist Vanguard, 1917-18, 1920.
title: ‘Memories of the Life of an Agitator: Autobiography of C.A. Glyde’, The Yorkshire Factory Times and Workers’ Weekly Record, 28 Sept 1922 – 30 Aug 1923

residences: Beccles (1879-1900); Tonbridge; Frome, Somerset; Beccles; Tiptree, Essex; Luton; Plymouth; London; Lowestoft; Oxford (1942); Watford (1942); Lowestoft (1955-62); Hythe, Kent (1962-4); Bushey, Herts
career_raw: Apprentice compositor (1893-1900). Remained in printing trade all his life, working variously as reader, overseer and manager of printing shops. Retired 1947.
affiliations_raw: Self-improver; occasional contributor to local publications; Conservative (came out on strike only once in entire working life); family life.
content_tone: Written in 1933, the narrative provides a detailed account of the author’s life up to his 54th year. Raised in a staunchly Methodist family the author describes a happy childhood, with full descriptions of the home; domestic conditions; schooling; childhood games (’cat’; ‘toot’; ‘Spanish fly’); outdoor sports and courtship. His working life is accorded the same detail with much information on wages, hours and conditions in the printing industry from the early 20th century on. The original MS was re-typed by the author’s son in 1973, incorporating new material obtained from correspondence with his father. This required some of the original to be cut and rearranged to keep the material in sequence, but editing was kept to a minimum and the writing throughout remained the author’s.
title: ‘A Grey Life’

father_raw: Son of a pensioned soldier and a village schoolmistress.
career_raw: Worked as a farm labourer and bookbinder in America before becoming a temperance lecturer in 1843.
affiliations_raw: Published extensively on temperance. See also Platform Echoes (1885), Sunlight and Shadow (1881).
content_tone: Essentially a temperance tract in which the author describes his personal experiences of alcoholism before signing the pledge and eventually lecturing on the subject throughout England and America.
title: The Autobiography of John B. Gough, with a continuation of his life up to the present time

father_raw: 3rd child of a jeweller and an aspirant opera singer and dress-maker.
career_raw: Chorister (1865-8); schoolteacher (1871-96); freethought lecturer (1896-9); secretary and organiser of Leicester Secular Society (1899-1908); lecturer and propagandist for the Moral Education League (1910-).
affiliations_raw: Sunday School teacher; Radical; active as lecturer and propagandist for various freethought and radical associations; founder-member of the Ethical Society, Moral Instruction League and Moral Instruction Circle; town councillor; teetotaller; member of Labour Party; founder-member of Leicester Positivist Society; published extensively, including articles in periodicals, pamphlets and books.
content_tone: Mainly an account of the author’s association with various freethought and radical movements, including secularism, socialism and humanism.
title: The Life-Story of a Humanist

father_raw: Son of a grain merchant and proprietor, with wife, of a grocery store.
residences: Glasgow
career_raw: Appointed monitor (pupil-teacher) at South Side school (1879-82); started work for the National Telephone Company in 1882, with his first year spent cleaning batteries, but by attending evening classes he was promoted to the inspection staff in his second year; became an electrician in 1884/5, eventually setting up in partnership in an electrician’s business in the early 1890s.
affiliations_raw: Devout lover of opera and theatre; became active in trade unionism and politics in the late 1880s; founder and secretary of Electricians’ Union in Glasgow; member of local School Board; member of Barlinnie Prison’s Visiting Committee; member of Polmont Institution; contributed articles to various Labour periodicals and published various pamphlets.
content_tone: An interesting autobiography by a modest pioneer of social reform, though personal details subordinated to his account of the beginnings of the Socialist movement in Glasgow. Among the subjects discussed are children’s games; employment as an electrician; unemployment and local politics; the early struggles of the Socialist League, Scottish Labour Party, the Labour Army and the Independent Labour Party; the birth ofthe Labour Representation Committee; the South African War; the cultural side of socialism; School Board elections and activities; religious bigotry; the education system. The autobiography comprises pages 1-113, with the remainder entitled ‘A Few of the Prominent People Ihave Met’, reprinting articles on, among others, Keir Hardie; Harry Quelch; Bob Smillie; Jim Connell; G. K. Chesterton; Lloyd George; Gustave Von Holst; Eleanor Marx; Bruce Glasier.
title: My Seventy Years, with a foreword by John S. Clarke

father_raw: Father was a nomadic tinker, chair-bottomer and ‘jack-of-all-trades’, whom the author did not see until he was aged 7.
residences: Dublin (to age 7); Stockport (from age 7); Whittingham, near Preston (1885-7); Stockport (from 1887); led a wandering, Bohemian life until 1920, when he suffered a breakdown
career_raw: Was working for 4 hours a day before going to school (at age 8) as assistant chimney-sweep to his father; continued as a sweep until age 14, also playing the fiddle at his father’s Punch and Judy shows; worked for one year as a chair-bottomer in Canada (aged 14-15); performed general caretaking duties at Whittingham Asylum, near Preston (1885-7); returned to chimney-sweeping and playing the violin for travelling theatres and circuses; appointed leader of Stockport Theatre Royal Orchestra; employed at theatres in Blackpool and Southport, but repeatedly lost his job because of his political activities; travelled as a fiddler and socialist lecturer giving lectures and concerts in England and abroad.
affiliations_raw: Enjoyed reading in spare time; highly proficient violinist; founder-member and president of the Musicians’ Union in Stockport; flirted with Liberalism before joining the Independent Labour Party; contributed articles to the Labour Leader and Sunday Chronicle. Publications include Mr. James Watts’ Collection of Violins (Stockport, n.d.); Hampson’s Violin School (Stockport, 1901); A Wandering Minstrel I: Vagrom sketches by ‘Casey [1912?]; The Burston School Strike (1915).
content_tone: A most interesting narrative comprising a detailed chronicle of the author’s progress from childhood poverty in Dublin to becoming an accomplished violinist, combining concert-giving with lecturing on the socialist platform. Each stage of his life is given in full, and excellent accounts are provided of life as a child chimney-sweep (in defiance of the 1840 Climbing Boys Act); lunatic asylums (patients; methods of ‘treatment’); itinerant entertaining (theatre booths; circuses; fairs); and as a travelling musician and socialist propagandist. Other subjects covered include dress; diet; schooling; child labour; childhood fears; Labour politics and the ILP; reminiscences of World War I; mechanisation and dilution; profiles of William Morris, John Bruce Glasier and Katherine Bruce Glasier; the Suffragette movement.
title: ‘Reminiscences of ‘Casey”, Forward, 28 March - 31 Oct

residences: Camborne and Troon, and at the age of 61 had only once been out of Cornwall
career_raw: At age 9 drove plough for uncle and then worked as an assistant to a ‘tin-streamer’, throwing sand from the river; surface-worker at Dolcoath mine, dressing and preparing copper ore for the market (1830-2); underground copper-miner (1832-; upwards of 20 years); ‘tributer’ (labouring for a certain portion of the mineral discovered); scripture-reader in Falmouth (from 1857); employed as a writer (1875-6).
affiliations_raw: Sunday School teacher (from age 16) and librarian; Sunday School superintendent; local preacher; poet, with many of his verses being published (a full list of which is included in the volume).
content_tone: A most interesting piece that begins with an account of family history and references to rural traditions, festivities and superstitions, but then moves on to devote approximately equal attention to the ‘tyranny of labour’ in the copper mine and his escape from this through self-improvement and versifying. Most valuable for his comments on, and descriptions of, underground working.
title: My Autobiography

father_raw: 5th child of 6 of a journeyman baker.
career_raw: Worked for 7 years as a clerk in various offices before entering into a long period of service for the Baptist denomination, including Acting General House Secretary for the Baptist Missionary Society and editor of various missionary journals, including the Quest and Wonderlands.
affiliations_raw: Published several works, including Footprints in the Snow (1930); Sermons on the Christian Way [1945]; George Grenfell. Master builder of foundations (1949).
content_tone: A modest narrative with opening comments on parentage and schooling before moving on to a consideration of his life-long service for the Baptist faith.
title: Such has been my Life. An Autobiography, with an introduction by Hugh Martin

father_raw: Son of a labourer who died when author aged 9.
residences: Glasgow (1863-75); Newcastle upon Tyne (1875-96); Darlington (1896-1906); London (1906-35)
career_raw: Started to earn living as an errand-boy (aged 10); apprentice iron-moulder (from age 12); worked for Labour newspaper in Newcastle (1894-5); full-time agent for Liberal Party (from 1896). Elected Labour MP for Barnard Castle in 1903, and subsequently for Widnes (1919-22); E. Newcastle (1923); Burnley (1924-31); Clay Cross (1933-5). Parliamentary leader of Labour Party from 1908 and general secretary from 1911. Leader of the Labour Party (1931-2).
affiliations_raw: Teetotaller; converted to Wesleyan Methodism at age 16; lay preacher; joined Friendly Society of Iron-Founders (1883), soon becoming secretary of local lodge and district delegate (from 1892); secretary of North-Eastern Conciliation Board (1894); elected to Newcastle City Council as a Liberal (1893); elected to Durham County Council (1897) and Darlington Borough Council (1898); mayor of Darlington (1903). Treasurer of Labour Representation Committee and honorary treasurer of British section of International Association for Labour Legislation; president of Foundry Workers’ Union (from 1910); Privy Councillor (1915); JP; chairman of War Emergency Workers’ National Committee; president of Board of Education (1915-16); Home Secretary (1924); Foreign Secretary (1929); awarded Nobel Peace Prize (1934); published widely, including The Aims of Labour (1917); Labour’s Way to Peace (1935), and many articles in the Labour Magazine.
content_tone: A brief early life history to 1906 by one of the prominent figures of 20th century Labour Party politics.
title: ‘How I Got On: From Errand Boy to M.P.’, Pearson’s Weekly, 8 March 1906.

father_raw: Father a master tailor who died young.
residences: or near London all his life except for a brief period in Belgium
career_raw: Apprenticed to parliamentary printer, Luke Hansard (1805), and eventually became a compositor. Published pamphlets on his own account as well as for others (1822-); bookseller and newsagent.
affiliations_raw: Member of the Freethinking Christians (1798), the British Association for the Promotion of Co-operative Knowledge (c.1829), the First Middlesex Society (1830) and the Civil and Religious Liberty Association (1828), later the Radical Reform Association. Co-founder of the National Union of the Working Classes, the London Working Men’s Association and the Metropolitan Political Union (1830). Publisher of the unstamped Poor Man’s Guardian. Played an active but secondary role in the Chartist movement. Published a large number of radical papers and journals. Author of Principles and Practice contrasted; or, a peep into ‘the only true Church of God upon Earth’, commonly called Freethinking Christians (2nd edn., 1828); Cheap Salvation: or an antidote to priestcraft, being a succint, practical, essential and rational religion deduced from the New Testament (2nd edn., 1843).
content_tone: A note from G. J. Holyoake states that this manuscript was signed ‘J.W.’ [James Watson?] and yet ‘the handwriting seems to be Hetherington’s’. Although the text was written in the third person it has an intimacy that suggests autobiography. The narrative provides only a bare outline of Hetherington’s background and covers only his youth and not his later political activity. A short and little-known account by a leading campaigner for the unstamped press and universal suffrage.
title: Autobiographical fragment, MS, pp.8

father_raw: 3rd child born and second surviving of a hand-loom weaver.
residences: Dundee; Lochee; Broughty Ferry; Roundy Hill; Edinburgh; London (1860-8); Darlington (1868-)
career_raw: Assisted father at home from an early age by driving the ‘pirn-wheel”; hand-loom weaver; opened school at Smithfield, Dundee in 1844; left teaching to study and practice medicine, before returning to teaching; opened shop as druggist and stationer; missionary teacher; evangelist; pastor.
affiliations_raw: Newspaper correspondent; member of National Chartist Association, becoming secretary of the Lochee branch; member of Dundee Democratic Council; member of Forfar, Perth and Fifeshire Teachers’ Association; member of the ‘Literary Emporium’; temperance lecturer; independent Liberal. Publications include Sophia: a tale (1857); Thoughts in Rhyme (1859).
content_tone: A sad story of a life regularly afflicted by family deaths, illness and poverty. Hillocks’ tale takes us through his schooling; experiences of deprivation; Chartist activities; ‘tramping’; efforts at self-education; teaching; and also touches on dress; diet; low dwellings; popular demonstrations. A version of the narrative was a prize winner in an essay competition, ‘Lives of Working Men, written by themselves’, organised by the Commonwealth, 1856.
title: Life Story. A Prize Autobiography

residences: or near Ettrick, Selkirkshire (1770-c
career_raw: Cowherd (from age 7); shepherd; pursued a literary career (1810-16); tenant farmer, while continuing his distinguished literary pursuits.
affiliations_raw: Played the violin; poet, and writer of songs and ballads, establishing considerable fame as the ‘Ettrick shepherd poet’, with many publications, including The Long Pack (1817); The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner (1824); The Queen's Wake (1814). Proprietor of The Spy (1810-11). Secretary of the Forum Debating Society.
content_tone: A brief account of his early struggles for literacy but confined mostly to anecdotes relating to his progress in literary life, with reminiscences of contemporary literary figures including Galt, Cunningham, Lockhart and Wordsworth. Some mention is made of dress, but there is little comment on his early life, shepherding or the years spent in poverty.
title: ‘Memoir of the Life of James Hogg’, in The Mountain Bard; consisting of Ballads and Songs, founded on Facts and Legendary Tales. By James Hogg, the Ettrick Shepherd

residences: London (1745-50); Berkshire (1751); Rugeley; Cheshire; Newmarket (1757-60); London (1760-2); Liverpool (1764-5); London (1765- ?1770); Ireland (1770-1); London (1777-)
career_raw: Assisted parents in hawking various wares (1751-6); apprentice stocking-weaver (for short time only); stable-boy (1757-60); apprentice shoemaker (1760-64?); teacher (1764-5); began writing career as contributor to Whitehall Evening Post, subsequently writing many novels; prompter at a Dublin theatre (1770-1); strolling player in England and Scotland (1771-7); actor; author of many plays; set up printing business with brother-in-law (1803).
affiliations_raw: Taught to play violin at early age; editor of the Wits’ Magazine; member of Society for Constitutional Information (1792); indicted for high treason, but acquitted (1794); his many publications include Memoirs of Bryan Perdue (1805); Hugh Trevor (1794-7); Alwyn, or the Gentleman Comedian (1780).
content_tone: Although the autobiographical section deals only with the period up to 1760, Holcroft provides a most interesting account of his childhood as a pedlar/beggar and later as a stable-boy. Among the themes discussed are diet; dress; superstitions; public executions; and the Nottingham races. The remainder of his life is related by Wm. Hazlitt, compiled from Holcroft’s own writings, concerning his later activities in the fields of literature and theatre, though also including an account of the Gordon Riots (1780), and of his trial and brief imprisonment for high treason.
title: Memoirs of the late Thomas Holcroft, Written by Himself, and continued to the time of his death, from his diary, notes and other papers, with an advertisement’ by Wm. Hazlitt

father_raw: Father a whitesmith.
residences: Birmingham (1817-40); Worcester (c
career_raw: Went to learn father’s trade of whitesmith at age of 9; left foundry in 1839 and made a living by schoolteaching, public speaking, secretarial work and journalism; began a printing business with his brother (1851) which became a publishing house (1853) before closing in 1862.
affiliations_raw: Member of many organisations including the Association of All Classes of All Nations (1838); the London Atheistical Society; the Anti-Persecution Union; the Northern Reform Union; the London Political Union; the Reform League (1866); the committee established to finance the British voluntary expedition to support Garibaldi (acting secretary); the Association for the Repeal of The Taxes on Knowledge; the Liberty of Bequest Committee (president from 1893); the Travelling Tax Abolition Committee (president from 1887); the Peace Committee; the National Liberal Club (honorary member). Editor of the Oracle of Reason (1841-2); the Chartist Cause of the People (1848); Brighton Guardian (1878-80). Founded the Movement, 1843-5 (with M. Ryall); the Reasoner (1846-61); the Secular Review (1876). Promoter of the First British Congress on Co-operation (1869), and presided in 1875 and 1887. Founder and president of the Rationalist Press Committee. Published extensively, for details of which see G. W. F. Goss, A Descriptive Bibliography of the Writings of George Jacob Holyoake. With a Brief Sketch of His Life (1908). For further reminiscences see Bygones Worth Remembering (1905), 2 vols.
content_tone: Holyoake commences the narrative with a description of his early life in a whitesmith foundry, but the main value of this important work lies in the detail it provides of reform politics of the nineteenth century, with observations on all the main movements, people and events, from the Birmingham Political Union and Chartism to the Anti-Corn Law League and Gladstonian Liberalism. Although an ‘agitator” concerned with the freedom of individual activity and expression, Holyoake remained only on the fringes of radical politics, flirting with Chartism but preferring to ally himself to Owenism, co-operation with the middle classes and Gladstonian Liberalism. He was responsible for giving the secularist and co-operative causes national and international recognition, both being covered fully in the narrative.
title: George Jacob, Sixty Years of an Agitator’s Life

career_raw: Worked as assistant to father for short period (half-time); assistant groom and gardener, and then an indoor servant, beginning 57 years in service, interrupted in early stages by brief period as a railway porter. Employed in all grades of servants’ work, from footboy to valet, butler and house steward.
affiliations_raw: Chorister.
content_tone: A good account of life in service, with details of all grades of work and duties ‘below stairs’, and with comments on his employers and their ways of life.
title: What The Butler Winked At. Being the Life and Adventures of Eric Horne

father_raw: Father a railwayman, first a porter and later a foreman at Merthyr Goods Station.
residences: Merthyr Tydfil; Ynyshir; Mardy; London
career_raw: First job (at age 8) was as lather-boy in a barber’s shop; delivery-boy for a grocer; office-boy at the railway; collier; checkweighman (from 1919); elected president of South Wales Miners’ Federation (1936); appointed National Coal Production Officer (1945); general secretary of National Union of Mineworkers (1946-1959).
affiliations_raw: Well-known as the ‘Welsh boy preacher’, giving sermons in Baptist chapels at age 15; proficient at boxing, football, athletics; member of Independent Labour Party; chairman of Unofficial Reform Committee; member of Rhondda Socialist Society and Welsh Socialist Society; fought for Citizen’s Army in Ireland (1916); imprisoned as a conscientious objector; founder-member of Communist Party of Great Britain (1920), becoming part-time member of Political Bureau; helped to establish Miners’ Minority Movement in S. Wales; served on executive committee of Miners’ Federation of Great Britain (1926-7); unsuccessful Communist candidate for Rhondda constituency (1929, 1931, 1933); published South Wales Miner (1933); contributed many articles to various periodicals. Publications include Coal: the Next Round [1926]; Communism and Coal (1928); Trade Unions and Communism [1948].
content_tone: The miners’ struggles around the turn of the century formed the background to Horner’s early years, and the narrative soon develops into an excellent account of Labour militancy in the South Wales coalfields and of the politics and personalities of the miners’ trade unions. Among the many topics covered are the Tonypandy Riots (1910); the formation of the CP; the lock-out of 1921; the General Strike; the hunger marches. An invaluable source for 20th century Labour politics
title: Incorrigible Rebel

career_raw: Ploughboy (c.1843-5); assisted father as mortar-boy and timekeeper (1845-7); apprentice shoemaker (1847-51); journeyman shoemaker (1851-3); bricklayer (1853-9), then deputy foreman (to 1865); paid secretary of the Reform League (1865-9); launched a private Liberal Registration and Election Agency (1869), but was unsuccessful; paid secretary of the Representative Reform Association (1868-74); paid secretary of the Plimsoll and Seaman’s Fund Committee (1873-5); sought financial independence by setting up Adelphi Permanent Building Society (1870-1), but was unsuccessful; turned to writing as source of income, contributing regularly to the Beehive; London business agent for Manchester coal merchant (c.1882-5); MP for N. E. Bethnal Green (1885-95), supporting himself in these years by journalism; engaged to edit the Imperial White Books (1886-8); withdrew from political life in 1895 and devoted his time to writing.
affiliations_raw: Teetotaller; converted to Wesleyan Methodism (1848); Methodist Sunday School teacher; Chartist; member of improvement society affiliated to a Reformed Methodist chapel; helped to found St. James’s Square YMCA,; active in improvement societies, debating clubs and temperance organisations; member of London Order of the Operative Bricklayers’ Society, to 1871, when he resigned in favour of the Sheffield Lodge of the Manchester Unity of Operative Bricklayers; active in the launching of Operative Bricklayers’ Society Trade Circular, in 1861; elected to executive of London Trades Council (1861), and served as secretary (1861-2); one ofthe founders of the Trade Unionists’ Manhood Suffrage and Vote by Ballot Association (1862); member of National League for the Independence of Poland (1863), Garibaldi’s Reception Committee (1864), the Marquis of Townshend’s Universal League for the Material Elevation of the Industrious Classes (1864-5), and of the General Council of the International Working Men’s Association (1864-9); helped to establish the Labour Representation League, serving on its executive until 1876; chairman of the Working Men’s Committee for Promoting the Separation of Church and State (1871-2); member of executive committees of National Education League and the Liberation Society; financial agent of the Land Tenure Reform Association; secretary of the People’s Garden Company; served on parliamentary committee of TUC (1871), and as its secretary (1871-5); secretary of London School Board election committees (1876, 1879, 1882); parliamentary agent of Women’s Suffrage Committee (1878-9); founder and chairman of National Liberal League (1879-82); co-editor of the Common Good (1881); active in the management of the Labour Standard. Publications include many articles, and also, A Handy Book of the Labour aws (1876); Trade Unionism New and Old (1891); The Conflicts of Capital and Labour Historically and Economically considered (1878); Labour Legislation, Labour Movements and Labour Leaders (1902).
content_tone: An uncorrected and unedited draft autobiography in 6 volumes of compact manuscript, including much repetition. Volume F contains carbon copies of the bulk of the material contained in volumes A-E, and is perhaps closest to a completed version. Howell was constantly revising his manuscript and although begun in 1897 he was still seeking to revise it for publication in 1908, though this had to be deferred because of ill-health and was never achieved. Among the many subjects covered are ancestry; childhood; education; self- improvement; Chartism; temperance; Freethought Movement; coffee-houses; Milton Club; the building trade; London slums; Free Trade Movement; debating societies; Nine Hours Movement; the builders’ strike and lock-out; American Civil War; industrial and political combinations; opinions and biographies, often colourful, of men known to Howell; Plimsoll Movement (1871-5); Ballot Society (1860-72); London School Board; Land Tenure Reform Association (1869-74); Land Laws Reform League (1879); and parliamentary life. An extremely useful account of London life, mid-century radicalism and Labour agitation.
title: ‘The Autobiography of a Toiler. With an account of the movement with which he was connected, of the persons whom he met, of his aspirations and achievements during 50 years of active political and industrial life’ [one of the provisional titles listed in the manuscript], MS, 6 vols. George Howell Collection, Bishopsgate Institute, London.

father_occupation: foreman machine-ruler at a paper mill
father_raw: Son of a foreman machine-ruler at a paper mill.
career_raw: Machine-ruler at paper mill (1865-71); worked in same trade in various shops in London before setting up on own account, in 1878, as a printer and wholesale manufacturing stationer.
affiliations_raw: Joined the Volunteers when aged 16; member of Consolidated Society of Bookbinders and Machine Rulers (from 1911, the National Union of Bookbinders and Machine Rulers); one of the founders and president of the Fifty Club, formed in 1899; alderman; mayor of Shoreditch; supported every charitable organisation connected with his trade; Freeman of City of London; member of Stationers’ Mutual Benefit Society from age 21; member of Vintry Ward Club; Liveryman of the Stationers’ Company; Freemason; chairman (for one year) of Printers and Kindred Trades of the British Empire; member of City of London Trade Society; joint-founder and chairman of the Trade Rulers and Vellum Binders section of the London Master Printers’ Association.
content_tone: A reflection on changes in the trade of machine-ruling, with anecdotes of his youth and comments on the home; leisure (’penny readings’; circuses); transport; dress; policing; public houses; ‘tramping’.
title: The Life Story of T. J. Hunt. An Autobiography

father_raw: One of 9 children of a woolcomber.
residences: Derby (1723-38); Nottingham (1738-49); Southwell (1749-50); Birmingham (1750-)
career_raw: Started work in a silk mill (1730-7); apprenticed to uncle as a stocking-maker (1738-44); journeyman stockinger; taught himself bookbinding, and set himself up as a binder; became successful in business, running a paper warehouse; invested money in business ventures and land and property purchases.
affiliations_raw: Dissenter; interested in music; Commissioner of the Court of Requests (1772-91); Commissioner of the Lamp and Street Act (1773); poet; Fellow of the Antiquarian Society of Scotland (FASS); opened a circulating library in Birmingham (1751); local historian and author of many works including An History of Birmingham to the end of the year 1780 (Birmingham, 1781); A Trip to Coatham in Yorkshire (1810); The Court of Requests...with a memoir (Edinburgh, 1840).
content_tone: Written in the form of an annual diary, Hutton tells of a successful life, rising from a child mill-worker to an eminent businessman and property-owner. Among the themes and topics discussed are ‘breeching’; childhood incidents; elections; experiences in the mill and as an apprentice stockinger; ‘tramping’; courtships; travels; with a detailed account of the riots in Birmingham, 14 July 1791. Hutton takes the narrative up to 1812 (p.286), and the story is brought to a conclusion by his daughter (pp.287-328), followed by a ‘History of the Family of Hutton, 1570-1798’ (pp.331-98).
title: The Life of William Hutton, F.A.S.S. Including a Particular Account of the Riots at Birmingham in 1791. To which is subjoined, The History of His Family, Written by Himself, and published by his Daughter, Catherine Hutton

father_raw: Father an enlisted (?)soldier.
residences: Bingley and Blackburn (1888-2)
career_raw: Placed in service with a collier and with a yeoman farmer; made ‘occasional ramblings’ through the neighbourhood of his birth (1865-75); herbalist (c.1880s-). | Poet and contributor to the Blackburn press.
content_tone: A brief sketch of the author’s life with no additional information or observations. Written in the third person.
title: ‘Autobiography of Thomas Ince’, in his Beggar Manuscripts: an Original Miscellany in Verse and Prose

residences: Knaresborough; Scriven (1908/9-10); Malton (1910-12); Scarborough (1912-13); Leeds (1913/14); Bath; London (1918-?); Sussex
career_raw: Part-time assistant at chemist’s (aged 9); newspaper boy; errand-boy (1904-6); apprenticed to a chemist when aged about 14; travelling salesmanfor chemist; enlisted (1914), but invalided out; organising secretary, then chief officer, for the London Hospital Saturday Fund (1918-21); House Governor of Charing Cross Hospital (1921-36), then chairman (1936-); chairman of British Broadcasting Corporation; chairman of the Central Board of Finance for the Church Assembly; chairman of the Hotels Executive of British Transport.
affiliations_raw: Chorister; member of Mutual Improvement Society; active member of Labour Party (to 1936); frequent contributor to Daily Herald; created a peer in 1946; member of Attlee’s Cabinet as Lord Privy Seal.
content_tone: A full account of the author’s life, from his early struggles and poverty through to success in public and business life. Among the themes covered are hiring fairs; home life; food prices; local parish history; courtship; youthful reading matter; hospital life and work (as an administrator); journalism and literary work; business ventures.
title: No Going Back. An Autobiography

residences: Dundee for much of his life
career_raw: Apprenticed to an uncle, an ironmonger (1 year); apprentice draper (4 years); journeyman and master draper.
affiliations_raw: Contributor to local newspapers; Christian; teetotaller; member of Gladstone Literary Society.
content_tone: The narrative commences with an explanation of the author’s desire to publish his memoirs, followed by an excellent account of his schooling. Much of the remainder is given over to detail on various aspects of the drapery trade, including conditions of employment; wages; apprenticeship; state of the trade; business life; and incorporating full accounts of the Dundee Drapers’ Association Annual Festivals (1879, 1880). Ireland also provides the full text of his first public lecture on Addison, Steele and Cowper. The final sections contain reviews of a volume published anonymously in Dundee, entitled ‘The Life of a Dundee Draper’, with advice on how to become a good and successful draper. A review states that the author of this was born in 1800 and came to Dundee in 1814 as an apprentice draper.
title: Passages in the History of a Town Draper, with an Account of the Drapers’ Festivals

father_raw: Son of a stonemason.
residences: Warmington (1858-64); Thrapston (1864-70); then travelled to where work demanded
career_raw: First employment was crow-scaring, then employed in printing and bookbinding, in an iron foundry, in osier-peeling, and as a butcher’s boy, carpenter and servant between ages 10 and 14. Then was apprenticed (unofficially?) to learn stonemason’s trade, in which he remained until called to the Gospel (1871-82). Worked as London City Missionary (1882-1927).
affiliations_raw: Much of the author’s youth was spent playing pranks and enjoying the pleasures of the countryside, attending feasts and fairs. His early working life was spent ‘tramping’ and it was not until 1877, and his conversion to Christianity, that these habits passed out of his life. From that time he desired to acquire knowledge and education, previously neglected, and wholeheartedly went into Christian missionary activity, through preaching and going among the poor to give them the Word of God.
content_tone: The first part of Ireson’s autobiography describes in romantic style his country childhood, a time of harvesting, gleaning, pig-killing, fairs and feasts, with rarely a suggestion of rural poverty and hardship. This is followed by an account of his apparently pleasurable time as a ‘tramping’ stonemason. These sections contrast with the pictures of squalor and deprivation met by Ireson when employed as a London City Missionary from the 1880s on. An interesting memoir from a witness rather than a victim of poverty. Written 1929-30.
title: ‘Reminiscences’, TS, pp.175

father_raw: One of 4 children of a compositor.
residences: London (1879-1909); Newport (1909-11); Leeds (1911-19); Newcastle upon Tyne (1919-21); London (1921-9); Three Bridges, Sussex (1929-?); Clare
career_raw: Reading-boy at large printing works (aged 13 1/2); apprentice compositor (1893-1900); after apprenticeship was unable to find employment as had been branded by employers as a socialist agitator; paid lecturer for Independent Labour Party (1909-11); lecturer for National Secular Society (1911-14); storekeeper at small engineering works (1914-19); lecturer for N.E. district of National Council of Labour Colleges (1919-21); employed by Communist Party, first as editor or sub-editor of party journals, then as agitator/propagandist, and subsequently as journalist for the Sunday Worker (1921-9); turned his attention to writing and local lecturing from 1929, contributing regularly to the Daily Worker; district lecturer for the Communist Party (1944-9).
affiliations_raw: Inherited from father an early interest in trade unionism, radical politics and Irish nationalism; joined Social Democratic Federation in 1900; member of Socialist Labour Party; started a branch of the Communist Party in Newcastle (1920); member of Communist Party central committee, with special duties in the field of education and propaganda (1924- 9); centrally involved in the disputes within the Communist Party in the 1920s; published extensively, with works on the Russian Revolution, Irish Nationalism, literature, and communist theory, including Ireland Her Own: an outline history of the Irish strugele for ational freedom and independence (1946); Charles Dickens: the progress of a radical (1937); Old Friends to Keep: Studies of English Novels and Novelists (1950).
content_tone: The two main themes of the text are work and politics, with accounts of the author’s time spent in a printing shop and of his participation in the Socialist and Labour movements of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Among the many subjects discussed are Irish politics and the Fenians; the Labour press; American Labour and the Industrial Workers of the World; policing and socialist agitation; Jews and the charge of ritual murder. The narrative ends with the formation of the Communist Party in 1920. Solo Trumpet was intended to be the first part of a two volume autobiography but the second volume never appeared owing to publisher’s difficulties.
title: Solo Trumpet, Some Memories of Socialist Agitation and Propaganda

residences: various parts of South Wales all his life
career_raw: Began as a pit-face worker at age 12, and worked on and off as a miner for 26 years; also variously employed as a forester; navvy; soldier; book salesman; cinema manager; hod carrier, as well as suffering from periodic bouts of unemployment. Entered the literary field as a freelance journalist and worked as an author and playwright from 1934.
affiliations_raw: Secretary-representive of local lodge of South Wales Miners’ Federation; member of the newly-formed Communist Party of Great Britain, acting as an agitator and propagandist; drifted away from communism into the Liberal Party; unsuccessfully contested the Neath constituency in 1929; awarded the CBE in 1948. Wrote many novels and plays, including Land of My Fathers (1937); Bidden to the Feast (1938); Lily of the Valley (1952).
content_tone: A graphic and lively narrative with fine detail of home and childhood in a South Wales mining community and also of his subsequent working life. Good descriptions are provided of the slums of Merthyr; pit life and work; leisure (childhood games; theatres; circuses); the chapel; barrack life and military adventures in South Africa and France; the General Strike; dress and diet, the early years of the CPGB; Oswald Mosley’s New Party.
title: Unfinished Journey, with a preface by the Rt. Hon. David Lloyd George

father_raw: Father worked as a ‘hobbler’ at Cardiff docks.
career_raw: Door-boy at local colliery (aged 12-13); hammer-boy (’Oliver-boy’) in colliery blacksmith’s shop (aged 13); collier-boy (aged 14); stoker; pit labourer (’the hardest and worst paid job’); haulier; fitter’s labourer; engine cleaner; gardener; gasometer painter; hawker of trinkets and domestic wares (aged 19-21); violinist in music hall orchestra; postman/telegram clerk; junior reporter; shorthand clerk; rent-collector; novelist and dramatist; private secretary to an accountant; city clerk.
affiliations_raw: Chorister; violinist; secretary of local branch of United Irish League. Novels include The Exploited Woman (1923); The Great Appeal (1909); The Perfect Wife (1913); Maurice (1905); Son of Judith (1901).
content_tone: A most interesting and highly readable volume which charts in fine and graphic style the author’s rise from pit-boy to successful novelist. Excellent descriptions are provided of childhood, home and working-class life and conditions in the Irish colony of Mountain Ash. Other topics covered include religion; schooling; diet and dress; childhood reading matter; the Fenian movement; courtship. Full accounts are provided of Keating’s varied employments with particularly good sections on navvies and navvying and on pit life and work, describing his first experiences underground with obvious pleasure, excitement and pride. The major theme of the remainder of the narrative is the author’s struggle for literary success, with hardship regularly alternating with prosperity.
title: My Struggle for Life

career_raw: Newspaper-seller; odd-jobs; cook and rope-boy on fishing smacks (aged 9-12); cabin-boy; merchant seaman; ran a tea business; employed by the Dominion and the Evening Post; in business as a newsagent.
affiliations_raw: Joined the Salavation Army; became mayor in New Zealand.
content_tone: A brief account of his early years as a street-urchin precedes a lengthy narrative of his adventures as a seaman, with some later comment on his conversion and life in New Zealand. The text has been rewritten from the original by Rita F. Snowden, though retaining Kelly’s style ‘as nearly as possible’.
title: Prodigal of the Seven Seas, edited with a preface by Rita F. Snowden

father_raw: 7th of 12 children of a cotton operative.
career_raw: Worked for short periods in a wide variety of occupations before turning to journalism, including assisting father in his newly-formed business venture of hawking ‘washing-liquor’ from a pony and cart (aged 9/10); newspaper boy (1893); half-time learner in a cotton mill (aged 11), and full-time from age 14; chain-horse lad for the London and North Western Railway (aged 15 1/2); casual labourer (aged 17); navvy; tramp; agricultural labourer; cobbler; carter; builder’s labourer; capstan man; commercial traveller (1903/4); manager of branch of Abel Heywood & Sons (publishers and stationers) in Preston (1906). Arrived in London in 1908/9 and was employed by the Independent Labour Party as manager of the Publications Department; publisher of Vanity Fair; Labour editor, then editor, of Daily Herald; writer for the New Statesman and Reynolds Newspaper; accepted post (in 1920) in the Political Intelligence Department of the Foreign Office, being employed in that service in various capacities thereafter.
affiliations_raw: Interested in literature and music; member of ILP and of the Shop Assistants’ Union; representative on Preston Trades Council; British representative to the Norwegian Press; attended the Stockholm conference of the Socialist International; member of the British mission to Poland. Publications include Men and Rails (1913); A Pedlar's Pack (1923).
content_tone: A highly interesting volume, with full detail of his life as a vagabond, tramp, and casual labourer, and of his later activities as a Socialist propagandist. The narrative commences with recollections of the home and schooling, moving on to highlight the horrors of child labour with graphic descriptions of his various labours, including mill-worker, navvy and farm hand. Kenney then provides a brief history of the British Socialist and Labour movement, before detailing his own activities as an activist for the ILP and as a socialist journalist. The text also includes some comment on dialect words. A useful work, with a very helpful index.
title: Westering. An Autobiography

father_raw: Illegitimate son of a watchmaker.
residences: a single room
career_raw: Supported self from very early age by taking jobs as an errand-boy, porter and messenger; was articled to a garment-dyer but soon left this employment to go ‘on the tramp’; later employed as a dyer; Socialist propagandist; joint-editor of Commonwealth.
affiliations_raw: Member of the Democratic and Trades Alliance Association, later the Manhood Suffrage League; founder of the English Revolutionary Society; an anarchist communist; assisted in formation of English section of Rose St. Social Democratic Club; delegate to International Revolutionary Congress (1881); secretary of Freiheit Defence Committee, and editor of English version of Freiheit; joint-founder of Labour Emancipation League (1882).
content_tone: Kitz provides a brief outline of his early life, but the bulk of the narrative is devoted to extensive comment on the national and international socialist and reform movements ofthe 1870s and 1880s. Among the themes discussed are the life and experiences of a tramp; Hyde Park demonstrations; the activities of the Manhood Suffrage League and the Socialist League; the Paris Commune; policing of the radical movement; and German refugees fleeing from anti-socialist legislation.
title: ‘Recollections and Reflections’, Freedom, Jan - July 1912

father_raw: One of 9 children of a railway timekeeper.
career_raw: Office-boy (aged 11/12); worked again for short time as office-boy (aged 14) before undertaking various jobs, including labouring in charcoal factory; wholesale grocer (1 year); coal-heaver, in partnership with brother (to 1883); manager of coffee bar; while in Australia, worked as a stonebreaker, van-driver at a slaughterhouse and farm servant; employed in father-in-law’s sawmill and veneer works in Whitechapel, eventually inheriting the business (1895-1914); from 1914 devoted time and effort to the Daily Herald, of which he was the editor, and Lansbury’s Labour Weekly (1925-7). Elected as Labour MP for Bow and Bronley in 1910, but resigned to fight (unsuccessfully) as an independent on the issue of votes for women; re-elected in 1922 and served until 1940.
affiliations_raw: Teetotaller; unpaid ward secretary to the Liberal Party; general secretary to Bow Liberal Party (1886); member of Social Democratic Federation, Independent Labour Party, Labour Party and Fabian Society; member of Gasworkers’ Union (from 1889); elected to Board of Guardians in 1892; member of LCC; first Commissioner of Works in MacDonald’s government (1929); elected as Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons in 1931 but resigned four years later over the question of using force against Italy for the attack on Abyssinia; Privy Councillor (1929); President of Peace Pledge Union. Published large number of articles and pamphlets. See also volume of reminiscences Looking Backwards and Forwards (1935).
content_tone: A well-known account by an important leader of the Labour movement in which he tells of the various incidents, activities and people with whom he was connected. Sections on his early life spent travelling, schooling, and life in London in the 1860s and 1870s, precede the lengthy descriptions of his political life, with comments on his ‘crossing over’ from liberalism to socialism; the movement of Labour from the 1880s on; parliamentary life; the Suffragette movement;.his work as a town and borough councillor and member of The Board of Guardians; the Daily Herald; his visit to the Soviet Union.
title: My Life, with an introduction by Harold Laski

father_raw: Elder of 2 children of an iron-moulder, later an insurance salesman.
career_raw: Half-time errand-boy at printing works (1879-1881); apprentice printer (1881-89); journeyman printer (1889-90); lay agent for East Anglia (1890-2); probationer for the Methodist ministry (1895); Halifax and Bradford District missionary (1896-7); West London missionary (1897-1902), transferring to the East End in 1902.
affiliations_raw: Was ‘conscious of God’ from a very early age; local preacher at age of 18; devoted life to mission work.
content_tone: Recollections of childhood, schooling, dress and Methodist home life in a late 19th century Lancashire mining village act as a short preface to the lengthy account of his life’s work as a Methodist missionary. A religious tone informs the whole narrative.
title: Lax: His Book. The Autobiography of Lax of Poplar(The Epworth Press, London, 1937), pp.328 + 4pp. index. Illustrated.

father_raw: Father a carpenter (died, 1817).
residences: Kettering
career_raw: Sent to learn shoemaking craft (1824), but trade was bad so was ‘placed in the loom’ under stepfather (till 1829), then apprenticed to a ribbon-weaver (to 1834); stayed with master for a further 3 years, then became a velvet-weaver (c.1837-1846/7); manufactured and hawked plain and fancy vests until accident and illness rendered him incapable of manual labour (1847-50); reporter for Northampton Herald and other local newspapers (1849-).
affiliations_raw: Devoted much of his spare time to literary pursuits; formed (with workmates) a Mutual Instruction Society, arranging classes and delivering lectures; a locally-celebrated poet, working with the ‘grossest society’ in the day and being ‘petted’ by the ‘genteelest’ families in the evenings; secretary of Kettering Chartist Association (for 4 years).
content_tone: Much of the narrative is concerned with apologising for his involvement with the radical movement, describing his time with the Chartist Association as ‘the bane of my youth’, and a time of ‘folly’ and ‘wild projects’. Similarly, his account of an association with another Chartist and self-confessed rick-burner was included to show not only the author’s disgust with such actions but also the humanitarian dilemma of not wishing to condemn the man to death by informing the authorities. Despite this attempt to distance himself from earlier beliefs, Leatherland does provide a solid account of work and literary pursuits.
title: ‘Autobiographical Memoir’ in Essays and Poems with a brief Autobiographical Memoir

father_raw: Father a footman.
residences: various times with aunt and grandmother
career_raw: Cow-minder (1836); servant; firework-maker; rope-spinner; rural postboy; apprenticed in a printing office at age 14; journeyman printer; editor and proprietor of various newspapers; co-operative printer; publisher; election agent (1868); writer.
affiliations_raw: Interested in amateur theatricals, poetry, literature, singing and self-improvement; an active Chartist, forming branches in Uxbridge and Windsor; joint editor of the Manuscript Newspaper and, with friends, produced Spirit of Freedom, and Working Man's Vindicator; contributor to the Christian Socialist; edited the Commonwealth; proprietor and editor of St. Crispin, The Westminster News; member of council of Reform League; Radical publisher; member of The First International; author of miscellaneous political pamphlets and poems.
content_tone: Leno deliberately neglected to write about subjects he thought would ‘weary’ the reader and consequently little is said about his early life beyond a list of employments. The main value of this autobiography therefore lies in the detail given by one actively involved near the top level of reform organisation and agitation, whether speaking on platforms, engaged in meetings with trade union leaders, politicians or others active in the radical cause (including Carl [sic.] Marx and William Morris) or writing political articles and songs.
title: The Aftermath: with Autobiography of the Author

residences: Germany until 1847, when he fled to London to escape compulsory military service; removed back to Germany (1848-56) before returning to London in 1856
career_raw: Apprentice tailor in Germany; remaining in the tailoring trade for almost 70 years.
affiliations_raw: Member of the Arbeiter-Verein (Workmen’s Educational Society; later, the Communist Workmen’s Club); member of the Union of the Just (the Union of the Communists); delegate to the International Socialist Congresses; imprisoned for his political activities (1853-6); helped to set up the paper Das Volk (The People), published in London in 1859.
content_tone: A close friend of Marx and Engels, Lessner tells briefly of his early years in Germany before moving on to deal with the activities of the pioneer Communist and Socialist movements. Among the themes discussed are the International Socialist Congresses; Chartism; the European Revolutions of 1848; the national and international political struggles of the 1860s and 1870s.
title: Sixty Years in the Social-Democratic Movement. Before 1848 and After: Recollections of an Old Communist, with a foreword by E. Belfort Bax and translated from the German by Thalmeyer

residences: London; Stratford; Kennington; Woodford (?-1842); London (1842- 9); Miteside, Northumberland (1849-52); Brantwood, Lake District (1852-5); London (1855-66); went to United States of America in 1866 intending only a brief visit, but settled there; revisited England at fairly regular intervals
career_raw: Apprenticed to a wood-engraver in 1828; entered into partnership with former employer in 1842, but was dissolved in following year owing to death of latter; established reputation as the best wood-engraver of the day; entered into various editorial and publishing ventures, including the Odd-Fellow, the Spectator; the English Republic; the Leader; the Illuminated Magazine; Pen and Pencil.
affiliations_raw: Chartist; took a prominent part in the founding of The People’s International League (1847); close friend of Mazzini and of other leading political, literary and artistic figures; poet; author of various works, including James Watson: A Memoir (1879); The Plaint of Freedom (Newcastle, 1852), published anonymously; A History of Wood-Engraving in America (1882). See also, “Who were the Chartists?, Century Magazine, Vol. 23, Jan 1882, pp.421-30, for profiles of various Chartist leaders including William Lovett, Henry Hetherington, James Watson, Richard Moore, John Frost, Thomas Cooper.
content_tone: Few personal details are provided, with Linton concentrating on detailing his formative influences and acquaintances, political and literary. A most useful history of mid-century Radicalism is provided, with extensive comment on the movement for a free press and Chartism. Pen pictures are provided of all the leading radical figures of the day, and reference is made to the activities of police spies and of the London Working Men’s Association. The other major topics in the volume are his travels at home and abroad; international politics and nationalist movements; London’s literary and artistic world.
title: Memories

career_raw: Started work at an early age winding weavers’ bobbins; subsequently worked as a shuttle-maker, ‘twister-in’, ‘jobber’; weaver (for 7 years); began to sell cheeses at the weekend (c.1815), eventually becoming a cheese wholesaler/cheesemonger and establishing a successful business; ran own printing establishment (1832-59).
affiliations_raw: Converted to Christianity at early age; wrote pamphlets, lectured and agitated on behalf of the Anti-Corn Law League; active in temperance and philanthropic movements; member of Select Vestry; member of Board of Guardians; Commissioner for Improvement of the Borough; elected to Town Council in 1835; active in the ‘Bedding Charity’; worked for the Preston Relief Fund during the Cotton Famine (1862-5); active in promoting the extension of education through Sunday Schools and Working Men’s Clubs; published numerous anti-Corn Law and temperance tracts and pamphlets; editor and publisher of various periodicals, including The Struggle (1842-6); The Moral Reformer (1831-4; 1838-9); The Temperance Advocate (1834-8); The Staunch Teetotaller (1867-8).
content_tone: A fascinating volume with excellent descriptions of the conditions of the working classes during the early and mid-19th century, firstly from a position of childhood experiences and struggles against his environment of ‘mental darkness and vice’ and later from the perspective of an active philanthropist. Among the many themes discussed are struggles for self-improvement; childhood games; superstitions; effects of the Corn Laws on food prices; sufferings and hardships among the working classes; customs/leisure (bull-baiting; ‘Collop Monday’); public duties; 1834 Poor Law.
title: Autobiography of Joseph Livesey

father_occupation: captain of a small trading vessel
father_raw: Son of a captain of a small trading vessel, who drowned before author’s birth.
career_raw: Apprentice rope-maker (c.1814-21); fisherman (one season); carpenter’s mate (1821); assistant to a cabinet-maker (from 1821); cabinet-maker (to 1828); opened a pastry and confectionery shop (1828); storekeeper of London Co-operative Trading Association (from 1829); ran a coffee-shop (1834-6); arrested and imprisoned on charge of seditious libel (1839- 40); opened small bookseller’s shop in 1840; journalist; publisher of Howitt's Journal, schoolmaster.
affiliations_raw: Member, and later president, of Cabinet Makers’ Society; member of ‘The Liberals’, a mutual improvement club (c.1825); member of committee of London artisans which successfully promoted Friendly Societies Act of 1829; secretary of British Association for Promoting Co-operative Knowledge; member of Radical Reform Association; member of central committee of National Union of the Working Classes (to 1832); member of Grand National Consolidated Trades Union; founder and secretary of the London Working Men’s Association; member of Association of Working Men to Procure a Cheap and Honest Press (1836); secretary of National Chartist Convention (1 839); declined to join National Charter Association and founded instead the National Association for Promoting the Political and Social Improvement of the People; member of the Democratic Friends of all Nations (1844); active in the People’s League; delegate to Sturge’s Complete Suffrage Conference (1842); leader of ‘moral force’ Chartism; an ‘indefatigable pamphleteer’; little involved in politics from 1850, turning his attention to work connected with the school established by the National Association.
content_tone: A well-known work that provides a full account of the various reform activities and associations of the 1830s and 1840s by one of the most prominent leaders of the political Labour movement. Invaluable for any history of the agitation for an unstamped press and of the early years of the Chartist movement. Other subjects discussed include schooling; diet; superstitions; the policing of the Radical movement; workshop customs; unemployment and poverty; the Calthorpe Street affair (1833); and prison life. The narrative was written between 1840 and 1874. The 1967 edition omits the last 3 chapters of the original, covering Lovett’s educational plans and general reflections on society, the church and progress.
title: Life and Struggles of William Lovett In his Pursuit of Bread, Knowledge & Freedom, with some short Account of the different Associations he belonged to & of the Opinions he entertained

father_raw: Son of a rural postman who died when author was a student in his early ‘teens.
residences: Scotland and the Shetland Isles for much of his life, with some time spent in London
career_raw: Was for many years a reporter on local weekly newspapers in Clydebank, Ebbw Vale, Cupar-Fife, Forfar and Montrose; served in Royal Army Medical Corps (1914-20); editor of Montrose Review (1920-9); editor of Vox (1929-?); reporter; writer/poet; precision fitter; deck hand and first engineer in the merchant service; lecturer; in receipt of a Civil List Pension.
affiliations_raw: Town and parish councillor; member of Education Authority; magistrate; unsuccessful Communist Party parliamentary candidate; active in formation of the National Party of Scotland; author of many volumes of poetry.
content_tone: The first of a proposed 3-volume autobiography (volume 3 was to deal with domestic life and marriage, but was never published). Not a conventional life history, with only brief comments on early life and ancestry, dealing instead with his intellectual and aesthetic development.
title: Lucky Poet: A Self- Study in Literature and Political Ideas, Being the Autobiography of Hugh MacDiarmid

residences: Ireland before travelling to Scotland in 1905; ‘tramped’ throughout Scotland for 7 years; lived briefly in London before returning to Glasgow; was writing from Windsor in 1914; settled in California in 1924/5
career_raw: Farm-boy (from age 10); joined a gang of potato-pickers in Scotland in 1905; spent 7 years as a gang-labourer, tramp and railway navvy; entered journalism by having occasional articles published in various newspapers, with the life of the navvy as the usual theme; full-time journalist (1909/10-); became a successful and well-known professional novelist.
affiliations_raw: Member of Glasgow Socialist Party; wrote many poems, songs and articles about navvies’ lives; his many publications include Songs of a Navvy (1911); The Rat Pit (1913); Lanty Hanlon. A Comedy of Irish Life (1912).
content_tone: Most of the story is autobiographical, though MacGill asks us to make allowance ‘for the pen of the novelist’. Given this qualification we are provided with a moving account of a poor and hard childhood in Ireland at the end of the 19th century, followed by excellent descriptions and anecdotes of the life and work of a navvy. Other themes discussed include rural customs and superstitions; schooling; hiring fairs; diet; dress; courtship; poaching. The text is written in the first person but the author calls himself Dermod Flynn, and includes extensive use of dialogue and some songs and ballads. 6 editions (10,000 copies) were published in 15 days.
title: Children ofthe Dead End. The Autobiography of a Navvy

father_raw: Father a hand-loom weaver.
residences: Edinburgh; Paisley; Glasgow; Dundee; Perth; Dundee
career_raw: Started work at an early age in a Dundee cotton mill (for 4 years); taught hand-loom weaving by father; was forced out of work by the introduction of machines and subsequently made a living from his dramatic and poetical recitals and from the sale of his poetry.
affiliations_raw: Leisure time was spent reading and improving handwriting; amateur dramatic actor; famous poet, known for his distinctive style of verse; published first small book of songs and poems in 1878.
content_tone: A short narrative with only outline details of his early life and work, concentrating instead on his life as a poet. The text includes several samples of his very distinctive poetry and reviews of his public appearances.
title: The Authentic Autobiography of the Poet M'Gonagall. Written by Himself

residences: Glasgow (c
career_raw: Apprentice shoemaker (bound to various masters for short periods), but did not remain bound for full period; worked as a shoemaker for several years before setting up on own account.
affiliations_raw: Converted to Christianity. Convicted of murder and sentenced to death.
content_tone: An apparently genuine gallows confession ‘...taken from M’Kaen’s own mouth, in the tolbooth of Glasgow ... [in] as near his own words as possible ...’. The narrative tells of his early family and work life; courtship; adultery and the birth of an illegitimate child; drunkenness and fighting; delivering recruits to the army. Following this is a full account of the events leading up to the drowning of his mother, for which he was wrongly accused of murder, and of the circumstances of his own crime, with chilling details of the act of murder, his flight, capture and subsequent conviction. The author concludes with remarks on his ‘just’ sentence and extends his thanks to the magistrates and keepers for their ‘kindness and indulgence’. A rare volume of particular merit.
title: The Life of James M’Kaen, Shoemaker in Glasgow, who was executed at the Cross of Glasgow, on Wednesday the 25th Jan. 1797. For The Murder and Robbery of James Buchanan, the Lanark Carrier

father_raw: Son of a colliery clerk.
