residences: Foleshill (1856-70); Birmingham (1870-6); London (1876-87); Newcastle upon Tyne and Bolton (1887-9); London (1889-1901); New Zealand and Australia (1901-10); London (1910-)
career_raw: Started work as a boy on the colliery farm (aged 9); went down the mines at age 10 (to 1870); printer’s devil (1870); apprentice tool-maker (1870-6); dock clerk (1876-80); turner/engineer; propagandist/lecturer/organiser for Social Democratic Federation (1887- 9); first president of the Dockers’ Union (1890-3); appointed secretary of the Independent Labour Party in 1894; co-founder and president of the International Federation of Ship, Dock and River Workers; editor of the Industrial Syndicalist (1910-11); spent many years abroad and travelling; general secretary of the Amalgamated Society of Engineers (later the Amalgamated Engineering Union), 1919-21.
affiliations_raw: Supported at various times the doctrines of Malthusianism, vegetarianism and teetotalism; interested in astronomy; president of the Shakespeare Mutual Improvement Society; joined the Social Democratic Federation in 1885; treasurer of the John Burns Election Fund; one of the 7 Labour members on the 1891 Royal Commission on Labour; first secretary of the London Reform Union; unsuccessful parliamentary candidate; largely responsible for founding the Workers’ Union (1898); joined the British Socialist Party in 1916; founder-member of the British Communist Party; chairman of the National Minority Movement (1924-32).
content_tone: An important autobiography by a prominent trade unionist and communist with comments on his early work life, workmates and strike activity; the Nine Hours Movement; early socialist activities and portraits of fellow travellers in the SDF; the fight for the Eight Hour Day (1886-9); labour unrest and agitation in the 1880s and 1890s; the 1889 Dock Strike; ‘New Unionism’; the Labour movement and the Churches (1890-4); police brutality during the strikes of 1910/11; an account of his trial for incitement to mutiny (1912). The text, which says little of his home life or non-political activities, is divided into three sections with details of his life in the Southern Hemisphere interrupting the period spent at home and in Europe The narrative ends in 1912.
title: Tom Mann’s Memoirs

father_raw: Illegitimate son of Sally Marcroft and Richard Howarth, a weaver.
residences: Heywood (1822-44); Oldham (1844-7); Failsworth
career_raw: Began work at age 6 gathering dung from the turnpike road; at age 8 was employed in the cardroom and thirstle-room of cotton mill; assistant to cotton cloth fustian-cutter for a short time before returning to mill to work as a piecer (to age 16); apprentice machine-grinder (1838-43); journeyman grinder, timekeeper and foreman in machine-making works (to 1861); dentist (1861-).
affiliations_raw: Secretary of local branch of Machine Grinders’ Society; teetotaller; member of Rechabites and Oddfellows; helped to promote the Oldham Industrial Co-operative Society (1850) and the Oldham Building and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. (1858), of which he became a director and treasurer; regular contributor to Co-operative News, Oldham Chronicle, Oldham Standard; author of several works, including Sun Mill Company Limited: its commercial and social history from 1858 to 1877 (Oldham, 1877).
content_tone: An extremely interesting volume, in which the author provides a full family history before discussing his own life and experiences, resulting in a vivid picture of working-class life in Lancashire in the early decades of the 19th century. Marcroft discusses his early life and childhood spent in cellar dwellings, the poorhouse and the cotton mill and comments on the Peterloo Massacre; the silk weaving trade; harvest feasts; homes and housing; customs in the cotton mill; dress; diet; superstitions and schooling. The narrative is written, in the early stages, in the third person, but soon reverts to the more conventional first person.
title: The Marcroft Family

forename: Memoirs of a Printer's Devil; interspersed with Pleasing Recollections
father_raw: Son of a soldier and a needleworker.
residences: Lincolnshire, Lancashire and Nottingham
career_raw: Started work at a young age for a whip-cord maker; subsequently worked in a brick manufactory before becoming a printer’s devil.
affiliations_raw: Chorister; studied fine arts and mechanics in his spare time.
content_tone: The text makes no mention of work life and instead deals in a lively style with family history, courtship and travels. The volume concludes with a 10-point ‘Printer’s Devil’s Creed’.
title: Local Descriptions, and Anecdotes

father_raw: Father, a sailor and master of a sloop, died when author aged 5.
residences: Cromarty (1802-23) and subsequently lived and worked in Niddry, Cromarty, Inverness
career_raw: Bound apprentice to a stonemason for three years (1819-22); worked as a mason until c.1832; bank accountant (1832-40); editor of Witness (1840-); public lecturer (1852-).
affiliations_raw: Adherent of Church of Scotland and strong advocate of non-intervention; member of (cholera) Defence Association; keenly interested in the natural sciences and geology, attaching to his retirement home a museum of specimens collected from his explorations; supplemented income from bank by contributing to various periodicals; a prolific author with most of his publications related to geology and science.
content_tone: A detailed and finely-remembered autobiography covering Miller’s childhood; ancestry; schooling; leisure interests in geology and the natural sciences. The text also includes interesting comments and observations on cock-fighting; religious controversy; Scottish working-class life; strike activity among masons and the beginnings of combination and trade unionism; gypsies; Reform Bill agitation; seasonal and temporary employments. This is a classic tale of self-advancement through talent and perseverance, with the author achieving distinction in the areas of science and literature.
title: My Schools and Schoolmasters; or, the Story of My Education(Johnstone and Hunter, Edinburgh, 1854), pp.v,537. Other edns.:

residences: London from 1891
career_raw: Errand-boy to a publishing firm (1855); worked for short periods as a printer’s devil and shop-boy; enlisted in British Navy by deception when under age (1857) and was soon discharged; apprentice sailor on a collier brig; subsequently worked as a ship’s pilot, cook and steward before becoming a ship’s captain. Gave up his command in 1891, and employed as superintendent of the working of steamers in the London docks (1891-1905).
affiliations_raw: Smuggler.
content_tone: Early comments on schooling and religious training precede a lengthy account of experiences, work and adventures as a seaman, with some mention of his smuggling activities and the period spent in Australia while digging for gold. The narrative includes much dialogue.
title: From Ship's-Boy to Skipper. With Variations

father_raw: Youngest of 7 children of a police constable.
residences: London
career_raw: Errand-boy (1902), then, shop assistant; switchboard operator; minor journalist; circulation manager of the first official Labour paper, the Daily Citizen (1912-15); part-time secretary of London Labour Party (1915-47); after 1915, politics, as either organiser or MP, was his sole occupation. MP for Hackney South (1923-4; 1929-31; 1935-59).
affiliations_raw: Member of Brixton Discussion Forum as a youth; joined Independent Labour Party in 1907, transferred briefly to the Social Democratic Federation before rejoining the ILP; secretary of South West London Federation of ILP branches (1910); mayor of Hackney (1920-1); alderman (1921-5); member of LCC (1922-45), serving as its leader from 1934-40; Minister of Transport (1929-31); Minister of Supply (1940); Home Secretary and Minister of Home Security (1940-5); Lord President of the Council, Deputy Prime Minister and Leader of the House of Commons (1945-51); Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs (1951); appointed a life peer (1959); Privy Councillor; Companion of Honour; president of British Board of Film Censors (1960); author of Socialisation and Transport (1933); Looking Ahead (1943); How London is Governed (1949); The Peaceful Revolution (1949); Government and Parliament: a Survey from the Inside (1954).
content_tone: Although the narrative commences with comments on childhood, schooling and early occupations, this autobiography is essentially political, with a full account of Morrison’s participation in the Labour movement from his time as a socialist activist at the beginning of the century, through his parliamentary career (1929-59, with two breaks) to his acceptance of a life peerage in 1959. The text is interesting for the comments it makes on his relations with colleagues in the Labour Party, and is a useful if not entirely reliable source for an institutional history of Labour, the struggles for national political representation and local government activity.
title: Herbert Morrison. An Autobiography by Lord Morrison of Lambeth, PC, CH

father_raw: Youngest of 6 children of a tenant farmer.
residences: Deerness (1887-9); Bu (1889-95); Garth (1895-1901); Glasgow (1901-?); Fairport; London (1919-21); Prague; Germany; Italy; Austria (1921-4); Buckinghamshire (1924-5); France (1925-7); Sussex (1928-32); Hampstead (1932-5); St
career_raw: Office-boy and clerk in various commercial and shipbuilding offices (1901-1919); assistant on the journal New Age (1919-24); critic, author, translator and poet (1924-42); worked for the British Council in Edinburgh (1942-5), and then Director of its Institutes in Prague (1945-8) and Rome (1949-50); warden of Newbattle Abbey (1950-5); professor at Harvard University (1955-6).
affiliations_raw: Attracted to the philosophies of socialism and Nietzsche; member of the Clarion Scouts; member of the Independent Labour Party; active in the Guild Socialist movement; contributor to the New Age; awarded CBE in 1953.
content_tone: Muir’s autobiography is perhaps most notable for the contrast it makes between the idyllic rural surroundings of the Orkney Islands of the author’s childhood and the slum dwellings of Glasgow of his ‘wretched’ adolescence. Following this startling change and the rapid deaths of his parents and two of his brothers, Muir was forced to undergo psycho-analysis. Many of his dreams are recounted in the text.
title: The Story and the Fable: An Autobiography(George G. Harrap & Co. Ltd., London, 1940), pp.264. Portrait. Enlarged and revised edn., An Autobiography

father_raw: Eldest child of a carpenter (see above).
residences: Walhowe (1847-6); Aberdeen (1861-77); London (1877-1934)
career_raw: Herd-boy for 6 weeks in 1858; Head of English Department at Aberdeen Grammar School (1869-77); journalist; barrister, Middle Temple (1881); Professor of Roman Law at University College, London (1883-1925); professor of Jurisprudence at University College, London (1901-25); Dean of Faculty of Laws, University of London (1914-8); Deputy Professor of Roman-Dutch Law (1914-24).
affiliations_raw: Unsuccessful parliamentary candidate; examiner at Oxford University and elsewhere; Deputy Regius Professor of Civil Law, Oxford University (1915-19); president of Society of Public Teachers of Law (1916-17); senator of University of London (1921-4); published numerous educational works and translations.
content_tone: A dramatic tale of sharp upward mobility from humble herd-boy to international distinction as a scholar and translator. Although much of the volume tells of Murison’s schooling and career as an educationalist, the early sections deal with his ancestry and include some comments on dame and parish schooling and working-class dress. The volume also contains brief autobiographical reflections by his father (see separate entry).
title: Memoirs of 88 Years

career_raw: Combined schooling with hawking bread and cakes and working on a local milk round (from age 7); check-boy at engineering works (1901); apprentice engineer (1901-8); engineer (1908-18, and again in the late 1930s); suffered periods of unemployment and hardship but managed to secure an income from his political activities as a writer; lecturer; freelance journalist; editor of The Communist International and The Communist Review; representative of the Communist Party of Great Britain on the executive committee of the Communist International; general secretary of the Socialist League (1934-6); organiser of the People’s Front Propaganda Committee (1936). He returned to the engineering workshop when in his forties.
affiliations_raw: Sunday School superintendent; adherent of ‘Muscular Christianity’; local Primitive Methodist preacher; came increasingly to question Christian doctrines, which he eventually abandoned; joined Amalgamated Society of Engineers in 1910; secretary of Engineering Amalgamation Committee in Sheffield; representative on district committee of ASE: delegate to Sheffield Trades and Labour Council; secretary of Sheffield branch of Daily Herald League; member of executive committee of the Socialist Labour Party; unsuccessful parliamentary candidate on many occasions; representative at the Third International (1920); member of provisional executive committee of the Red International of Labour Unions; member of executive committee of CPGB; CP delegate to 4th Congress of the Communist International; resigned from the CPGB in 1932; member of executive committee of local branch of Labour Party; member of the Socialist League; founder-member of the People’s Front Propaganda Committee.
content_tone: An excellent, detailed account of the Labour and Socialist movements in the first half of the 20th century, with references to the rapid growth of trade unionism and syndicalism in the early decades of the century; the Dublin Lock-Out of 1913; the wartime Shop Stewards’ Movement and the Sheffield strike of 1916; the impact of the 1917 Russian Revolution on British socialism; the Khaki Election of 1918; the early struggles of the CPGB; Irish republicanism and the IRA; inter-war Labour and Communist politics; raids on CP head-quarters and imprisonment; the General Strike. Murphy also makes very interesting observations on post-revolutionary Russia, witnessing in person the various stages of economic policy and the internal struggles for power.
title: New Horizons

father_raw: Son of a farmer.
residences: Ysceifiog; lived with aunt and uncle at Mold (c
career_raw: Engaged by uncle as shepherd/farm-boy (aged 13); casual dock labourer; cooper; sawyer; apprenticed self to printer (2 years); miner; printer (1860-).
affiliations_raw: Keenly interested in music and skilled at setting musical type; chorister and choir leader; teetotaller.
content_tone: Among the many themes discussed are ancestry; dress; schooling; public executions; chapel life; childhood incidents; electioneering; local characters; rural discontent; public houses; policing; tramping. The narrative is incomplete as the author died while working on it.
title: ‘My Recollections and Life’, MS, pp.27

father_raw: 3rd of 5 children of a basket-maker.
residences: London, Cambridge and Brasted, Kent
career_raw: Apprentice and journeyman basket-weaver (1864-82); master basket-maker (1882-96), combined with literary work and foreign travel; teacher of Italian, Toynbee Hall (1892- 1901); assistant examiner in Italian to the Civil Service Commission (1918); professor of Italian, Cambridge University (1919-28). Accepted commission in 1903 to write “The Story of Venice’ (published as writing and publication of similar works.
affiliations_raw: Keen reader; chorister; contributed to and distributed the Republican; member of debating society, the Milton Conversational Class; member of the South Place Chapel Religious Society, later the South Place Ethical Society; lecturer for the Ethical movement; member of Secularist Club; member of English section of the German Socialist club in Soho (c.1880); vice-chairman of Education Committee and organiser of Toynbee Traveller’s Club; school manager; Liberal. Successful author.
content_tone: The early sections are useful for descriptions of life in the East End in the 1850s and 1860s, with comments on schooling, dress, diet, and conditions of work as a basket-maker. The latter sections deal with his intellectual and spiritual ‘vagrancy’, his literary pursuits and travels abroad, notably in Italy. Okey was eventually able to relegate basket-weaving to a recreation and, by becoming Professor of Italian at Cambridge University, offers his testimony to the work of the University Extension movement.
title: A Basketful of Memories. An Autobiographical Sketch(J.M. Dent & Sons Ltd., London, 1930), pp.viii,152. Illustrated.

residences: Newtown (1771-81); Stamford, Lincs (1781-6); London (1786-8); Manchester (1788-1797); Glasgow (1797-1800); New Lanark (1800-24); America (1824-9); London (1829-44); America (1844-7); London (1847-53); Sevenoaks, Kent (1853-8)
career_raw: Assistant to wholesaler (aged 9-10); apprentice to high-class linen draper (1781-5); assistant in a haberdashery (c.1786-9); entered into partnership making ‘mule’ spinning machines (at age 18); and on own account at age 19 running a small cotton-spinning establishment; manager of large cotton mill (1790-1794/5); entered into business partnership (1794/5), and became part proprietor, and ultimately sole manager of the New Lanark factory in 1797. Set up experimental community in America (1824-9). Returned to England to take active part in the working class movement, touring the country as a lecturer and attending union meetings. Was employed lecturing, writing and organising.
affiliations_raw: Committee member of Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society. Progressed from system of management based on paternalism and philanthropy to one based on Co-operative Socialism, attempting a utopian experiment in community organisation in America (1824-9). Unsuccessful parliamentary candidate in 1819 and 1820. Founder of the Institution of the Industrious Classes (1833) and the National Equitable Labour Exchange (1832-4); assisted in the launching of the Society for Promoting National Regeneration (1833); founded The Crisis (1832-4), and the New Moral World (1834-45). Published extensively, with a comprehensive guide to his works contained in J.F.C. Harrison, Robert Owen and the Owenites in Britain and America (1967). See also the autobiography by his son, Robert Dale Owen, Threading My Way. Twenty-seven years of Autobiography (1874).
content_tone: A full account of the life of the pioneer of Co-operative management up to his departure from New Lanark for America in 1824. Owen charts his rise from humble beginnings to successful businessman and manufacturer by the age of 19. Systems of management and organisation in the cotton industry are described in detail, with particular attention given to the reforms initiated at the celebrated New Lanark village and manufactory. Other themes include diet and courtship. The author refers to a proposed supplementary volume, but this never materialised owing to his death.
title: The Life of Robert Owen, written by himself. With selections from his writings and correspondence, vol.1, 2 parts [vol.2 not published]

residences: Struthers (1805-12); Maybole (1812-c
career_raw: Stable-boy (c.1815); farm-boy (1817); apprentice printer (1818-24); journeyman (1824-6); set up in business as a stationer and printer (1826-); co-proprietor of the Kilmarnock Chronicle (1831-2); Dublin correspondent for the Glasgow Liberator (1835); employed writing the letterpress and many of the biographies for Kay’s ‘Edinburgh Portraits’ (1837- 9); editor of the Ayr Observer (1839-46); subsequently supported himself by miscellaneous writing.
affiliations_raw: Contributor to Thomson’s Miscellany at age of 13; poet; participated in the struggle for the emancipation ofthe working classes between 1826 and 1834, but soon lost faith in the ability of that class to manage its own affairs; published widely, including History of the County of Ayr (Ayr, 1847); The Life and Poems of William Dunbar (Edinburgh, 1860); Origin of the Scots and the Scottish Language (Edinburgh, 1855).
content_tone: Full details of the author’s life and work are regularly broken up by sketches of people, places and events, with recollections of local characters; pedlars; packmen; lunatics; beggars; Irish; radical politics, 1819-20; leisure; Chartism; policing. The narrative also includes extracts of verse written by the author.
title: Autobiographical Reminiscences: including Recollections of the Radical Years, 1819-20, in Kilmarnock; the First Election for the Kilmarnock Burghs, 1832; Kay's Edinburgh Portraits - how they were got up in 1837-9

father_raw: Deserted by father (master baker) before he was aged 2.
residences: Aberdeen and Glasgow for most of his life before moving to London in 1924
career_raw: First job was in a newspaper office, nominally attached to the composing room (1899); apprentice compositor (1900-?), but sacked from this work; worked briefly in a drapery warehouse before becoming an apprentice baker; abandoned this trade by age of 16 to work as a lather-boy in a barber’s shop and remained in this trade for most of the period up to 1919, though interrupted by spells selling false teeth and as a milkman; Northern organiser for the Independent Labour Party (1919), becoming the Scottish organiser (1920-4) and the national organiser in 1924; general secretary of the ILP (1927-33); editor of the New Leader and the Penal Reformer; MP (Lab) for Norwich (1945-64).
affiliations_raw: Had a passion for athletics (as ‘protection against practical [sexual] experiment’); became influenced by the writings of Robert Blatchford and the Clarion; joined the Clarion Club; member of the Shop Assistants’ Union; long-serving member of the ILP, though leaving briefly to form the Glasgow Anarchist Group and permanently in 1933 over his opposition to what he regarded as its pro-Communist policies; member of Institute of Trichologists; member of Aberdeen School Board; honorary secretary of the Aberdeen ILP and the Northern Federation; unsuccessful parliamentary candidate (1922, 1923); secretary of the International Committee of Independent Revolutionary Socialist Parties; author of Wealth, Work and Wages [1929].
content_tone: A well-written and absorbing description of a ‘rough ... but healthy and colourful’ childhood, of his work life and of his growing involvement in the Labour movement. Marvellously detailed descriptions are given of the house/shop; the ‘vicious circle’ of working-class poverty, from pawnshop to pay-packet; dress; schooling; awakening sexual awareness and adventures; ‘flitting’; tenement life; street ‘parading’; gambling; the work and sharp practices of the barber and milkman; and with an introduction to the activities and membership of the ILP. The volume ends in 1919 with the author abandoning his trade as a barber to become a full-time organiser of the ILP. A profitable and enjoyable volume.
title: Proletarian Pilgrimage. An Autobiography

father_raw: Father a stay-maker, variously running his own small business and employed in a stay factory.
residences: London (1831-6); St
career_raw: Took work to domestic workers for mother, who was acting as a ‘middlewoman’ (1843); errand-boy and general assistant in father’s stay workshop; cutter in a stay factory (1853-7)
affiliations_raw: Had a ‘strange fascination’ for books; poet and essayist; regular correspondent to newspapers and periodicals on wide variety of topics; had printed anti-trade union tracts; published miscellaneous other works, including Our Colonies: being an essay on the advantages accruing to the British Nation from its possession of the Colonies (1864); Strikes: their causes and their evils; especially with regard to the machine question in Northamptonshire, Staffordshire, and other places (1859); Reduction of the Hours of Labour, as proposed by the Nine Hours Movement. A Reply to the prize essay of the United Building Trades (1859).
content_tone: A concise account of the author’s life and literary interests, though perhaps most interesting for his anti-trade unionist writings, prompted by the exclusion of his brother from the shoemaking trade in Kettering by closed shop practices. One result of this heated local dispute was that an effigy of the author was burnt, his infirmity (deafness) ‘cruelly caricatured’, and his life threatened.
title: ‘An Autobiographical Sketch of the Author’s Life’, in his Songs of Labour. Northamptonshire Rambles and other Poems(W. Tweedie, London; Thomas Waddington, Kettering; 1860), pp.ix-xxxiv.

residences: Fleetwood all his life
career_raw: Started work in a ropewalk (1870-86); casual dock labourer, employed by the Railway Company, and later a checker.
affiliations_raw: Wrote articles for the Fleetwood Chronicle; very interested in local history; walked miles exploring the Fylde.
content_tone: Written in 1928, the narrative gives only brief details of the author’s life and is rather a history of Fleetwood in the second half of the 19th century. Porter describes places; trades; events (floods; shipping disasters; 1868 election); leisure (Sunday School excursion; visit of the circus); and dock life (wages; hours; fishing industry; dock construction).
title: ‘Recollections of Fleetwood. By a Native’, TS, pp.35

father_raw: 2nd son of an engineer working in a paper mill.
residences: many different places, leading an itinerant way of life
career_raw: Sent to work at the paper mill at an early age; bound apprentice to father (aged 16); ‘tramping’; employed in flour mill at Watford; in business for a short time selling groceries and Italian wares; returned to work as an engineer; worked for one year for the London and North Western Railway Company at the Wolverton Works; employed shaping iron at the Canada Works, near Birkenhead; rented a shop and started in business as a bookseller, but soon forced to return to his trade; obtained small income by publishing books, selling verse and lecturing; employed at Crewe Railway Works and then at Brighton as a turner; proprietor of short-lived monthly periodical, Powell’s Domestic Magazine; opened a small shop for the sale of periodicals and newspapers, but this came to a speedy end; started in the late 1850s/ early 1860s as a lecturer in Electro-Biology, or mesmerism.
affiliations_raw: Occupied youthful leisure time by reading, drawing, painting; member of Amalgamated Society of Engineers; member of Mechanics’ Institute; author of various works, including Phases of Thought and Feeling. Poems and Lyrics (1857); Spiritualism, its facts and phases (1864); Woman, at home and abroad: a glance at her domestic and social condition (Brighton, [1861]). See also The Village Bridal ... with a fragment of autobiography (1854).
content_tone: Plagued throughout his early life by a weak constitution and recurrent illness, Powell tells a story of childhood hardships and deprivations; ‘tramping’; unemployment; temporary work; deaths; poverty. A major part of the narrative is given over to an account of his migratory life as a lecturer in Electro-Biology, or mesmerism. Other topics covered include anecdotes of childhood; descriptions of his various jobs in a paper mill (mid 1840s); the Engineers’ Lock-Out.
title: ‘Life Incidents, in Life Incidents and Poetic Pictures

father_raw: Son of a hosier and lace manufacturer who lost his trade and was bankrupted through his agitation for political reform, but later set up as a newspaper printer and publisher of political tracts.
residences: Nottingham (1808-9); Birmingham (1809-22); Leicester (1822-6); Nottingham (1826-?); New Lenton, near Nottingham (?-1839); Birmingham (1839-)
career_raw: Started work in father’s printing office (1819-22); apprenticed to uncle as a hosier (1822- 29?); shopman/bookseller’s assistant (18292-39); editor of the Birmingham Advertiser (1839- 46?); set up in business as a printer and bookseller (1846?-58); minister (1858-).
affiliations_raw: Wrote poetry, having his works published in local newspapers and by subscription; Dissenting local preacher; Conservative; wrote leader articles for a Leicestershire newspaper while working as a shopman; assisted in founding a Protestant Association and a Church of England Young Men’s Association.
content_tone: The story of the author’s battle against his humble origins and the Republican and ‘Infidel’ teachings and influence of his father, to achieve a position of ‘eminence and honour’ as a literary writer and devout Christian. The text, which includes extracts of his poetry, tells of his conversion, the state of the lace-making trade, and includes comments on social ordering and Birmingham Chartism.
title: God’s Dealings with an Infidel; or, Grace Triumphant: being the Autobiography of Thomas Ragg, author of ‘Creation’s Testimony to its God

father_raw: Son of a carpenter.
residences: Bath (1889-1906; 1907- 11); Weymouth (1906-7); Bournemouth; Bristol; Torquay; Wallasey; St
career_raw: Pupil-teacher (1904-7); second-hand bookseller (1907-11); teacher for the International Correspondence Schools (1911-16); served in Artists’ Rifles OTC (1916-19); journalist; newspaper director; postal censor (1939-42). MP (Ind), Wallasey (1942-5).
affiliations_raw: Member of Wallasey Borough Council (1922-50); mayor (1936-7); JP (for 20 years); Juvenile Court magistrate (for 13 years). Published various booklets on education.
content_tone: Brief mention is made of the author’s schooling and pupil-teacher training, but otherwise the narrative is located in the 20th century and is concerned with Reakes’ political life as local councillor, mayor, magistrate and MP.
title: Man of the Mersey

father_raw: Born 1875 in London, the illegitimate son of a draper.
residences: London; Nottingham; Leicester; Coventry; London suburb (1895-6); Huddersfield (1896); Stockport; Halifax; Manchester (1898-)
career_raw: Apprentice assistant in draper’s shop (1889); remained a shop assistant until 1898 when he became a storekeeper for the Manchester Vegetarian Society; minor commercial traveller; money-lender’s clerk; desk clerk at Manchester Co-operative Wholesale Society, becoming sub-editor and then managing editor of that society’s publications, and its historian (to 1938).
affiliations_raw: Labour Church speaker; secretary of Manchester Tolstoy Society; member of Shop Assistants’ Union, the Social Democratic Federation and the Independent Labour Party; contributed verses to Justice. Author of various works including Tolstoy: a study (1907); The Story of the C.W.S.(1913); Co-operation for All (Manchester, 1914); John T. W. Mitchell (Manchester, 1923).
content_tone: Redfern bares his philosophical, theosophical and political soul in a staccato style that inhibits easy reading. An outline of the author’s life can be extracted from various parts of the text, but personal details are few.
title: Journey to Understanding, with a foreword by Albert Mansbridge

residences: Castle Eaton (1777-1822); Highworth (1822-7)
career_raw: First job was assisting mother and sisters in spinning and carding wool; general and agricultural labourer (living-in from age 16); skilled rickmaker and thatcher; carpenter and ‘wheeller’; gamekeeper (c.1797); land-surveyor; set up shop as printer, and later (1822) as druggist, printer, stationer, bookseller, bookbinder, music seller; ‘Patent Medecine Vender’; dealer in general provisions. He also sold harp strings and performed veterinary services.
affiliations_raw: Chorister (1793-death). Read medical guide when confined to bed (1799) and became the unqualified parish doctor; set up own (illegal) malt kiln (c.1794); made and sold musical instruments; master of first musical band in the neighbourhood.
content_tone: An interesting narrative with comments on schooling; canal-building and navvies; illegal brewing; poaching and Game Laws; agricultural labouring (late 18th/early 19th centuries). Written in a simple style with little regard for conventional punctuation and spelling. The published transcript was annotated by Rev. J. A. Harrison, and contains additional notes by K. H. Rogers.
title: ‘Notes on the Life of Joseph Ricketts, Written by Himself, c.1858‘, Wiltshire Archaeological and Natural History Magazine, Vol. 60, 1965, pp.120-6. MS in Devizes Museum Library.

residences: various places in Scotland, including Langshawburn; Capplefoot; Deloraine; Glencotho, but eventually settled at Teviothead in 1831
career_raw: Started work as a cowherd and shepherd at early age, working the summer months and attending school in the winter; became a licentiate of the Church of Scotland in 1830 and the incumbent of Caerlanrig Chapel in 1833; confined to Crichton Royal Institution, Dumfries, for insanity (1841-4); on his discharge he led the life of a recluse, interrupted only by occasional lecturing, and devoted himself to his literary work, maintained by an annual grant from the Duke of Buccleuch.
affiliations_raw: Honorary member of Border Counties Association (1866); published widely in periodicals on religious and agricultural matters, and lived to see many of his poems appear in print.
content_tone: Riddell wrote his autobiography in 1854, and this version is abridged from Dr. Roger’s “Modern Scottish Minstrel’. Beginning as a shepherd/poet, the narrative tells of his move to secure a good education and eventual entry into the ministry.
title: Autobiography, in The Poetical Works of Henry Scott Riddell, edited with a memoir by James Brydon

father_raw: 4th of 11 children of a tenant farmer.
residences: Cwmcammas; Bala (1847- 9); Anglesey; Castle Caereinion; Llanflechid (1853); Amlwch; Ruthin (1855); Bala (1860); Rug, near Corwen; emigrated to Australia in 1861; returned to Wales in 1875, and lived in Bettws; Isle of Man (1879); Wolverhampton (1879-c
career_raw: Farm-boy (farmer’s ‘drudge’); porter; schoolteacher; private tutor; ordained deacon (1859); compelled to give up curacy in 1861; returned to Wales to work as a private tutor and teacher.
affiliations_raw: Outstanding, though unrecognised, Welsh scholar; leader writer for the Gwalia; keenly interested in lexicography.
content_tone: A detailed and descriptive portrait of social and religious life in mid-19th century Wales, with an interesting account of the economic conditions of Welsh hill farmers in the ‘Hungry Forties’ and of the struggle for education. The narrative ends in 1863, when the author landed in Australia. The text includes a good deal of dialogue. The editor claims that much of the material in the early chapters is a reconstruction, drawing a ‘typical’ picture of the social and economic life of the time.
title: The Life and Opinions of Robert Roberts, A Wandering Scholar, as told by Himself, edited with an introduction by J. H. Davies

father_raw: Father a sailor, linen draper’s assistant, dock labourer.
residences: East London to 1901, then moved to New Cross, London
career_raw: Errand-boy (1856); sandwich-boy; indoor work at firm of stationers (from 1860); vellum-binder (to 1884); commercial traveller for publishing firm (from 1884); returned to the workshop in 1887 as foreman of department of Co-operative Printing Society. Was unemployed for a couple of years in the 1880s, when he worked part-time as ‘hack’ writer for the Press and ‘hack’ for the Liberal Party.
affiliations_raw: Early life marked by constant spinal trouble; co-secretary of the University Extension movement in East London; involved in London School Board in its early years, as school manager and election worker; elected non-resident associate of Toynbee Hall in 1886, serving on its Education Committee from 1890-8; vice-president of Elizabethan Literary Society (1886-1915); active journalist, contributing articles to many journals and papers, including the Weekly Dispatch and Pall Mall Gazette; converted to Anglo-Catholicism in 1890s; member ofthe Vellum Binders’ Trade Society from 1873 (later, amalgamated to form National Union of Bookbinders and Machine Rulers), and president of the society (1892-8); delegate to TUC (1892, 1895-8); secretary of National Committee of Organised Labour for the achievement of old age pensions; member of executive committee of London Trades Council (1901, 1903); organising secretary of National Committee of Organised Labour (1899); present at founding conference of Labour Representation Committee (1900), being elected as its first chairman and subsequently as an executive committee member and treasurer; accepted Conservative nomination as alderman of LCC (1910-11). Published large number of books and pamphlets, including James Allanson Picton. A Biographical Sketch (1883); The Art of Bookbinding (1894); The Church in the Modern State (1914).
content_tone: The text begins with early memories of life in the East End of London, with interesting recollections of Fairlop Friday; a prostitute’s funeral; a public execution; street-sellers; ‘low’ public houses and ‘cheap’ theatres. Afflicted by ill-health as a youth, Rogers developed a keen taste for drama and literature which he was to retain throughout his life and which is evidenced by many passages in the text. Much of the narrative is given over to detailing his interest and activities on behalf of popular education; workmen’s clubs; the University Extension movement; women’s trade unionism. Other topics discussed include Ireland; the Co-operative movement; the bookbinders’ strike of 1891-2; old age pensions; ‘New Unionism’. Many of the chapters first appeared in serial form in the Anglo-Catholic Treasury.
title: Labour, Life and Literature. Some Memories of Sixty Years

residences: London, St
career_raw: First job was as a telegraph messenger (aged 13 - 14 1/2), then ‘fiddled about at various jobs’ until apprenticed to local printer. Released from apprenticeship at age 19 but remained in the printing industry, except for period of military service (1914-19), in various capacities including compositor; editorial proof-reader; freelance journalist and writer; London correspondent for Newspaper News (for 14 years) and editorial work.
affiliations_raw: Member of Typographical Association (from age 21) and of the Independent Labour Party. Published articles in various journals and wrote detective short stories for a ‘popular’ journal.
content_tone: The early part of the narrative tells of a poor childhood, with valuable comments on domestic budgeting; Saturday working (for 14 hours at a local greengrocer’s shop); childhood leisure activities such as ‘penny readings’, music hall and boys’ magazines; and Boer War celebrations. However, the author soon entered the printing trade and from then on the memoirs are exclusively given over to full descriptions of work and personalities in that trade. Personal details are lacking, except for a brief anecdote on his disability (artificial limbs), in favour of what becomes a potted history of the print trade, with chapters on the ‘tramping’ printer, the jargon of the industry, profiles of trade union leaders and a survey of print trade unionism. Written in 1968.
title: ‘Chaps among the Caps’, TS, pp.210

career_raw: Employed in wide variety of unskilled jobs from age 11/12, including in a printer’s; for a money-lender; as a newspaper boy; errand-boy; street-seller; general and day nurse; motor-van boy; roundsman. Enlisted in the cavalry in 1909, serving until 1917. Resumed unskilled employments after 1917, as an indoor messenger, storekeeper and clerk. Obtained skilled work, by deception, as a tool- and gauge-maker. Subsequently worked as a coach-builder, postman and salesman.
affiliations_raw: Wrote stories, many published in newspapers and periodicals.
content_tone: The narrative commences in 1902 and is essentially a descriptive list of his many employments. Royce had a clear preference for story-telling and the text relies heavily on anecdotal adventures, incidental detail and dialogue.
title: 7 Stand Nude

father_raw: Both parents were of Irish extraction, and worked as hawkers and umbrella-menders.
residences: Newcastle upon Tyne (1856-7); St
career_raw: First employment was punching holes in clog irons (for 1 week), followed by a job at the local glass works. Stowed away on a sailing ship (1868) and became a sailor; laboured at a chemical factory (for 3 years); returned to the sea (until 1877); casual dock labourer, but was marked out as an agitator and found it difficult to find employment. Worked for a short time as a steamship painter before beginning own business, running a coalyard, with donkey and cart. MP for St. Helens (1918-31).
affiliations_raw: Member of Liverpool branch of American Knights of Labour; president of local Home Rule organisation; one of the first members of the National Union of Dock Labourers (1889); general secretary of same union (1893-1922); founder-member of the Independent Labour Party; elected to city council (1905); member of parliamentary committee of TUC (1900-5; 1907; 1909-21); member of management committee of Ruskin College; member of General Council of TUC (from 1923). Appointed CBE (1917), and later knighted (1931). Contributed articles to various periodicals, Unionist, and Workman’s Times. Including Seaman’s Gazette; Clarion; Trade Unionist, and Workman´s Times.
content_tone: A full autobiography by one actively involved in the early struggles for organistion among dock workers and for the formation of an independent Labour Party. The narrative begins with a good account of domestic circumstances and (slum) living conditions, and then provides interesting details of his time as a sailor and dock labourer, with valuable observations on job demarcation - or ‘the caste system’ - in operation on the docks. The dock workers’ strike of 1889 and the seamen’s strike of 1911 are given much attention, with anecdotes of people and events. Profiles are provided of the leading Labour activists of the time, including T. P. O’Connor, Bernard Shaw, Bob Smillie, Keir Hardie, James Larkin and others. Sexton was also active in the Home Rule agitation and part of the narrative deals with the Irish Republican Brotherhood (Fenians) and its fluctuating fortunes in England.
title: Sir James Sexton, Agitator. The Life of the Dockers’ MP. An Autobiography, with a preface by the Rt. Hon. David Lloyd George, MP

father_raw: Son of a painter and gilder.
residences: Tunstall during his early life
career_raw: Started work as a ‘mould runner’ for a ‘muffin-maker’ in a pot works (aged 7); handle-maker in pot works (aged 8-10); toy-maker at manufactory in Burslem (1842-?); local preacher for the Methodist New Connexion church; spent some years running a cotton-spinning business before returning to work for the church; leader-writer for the radical Oldham Express. Retired in 1904.
affiliations_raw: Strong supporter of the Liberal Party; member of Mutual Improvement Society.
content_tone: An excellent and moving account of life, work and conditions in the Potteries in the 1830s and 1840s. Full descriptions are given of child, female and adult labour in the pot works, including workshop practices; Saint Monday; wages and methods of payment; and with comments on the absence of radicalism among pottery workers. Strike activity and the beginnings of trade unionism among neighbouring colliery workers is detailed, with an account of the reform agitation of 1831-2, and of the Chartist demonstrations and riot in Burslem (1842). Shaw also provides good detail of home and village life, with observations on poverty; schooling; diet; dress; superstitions; leisure (Wakes; beershops; horseplay; dog- and cock-fighting); policing; village ‘idiots’; religion. Arnold Bennett used an almost verbatim transciption of the account of Shaw’s workhouse experience in his novel Clayhanger.
title: When I Was a Child, by An Old Potter, with an introduction by Robert Spence Watson

father_raw: 6th child of 8 of an electro-plate polisher.
residences: Birmingham (1884-90); Leicester (1890-2); Birmingham/Erdington Workhouse (1892-4); London (1894-8); various farms near to Llandovery (1898-1904); Llandebie (1904-27); London and Scotland (1927); Llandebie (1928-37); London (1937); Midlands (1837-40)
career_raw: Domestic poverty caused author to work at early age in ‘sweated’ trade of carding hooks and eyes and also as a street-seller of matches (aged 8); committed to Industrial School for street-trading, where he trained as a tailor; served out his sentence on a farm in Wales (1898- 1900); farm-boy (1900-4); miner’s assistant (1904-6), and a full collier within two years (to 1925); made a living from writing and propaganda work; employed by a ‘big London organisation’ as a lecturer (1927); book salesman (1931-4); soap-box orator (1937-).
affiliations_raw: Local correspondent for South Wales Daily Post; member of Church Defence League; Conservative; active anti-socialist, engaged in street corner oratory and propaganda work.
content_tone: Very interesting detail is provided of the various stages of the author’s life, with good descriptions of childhood hardships; dress; schooling; youthful escapades; street life; time spent in an Industrial School; farm labour; courtship; religious and chapel life; work and conditions in South Wales coal mines; unofficial strikes; General Strike (’crazy business’). Valuable comment is also provided on the attitudes and activities of a collier and fervent anti-socialist. The text includes much dialogue and some dialect.
title: Guttersnipe, with a forword by Bertrand Watson

career_raw: Printer’s devil (1817-18); apprentice printer (1819-26); journeyman printer/compositor, and eventually a printer’s reader, though periodically leaving the trade to work as an English tutor to the Parisian middle classes (1828); teacher/usher at grammar school (1834-5). No detail is provided of his career after 1840, though he derived some income from his various publications.
affiliations_raw: Read widely, and taught himself various foreign languages; member of Mutual Improvement Society; played the fiddle; published vignettes of working-class life in London, which appeared first in periodicals and later as books, including Curiosities of London Life: or, Phases Physiological and Social, of the Great Metropolis (1853); The Little World of London; or, Pictures in Little of London Life (1857).
content_tone: Written at the suggestion of the proprietor of Tait’s Edinburgh Magazine, Smith’s narrative of his life and opinions falls firmly into the tradition of the ‘respectable’ artisan. Although suffering from periodic unemployment the author never abandons his adherence to ‘honest and decent’ principles and roundly condemns his ‘tramping’ workmates (‘...a tide of lazy and filthy vagabonds) and also any radical political activity, notably the Bristol Riots of 1831 ('mob’; ‘drunken riot’; ‘frolic’; ‘disgraceful atrocities’). Nevertheless, a very good account is provided of conditions operating in the print trade in the 1830s, with comments on seasonal unemployment, methods of payment and trade customs (’weigh-goose’; wedding ceremonies; ‘footing’). His time working as a printer and teacher in France is recalled in fine detail, including his personal experience of the 1830 revolution, and comments are also offered on smuggling and public executions. The reminiscences cover the period from about 1818 to 1840.
title: The Working Man's Way in the World: being the Autobiography of a Journeyman Printer

father_raw: 2nd daughter and 4th child of a boot- and shoemaker.
residences: Cropredy (1822-42); Brough, Westmorland (1842-7); Carlisle; Scotby (for some years about 1848); Carlisle; for a short time at Richmond and Twickenham when in her sixties, before returning to Carlisle
career_raw: Managed, with her brother, a grocery and provision shop; housekeeper/nursemaid/governess (1842-), combined with school teaching; set up her own school in 1852.
affiliations_raw: Adopted a spiritual way of life when in her twenties, and would have entered the Nonconformist ministry if she had been a man; disciple of the principles of self-help; published two volumes of poetry; contributed articles and verse to various periodicals and newspapers including the People’s Journal, the Observer, the Carlisle Express; spoke publicly in support of the Married Women’s Property Bill.
content_tone: Although concerned chiefly with her work and religious life, the narrative also includes some comment on family life; romance and courtship; dress (contrasts between the north and south); impressions of northern England; the Great Exhibition of 1851. The text is perhaps most useful, however, for observations on education, schooling and Nonconformity.
title: The Autobiography of Mary Smith, Schoolmistress and Nonconformist, A Fragment of a Life. With Letters from Jane Welsh Carlyle and Thomas Carlyle

father_raw: Father a lime-kiln worker and farm labourer.
career_raw: Variously employed as farm labourer (c.1823); lime-kiln worker; wood sawyer (1827); drain-digger; stone quarry worker; soldier (1831); shopkeeper (1833); journalist.
affiliations_raw: Joined the Royal North British Dragoons, 1831. Was court-martialled for writing to the press about support from the soldiers for the Birmingham Political Union and for his comments on the role of the military in quelling popular demonstrations. Became a cause celebre of the Reform movement. Moved into journalism and publishing and became Cobden’s adviser on agricultural subjects. Publications include the volume on agriculture, The Whistler at the Plough (Manchester, 1852), and the anti-Chartist pamphlet, Public and Personal Affairs (1839).
content_tone: The autobiography comprises three main themes, opening with an affectionate and descriptive account of growing up in rural poverty in Berwickshire and including much detail on the temporary, seasonal nature of agricultural employment and on working-class customs generally. This is followed by a large section on Somerville’s time with the Scots Greys, leading to his court martial for political activity during the 1832 Reform Bill crisis, and his subsequent flogging, which became a cause celebre. His politics took on an increasingly conservative tone, evidenced by his comments on London’s first major trade union demonstration (1834), and on the Owenites and Chartists.
title: The Autobiography of a Working Man, by ‘One who has whistled at the plough’

father_raw: Father a manager of firm of tobacco and cigar manufacturers.
residences: various parts of London all his life
career_raw: ‘Learner’ at sawmills (1856-61); apprentice carpenter and joiner (1861-4); worked in partnership in business; saw-operator and general superintendent at sawmill; manager of sawmill; proprietor of weekly newspaper, The Radical (1881-2); deputy manager of sawmill(1882-?); speaker for the Free Trade Union (1903-14).
affiliations_raw: Teetotaller (from age 15); member of Bermondsey Council; chairman of General Purposes Comittee secretary of Radical Association in Southwark.
content_tone: Although born into the middle-classes, the death of his parents forced Soutter to enter employment from the age of 12. He became actively involved in the Labour movement at an early age and much space is given to accounts of the attempts to secure local and national Labour representation, including the election attempt of George Odger (1869). Detail is provided of his endeavours to abolish Church Rate and Rector’s Rate, to expose the abuses of the Vestry system of local government (Bermondsey Rioters, 1889), and of his support for the movements for Women’s Rights and Irish Home Rule.
title: Recollections of a Labour Pioneer, with an introduction by T. P. O’Connor, MP

residences: Swindon (1872-91); Isleworth (1892-4); Nottingham (1894); Plumstead (1894-9); London (1899-1912); Liverpool (1912-23); London (1923-)
career_raw: Pupil-teacher and part-time library assistant (1886-91); teacher (1894-99); worked with Sidney and Beatrice Webb, researching into British Local Government (1899-1903, full- time), combined with some teaching and journalism (1903-5); head of Day Department at City of London College (1906-12); HM Inspector of Schools (1912-22); Chief Inspector under the London Education Committee, from 1922 until retirement in 1933.
affiliations_raw: Social life, as a child, revolved around the Sunday School; a ‘blue ribbonite’ at the Band of Hope; member of Sandford Institute; Nonconformist; St. Young Men’s Society; regular visitor to Mechanics’ Liberal, though later becoming a Fabian.
content_tone: One of the last pupil-teachers, Spencer’s narrative provides a full and entertaining account of all aspects of schooling and education, from his time at dame school to his post as an HMI. He begins his story of escape from poverty and ‘the factory’ with detailed descriptions of his native town (Swindon), home, family and ancestry.
title: An Inspector's Testament

father_raw: 4th child of 7 of a gardener.
residences: Cardiff to the age of 22, then Bradford (3 1/2 years); Manchester (1915-31); London (1931-9); Falmouth (1939-)
career_raw: Butcher’s errand-boy (aged 12); office-boy (aged 12); messenger-boy for a Cardiff newspaper, then journalist (aged 13-22); journalist for the Yorkshire Observer (aged 22- 25/6), the Manchester Guardian (for 15 years); employed by the Beaverbrook Press (1931-).
affiliations_raw: Interested in reading and writing; novelist, works including Shabby Tiger (1934); O Absalom! (1938); Fame is the Spur (1940).
content_tone: Reminiscences of the author’s early years, with descriptions of the home; schooling; childhood games; Sunday School; home life; social life and holidays. Names in the text have been altered.
title: Heaven Lies About Us: A Fragment of Infancy, with drawings byGill Lancaster

father_raw: Son of an iron-moulder.
career_raw: Left school at age 13 to work in a newspaper office; moved from there to a glass works; served his time as a moulder; then employed by a magazine and newspaper combine.
affiliations_raw: Interested in reading and writing; author of several novels, including Return at Dusk (1947); Slum [1934]; Violence [1933]. Active trade unionist.
content_tone: A finely-remembered account of the author’s infant and childhood years, with much emphasis placed on recording the amusing incident and anecdote. The text does, however, contain interesting comments on working-class life in Lancashire in the 1880s and 1890s, with observations on dress, the home, diet, play and leisure. The narrative ends with the author still at school.
title: So Long Ago...

residences: Denbigh (1841-7); St
career_raw: Given employment by cousin as a pupil-teacher at Brynford (1856); assisted aunt who kept a farm and an inn; assistant in haberdasher’s shop; butcher’s boy; cabin-boy; store assistant (in America, taking name of Henry Stanley from his employer and adopted father); fought in the American Civil War (1861-5); journalist and correspondent; established world-wide reputation as an explorer; lecturer; author; MP for N.Lambeth (1895-1900).
affiliations_raw: Perhaps best-known as the man who found David Livingstone, Stanley’s main activities were devoted to literary work and explorations of the ‘dark Continent’, earning titles and honorary conferments from a range of learned societies and institutions.
content_tone: A full account of the various stages of the author’s remarkable career, dealing largely with his time in America and his later explorations, but with an interesting opening section of his early struggles and exposure to the ‘brutal tyranny’ of a workhouse schoolmaster.
title: The Autobiography of Sir Henry Morton Stanley, edited with a preface by Dorothy Stanley

father_raw: 10th of 12 children of a farm foreman (from 1879, a carter) and a hand-loom weaver.
career_raw: Half-time ‘shifter’ in a jute mill (aged 10-13), combined with ‘chapping’ (i.e. knocking-up people for work); full-time mill worker (aged 13-16); apprentice joiner, becoming a journeyman c.1897; full-time organiser of the Scottish Prohibition Party and part-time editor of the Prohibitionist; full-time activist for the Prohibition and Reform Party (later, the Socialist Prohibition Fellowship); Scottish organiser for the British Communist Party (1921-).
affiliations_raw: Member of Independent Order of Good Templars, becoming the Chief Templar in Dundee; member of Amalgamated Society of Carpenters and Joiners; elected to Dundee Town Council in 1908; one of the founder-members of the Prohibition and Reform Party; author of political pamphlets; poet; unsuccessful parliamentary candidate; member of executive committee of the Communist International.
content_tone: The first section provides a most useful portrait of working-class life in Dundee in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with observations on family life and domestic struggles; diet; dress; tenement dwellings; schooling; child labour and mill work; the process of jute manufacture; employments; workshop customs; working hours and wages; Chinese labour; unemployment. The remainder of the narrative is concerned chiefly with his political activities and public life, providing good detail on the early 20th century Socialist movement. Among the themes covered are the anti-war movement; war-time industrial militancy and dilution; the internal workings and public and electoral activities of the Communist Party; the raid of the CP offices (1921); inter-war Labour governments; the Zinoviev letter; the General Strike. The illustrations include cartoons. The memoirs were dictated onto tape and then edited and prepared for publication by Dave and Elizabeth Bowman.
title: Breaking the Fetters: The Memoirs of Bob Stewart

residences: Manchester all his life
career_raw: Apprentice bookbinder (1827-34); journeyman (1834-).
affiliations_raw: Poet.
content_tone: Written in the third person, this (autobiographical?) preface provides only an outline sketch of the author’s life.
title: ‘Memoir’, in Songs for the Millions and other Poems. By Benjamin Stott, of Manchester, Bookbinder

father_raw: Son of a coal trimmer.
residences: Seaham Harbour (1861-81), then at Felling; Jarrow; South Shields; Hartlepool and Newcastle upon Tyne before settling in Sunderland
career_raw: ‘Weekend-boy’ in barber shop and errand-boy to a grocer (aged 12- 13); apprentice printer (1874-81); journeyman printer; journalist; started own printing business (1894); MP for Sunderland (1906-10).
affiliations_raw: Influenced by Smiles’ Self-Help and Blatchford’s Merrie England; came to socialism and the Independent Labour Party via Conservatism and Gladstonian Liberalism; member of Typographical Association; secretary to Sunderland Trades Council; helped to found Tyneside and National Labour Union (later, National Amalgamated Union of Labour); elected to Sunderland Borough Council (1892-1910); active member of Housing Reform Council, the Land Nationalisation Society and the Labour Information Bureau; secretary to the League of the Blind; author of Afforestation: the unemployed and the land (1908).
content_tone: A brief life history with little detail or comment.
title: ‘How IGot On: From Barber s Shop to Parliament’, Pearson’s Weekly, 22 March 1906.

career_raw: Started to earn own living at age 8 by selling newspapers, delivering milk and cleaning out herring boats; ran away to sea at age 12; assistant in pork butcher’s shop (aged 13); apprentice on a Swansea Copper Oresman (aged 14-18); enlisted in the army ( 1907); postman (c.1910); joined the British South Africa Police in 1912; employed in various occupations in South Africa (1919-22); travelling book salesman (1926), and subsequently employed as a salesman for miscellaneous items; was destitute and homeless in 1932 but by the following year was a successful author and soon to become a freelance journalist and broadcaster.
affiliations_raw: Author of various works including African Adventures [1949]; Dauniless Jock [1951]; My Friends the Beasts [1949].
content_tone: A lively and enjoyable work which offers a good portrayal of working-class life in Scotland in the late 19th century. Among the themes mentioned are overcrowding, diet, home life and marriage ceremonies. Similar detail is provided of the other main features of the authors life, including his South African adventures, war experiences, prison life and punishments. Dialogue is used extensively.
title: From à Glasgow Slum to Fleet Street with a foreword by Alvin Redman

father_raw: Son of a blacksmith and landlord of public house.
career_raw: Began employment as a newspaper-seller (at age 9), and then as grocer’s errand-boy before becoming apprenticed to a blacksmith; colliery blacksmith, subsequently working at the coal face; part proprietor at printing business; MP for Chester-le-Street (1906-19).
affiliations_raw: Primitive Methodist local preacher; secretary of Annfield Plain lodge of Durham Colliery Mechanics’ Association, being elected to its executive committee in 1882, and serving as treasurer (1891) and general secretary (1897-1923); member of Annfield Plain UDC (1899-1933, except for period in Westminster); pioneer of Independent Labour Party in Durham; member of Durham Education Committee and of Durham Mining Federation and Conciliation Boards; chairman of local Co-operative Society for 17 years.
content_tone: A brief life history with little detail or comment.
title: How I Got On’, Pearson’s Weekly, 3 May 1906.

career_raw: Errand-boy (1901); van-boy (1902); grocer’s boy (c.1902): oiler and greaser, then assistant brake fitter in carriage and wagon department of the Great Central Railway (1904-8); public orator, making a living from collections though also supplemented by begging; fortune-teller; quarryman in a conscientious objector’s camp in Aberdeen (c.1916-20); ‘quack’ doctor and birth-control advocate (1919-20); returned to platform as advocate of revolutionary socialism (c.1922/4); abandoned the open socialist platform to speak freelance and politically unattached (1926-).
affiliations_raw: Socialist; conscientious objector; member of Newcastle Clarion Dramatic Society; launched, with Harold Kelly, the short-lived Black Hat newspaper (1930).
content_tone: The story of a bohemian life as a tramp and public orator with the author turning to socialism and oratory as a means of escaping unremunerative labour. The narrative begins with recollections of childhood years in Ulster spent playing truant, bird-nesting and falling in love, and includes comments on religious influences; local characters; lunacy; religious mania; self-education and books; courtship. Thompson tells also of his trial for conspiracy in 1908, which achieved some national notoriety, his subsequent conviction for committing wilful and malicious damage aand imprisonment.
title: Hyde Park Orator, with a preface by Sean O’Casey

career_raw: Half-timer in cotton mill at age 10; errand-boy; worked in printing establishment and learned bookbinding; writer; novelist; script-writer; broadcaster.
affiliations_raw: Active member of trade union, serving on local committees, acting as local secretary and as member of national executives and of Joint Industrial Councils.
content_tone: Details of family, background and dates are mostly absent from this narrative.
title: Lancashirere for Me. A Little Autobiography

father_raw: 7th son and 14th child of father, and 4th of mother.
residences: Scotland all his life, chiefly in the region of Kilmarnock and New Cumnock
career_raw: Ploughboy and farm-boy (1835); ‘washer-off` in a tileworks (1838), becoming a moulder, tile-burner and assistant manager; in partnership with brother-in-law owning a brick and tile works at Dalquharran; started a successful literary and journalistic career in 1864 as a newspaper correspondent and author. Worked as a journalist for more than 60 years.
affiliations_raw: Author of volumes of poetry and novels, with his first book published in 1846; member of large debating society.
content_tone: The text commences with fond memories of a rural childhood, recalling schooling and in life and labour. Interesting observations are made on wages and conditions in a tileworks and on seasonal employments (tile-burning in summer, followed by harvest work in autumn). Other themes discussed include literature and reading matter; authors and authorship; literary life.
title: ‘Recollections of a Long Life’, in The Poetical Works of A. B. Todd with Autobiography and Portrait

residences: London when not travelling
career_raw: Clerk in a firm of manufacturers and traders (aged 13); journalist.
affiliations_raw: No details of interests or activities.
content_tone: Recollections of a childhood spent in the East End of London in the 1880s and 1890s precede lengthy anecdotes of his journalistic adventures and travels. An insubstantial work except for the opening sections.
title: A Mingled Yarn: Autobiographical Sketches

father_raw: 2nd son of hand-loom weavers, with a Luddite and Chartist ancestry.
residences: Holmfirth (1863-c
career_raw: Assistant to aunt and other domestic hand-loom weavers (aged 9 1/2); half-timer in the mill (aged 10-13); full-time mill worker (aged 13-); supplemented income during periods of unemployment by journalism for various radical newspapers, and as a drapery salesman and insurance agent; from 1889 was employed on the Yorkshire Factory Times and the Workman‘s Times; paid trade union official from 1922; MP for Dewsbury (1922-4, 1929-31).
affiliations_raw: Member of Mechanics’ Institute; member of Manchester Unity of Odafellöws; poet; active in the movement against compulsory vaccination; member of Leeds Socialist Party; joined the recently formed Weavers’ Union in 1882 (later, the General Union of Weavers and Textile Workers); appointed an officer in his union in 1889, serving as president (1902-22), and for the National Union of Textile Workers (formed from the amalgamation of 3 unions) from 1922-33; president of the National Association of Unions in the Textile Trade (1917-29); member of the Social Democratic Federation and of the Fabian Society; one of the founder-members of the Independent Labour Party; served for 17 years on the National Executive of the Labour Party; Parliamentary Secretary for Mines (1929-31); served on Batley Borough Council for 48 years; alderman; mayor; served on General Council of the TUC (1921-8), and as chairman (1927-8); president of TUC (1928); awarded OBE in 1917, CBE in 1930 and knighted in 1931.
content_tone: An important work by a pioneer of the Labour movement in Yorkshire. Among the many themes and topics discussed are ancestry; childhood memories; diet; dress; schooling; traditional songs (some in local dialect); child labour and mill work; domestic chores; childhood games and leisure; the ‘Shop Book’ (credit and thrift); the home. Apart from this many-sided look at working-class life in Yorkshire during the Cotton Famine and after, the narrative is also most valuable for its account of the early struggles of Labour in the district, with references to strikes and lock-outs (1872; 1883; 1925), 20th century Labour agitation and parliamentary activity.
title: About Myself, 1863-1930, with a foreword by the Rt. Hon. J. Ramsay MacDonald

father_raw: Son of an actor and actress.
residences: London and South Africa
career_raw: Worked at various jobs between the ages of 12 and 18, including a printer’s boy; newsboy; in a shoe shop; in a mackintosh cloth factory; on a Grimsby trawler; as a milk roundsman; road-maker; builder’s labourer; enlisted in the army when aged 18; later became a correspondent for Reuters and for the Daily Mail; editor of Rand Daily Mail (1902); returned to England and worked for the Daily Mail, established himself as a distinguished novelist, playwright and journalist.
affiliations_raw: Published poems and articles in various South African and British periodicals and newspapers; chairman of the Press Club (1923-5); one of the founder-members of the Company of Newspaper Makers; unsuccessful parliamentary candidate (1931); published more than 170 books, including The Four Just Men (1905); Bones (1915); The Crimson Circle (1922).
content_tone: A tale of upward mobility with recollections of childhood and schooling preceding a lengthy section on his time in South Africa.
title: People. A Short Autobiography

father_raw: 2nd of 8 children of a collier, later, a railway horse-keeper.
residences: Newhall, and for a short time at Derby and Wisbech; Keighley (1873-98)
career_raw: A Half-timer in woollen factory (1873-8); full-timer (1878-80); clerk at Midland Railway Company (1880-95); editor of Keighley Labour Journal (1893-7); editor of Railway Review (1897-1918); parliamentary secretary to Board of Trade, and later, Ministry of Labour (from 1917). Elected Labour MP for Stockport in 1906. Resigned his office and parliamentary seat in 1920 owing to ill-health.
affiliations_raw: Sunday School teacher and Methodist lay preacher in early manhood; member of Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants; served on executive of Labour Party (1913-19); following retirement, took active part in social life and charity work. Author of Problems of the Age and other Poems (1897); The Principles of Association (1914); À Railway Garland [poems] (1904); Railway Nationalisation (1908); ‘The Way to Industrial Unity’, in S. M. Watts (ed.), The Industrial Future in the Light of The Brotherhood Ideal (1919); evidence before Joint Commission on Railway Agreements and Amialgamations (1911).
content_tone: A short life history with brief comments on his passion for ‘reading and scribbling’ as a youth, and on the 1897 engineers’ strike.
title: How I Got On, Pearson’s Weekly, 22 Feb 1906.

career_raw: At age 12 was bound to clergyman as general servant, but indentures cancelled after 6 years owing to death of master’s wife; warehouseman at drysalter’s (c.1817-22); shopman to Mr. Carlile, and later manager of his business (1822-6), though interrupted by periods of imprisonment for selling liberal and freethinking literature; compositor (1826-8); manager of a co-operative store (1828-9); bookseller (1830); printer and publisher (1831-).
affiliations_raw: Adherent to principles of self-improvement; active in spreading radical literature and attending and leading meetings and discussions to agitate for the right of free discussion; active in the Co-operative movement; member of The National Union of the Working Classes (1831); led the agitation for an unstamped press; assisted in the formation of Working Men’s Associations (1836-8); helped to draw up the People’s Charter.
content_tone: A brief memoir by one of the best-known of the radical politicans of the early to mid-19th century who, alongside such men as G. J. Holyoake and Henry Hetherington, fought strenuously for the rights of organisation, free speech and representation for the working class. This account of struggles and clashes with the State leaves one regretting its brevity.
title: Autobiographical speech, The Reasoner

father_raw: Son of an agricultural labourer.
career_raw: Part-time errand-boy; garden-boy (1880); school monitor (1881); apprentice builder (1882), remaining in the same trade for the rest of his working life; clerk of works, supervising the erection of a spinning mill (1905); appointed first manager of Manchester Corporation Direct Works Department (1920-3), and then held the same post in Barnsley.
affiliations_raw: Member of minstrel group (1885); contributed to the Owl; joined the Operative Bricklayers’ Society in 1890, becoming branch president; delegate to Grimsby Trades Council; president of Stalybridge branch of OBS (1896); delegate to Ashton and District Trades Council; secretary of North-Western area of OBS (for 2 years); member of national executive of the OBS, serving as chairman to 1920, when he took an appointment with the Manchester Corporation; president of the Ashton League of the Blind; for several years an offical of the Ashton Labour Party; member of Hurst UDC (for 3 years); church warden (for 2 years); member of Radical Association and secretary and curator of Radical Club (1894); resigned from the Liberals in 1898; joined the Independent Labour Party in 1900; member of Anti-Vaccination League; elected to executive committee of Land Reform Council (1906); chairman of Ashton Labour Church (1906); member of sub-committee of Ashton District Distress Fund (1914); chairman of Land Nationalisation Society (1915); chairman of Ashton Tenants Defence League (1918).
content_tone: A valuable memoir, with full accounts of childhood, work and public life, providing both a graphic account of late 19th century village life and a document of Labour’s early struggles. Among the many subjects discussed are the home; domestic budget; hiring fairs; diet; dress; childhood games; agricultural trade unionism and Joseph Arch; schooling; wages in various trades; courtship; village festivals; superstitions and legends; Jubilee celebrations (1887); public activities and local politics; elections; provincial socialism. The narrative ends c.1917.
title: ‘The Autobiography of A ...’, TS, pp.57

father_raw: Father was employed in the leather bag industry.
residences: London
career_raw: Employed in a tea broker’s establishment (1894); leather-bag maker (1895-1904); appointed secretary of the Bible Training College (1904); editor of the Berean Expositor for more than 50 years; Principal of the Chapel of the Opened Book, Finsbury Square, London.
affiliations_raw: Member of the Bermondsey Settlement; published extensively on religious matters.
content_tone: A rather jumbled narrative, with the text frequently interrupted by random thoughts, verse, extracts from correspondence and extensive quotations from religious and other sources. Some comment, however, is made on the home and street life.
title: with a preface by Ruth Baker

father_raw: Eldest of 4 children of a taper, or sizer, in a cotton mill.
residences: Nelson (1879-1904); Edinburgh 9047); Nelson (1907-14?); London
career_raw: Half-timer in cotton mill (1889-92), and full-time at age 13; rose to position of undermanager in the mill; returned to work in the mill part-time after leaving university, combined with part-time teaching and lecturing for local Co-operative Societies and churches; worked for some years for the Independent Labour Party, supported by his wife, a music teacher and popular soloist; MP for Stourbridge (1927-31); joint managing director of Peace News, to which he regularly contributed (1940-).
affiliations_raw: Sunday School teacher at age 15, and preacher at the age of 20; president of the Young People’s Christian Endeavour Society; contributed regularly to the Indian Journal, Modern Review; joined the No-Conscription Fellowshipin 1914; started the anti-war broadsheet, the New Crusader; imprisoned, 1917-19; founder and chairman of the India Committee, devoted to the cause of Indian independence; served on various Select Committees; member of national committee, and for some years chairman, of the No More War Movement (merged in 1936 with the Peace Pledge Union); chairman of Society for Democratic Integration in Industry (now, the Industrial Common Ownership Movement); wrote large number of pamphlets and hundreds of articles, mostly on India and peace; was described as ‘... one of the greatest living interpreters of Gandhian philosophy...’.
content_tone: Written at the age of 80, the narrative tells briefly of Wellock’s happy childhood, half-time working, church activities and of his thirst and struggles for knowledge. The major part of the text is, though, devoted to the author’s ‘search for truth’ by means of pacifism and the application of Christian principles to social, economic and political life, in which he confronted the moral issues facing post-war Britain, America, Russia and India.
title: Off the Beaten Track. Adventures in the Art of Living, with a foreword by Jayaprakash Narayan

career_raw: First job was in the gardening department of a seed warehouse; gardener’ s assistant (aged about 17-22); post office employee (c.1873-1887); entered business on own account as bookseller and publisher.
affiliations_raw: Chorister; Malthusian; public lecturer. Publications include Marriage and its Mysteries (n. d.); Man: His Diseases and How to Cure them (1893); Man! Know Thyself [1905?].
content_tone: Few details are recorded of the author’s work or social life, with the tone of the text being a tract against puritan cant and hypocrisy. Arrested for selling and publishing ‘obscene’ books, the author’s advocacy of Malthusian doctrines remained undimmed. The narrative also contains comments on policing and Jews.
title: Prosecutions and Persecutions. Story of My Life

father_raw: Eldest of 9 children of a collier.
career_raw: Started work in the pit as a door-boy before the age of 9; a pony-driver by the age of 12, and a ‘full-blown’ collier by the age of 16; subsequently elected checkweighman; agent for the Somerset miners (1888-1917).
affiliations_raw: Secretary of miners’ lodge (1867); official with the Amalgamated Association of Miners; agent to West Bromwich Miners’ Federation, and one of the founders of the Midland Miners’ Federation, and secretary from 1886-8; member of national executive of Miners’ Federation of Great Britain, six times between 1889 and 1912; representative of the Midland Federation at the Rosebery Conference; member of West Bromwich School Board; member of Radstock (Somerset) UDC (1893-8); member of Clutton Board of Guardians for many years; supporter of Co-operative movement; Liberal; on staff of Labour Tribune, acting 2 as sub-editor in 1887.
content_tone: A short piece describing early life in a mining community in Staffordshire, with detail on pit life and conditions (child labour; accidents; trade unionism); diet; leisure; the influence of Methodism; and with a potted history of Labour agitation and organisation (Dorset and Manchester martyrs). Although the November issue states that the memoirs are to be continued, this does not appear to have been the case.
title: ‘Some Incidents in the Life of an Agitator’ The Beacon, May, July, Nov 1909.

father_raw: Father was an artisan.
career_raw: Employed as a button-cobber at age 7, followed by some time spent in a brass foundry; apprenticed to a rule-maker for 8 1/2 years (at age 12 1/2) but cancelled indentures prematurely; worked for a time as a rule-maker before entering into partnership as a manufacturing jeweller; commercial traveller; undertook various business ventures; bookmaker at race-meetings for much of adult working life, but also engaged in numerous commercial undertakings and running a newspaper, for which he did much of the writing and editing; was also a direotor of two public companies.
affiliations_raw: Poet; member of educational classes, mutual improvement societies, literary and debating clubs; heavy gambler; member of King’s Norton Board of Guardians and the Rural Sanitary Authority; member of Balsall Heath Local Board; claimed to have originated the first halfpenny newspaper, the Banner; later founded the penny weekly, South Birmingham News.
content_tone: Described as ‘..a chronicle of racing life from the early sixties to recent times, with reminiscences and anecdotes of many Turf celebrities’, including full exposures of ‘welshers’ and ‘sharpers’ engaged in illegitimate practices. Only brief reference is made to subjects other than the racing world and gambling.
title: A Wasted Life

father_raw: Father (an engineer) died before the author was born, resulting in reduced circumstances and status for his surviving family.
residences: a lower middle-class district in S
