career_raw: Reading-boy at publishing house (aged 14); silk hatter (from age 14); assistant manager in a hat manufactory (aged 24).
affiliations_raw: Amateur actor; author of London General (1953); 101 Jubilee Road A book of London Yesterdays (1948).
content_tone: Experiencing downward mobility following the death of his father, Willis offers a wry look at life and manners in a lower middle-class district of London and general reflections on late 19th century society. Among the themes discussed are family life and ancestry; leisure; transport; schooling; childhood games; diet; excursions and ‘jollifications‘, dress and fashion; retailing; early employment. The narrative ends in 1914.
title: Peace and Dripping Toast

residences: Skircoat and Halterhebble all his life
career_raw: Began work ‘when very young milking cows’‚ then farm-boy during day and in a card shop, carding teeth, by night. Later worked as a bobbin-winder (c.1838); woollen weaver; comber; railway navvy; quarryman; and, finally, as an expert horticulturalist.
affiliations_raw: Active in the Chartist and Co-operative movements, and later for the cause of Liberalism. Teetotaller. Published articles in the Halifax Courier relating to the social and political history of Halifax and district.
content_tone: The narrative begins with Wilson’s introduction to, and involvement in, radical politics, and what follows provides a most valuable account of the history of Chartism and radical politics in the mid-19th century. Among the topics covered are the Peterloo Massacre; electioneering practices; Plug Plot Riots, 1842; origin and struggles of the Halifax Co-operative movement; Reform League agitation; Hyde Park demonstrations and the 1867 Reform Bill. A major part of the text deals with aspects of the Chartist movement, including profiles of its leaders; comments on the trials at Leicester, 1843; physical force; the Land Scheme and its popular appeal.
title: The Struggles ofan Old Chartist: What he knows, and the part he has taken in various movements

father_raw: 3rd son of 7 children of a foreman draper.
career_raw: Part-time newsboy (aged 6); grocer’s errand-boy (aged 8/9); printer’s devil (aged 9/10); apprenticed to a lithographic printer (aged 13), but ran away to sea after a few mouths; apprentice seaman; worked for 11 years as a boy steward, cook and able seaman; served for 5 years in the Royal Naval Reserve; opened a small ‘cook shop’ in Monkwearmouth (1882); opened ‘Wilson’s Temperance Hotel and Dining Rooms’ in Sunderland (1884); general secretary of the National Amalgamated Seamen’s and Firemen’s Union of Great Britain and Ireland (1887-94), and then president of the new union from 1894; MP for Middlesbrough (1892-1900; 1906-10), and for South Shields (1918-22).
affiliations_raw: Member of Sunderland Seamen’s Union; delegate to Sunderland Trades Council; helped to establish the National Union of Labour; member of the North of England Sailor's and Seagoing Firemen’s Friendly Society (c.1883), serving as president (1885-7); member of parliamentary committee of TUC (1889-98); assisted in foundation of the International Transport Workers’ Federation (1896); vice-president of the British Workers’ League; member of the National Alliance of Employers and Employed (1917); awarded CBE in 1918; made a Companion of Honour in 1922; war caused him to adopt increasingly conservative political and industrial positions, coming to characterise the General Strike as a communist plot; gave evidence before various Royal Commissions and Departmental Committees concerned with sea labour; contributor to Seafaring, Seaman’s Chronicle and Seaman; publications include Objections to joining the Union answered [1897]; The Dublin Dispute: a statement of the seamen's case [1913]; The Red Hand Exploiting the Trade Union Movement: the Communist Offensive against the British Empire (1926); The Real Truth about the Soviet Government of Russia (1927).
content_tone: An important work by the founder of the NASFU, commencing with childhood recollections and comments on his adventures at sea and his various ‘berths’. The narrative then moves on to give a full account of his efforts at organising the seamen and firemen into a national union, and the early struggles of the NASEU in the law courts, in industrial action and against employers’ organisations and strike breakers. The narrative ends with the author’s entry into public office (1892) and with the voluntary liquidation of the union (1894). The intended second volume of memoirs was never published.
title: My Stormy Voyage Through Life, with a foreword by Sir Walter Runciman

father_raw: 2nd son of 6 children of a hand-loom weaver.
career_raw: At age 6 was sent to a cotton factory, but taken away by mother because of the beatings received there; put to the loom at about age 11, working first a cotton loom then ‘promoted’ to a worsted loom (for ‘a number of years’); schoolmaster (for 14 years), interrupted by spells when he ran own grocery shop and worked as assistant overseer to the poor. Then was engaged to compile the first Directory of Bradford (1845), and later became agent and correspondent for various provincial newspapers, becoming a regular journalist (for 5 years), and then reporter to the West Riding magistrates (for 25 years).
affiliations_raw: Dedicated to the cause of self-improvement; Sunday School teacher; member of chapel choir; lay preacher; poet; agent to Bradford branch of the Church Defence Association; scripture-reader; member of Great Hortona Temperance Society (for almost 20 years, 7 years as president).
content_tone: An interesting aaccount of self-improvement and upward mobility, with observations on the manners and customs of Bradford hand-loom weavers; diet; religious quarrels and disturbances (including the rupture among the Wesleyans, 1850); traditional customs (the ‘Denholme Wedding’).
title: Autobiography of John Wood, an old and well known. Bradfordian, Written in the 75th Year of his Age

father_raw: Father a weft manager.
career_raw: It was said of the author that he had been ‘everything by turns, and nothing long’. First job was as a warp-dresser, an occupation which he frequently fell back on when seeking work. Also worked as a sailor; apprentice to a mason; player with a travelling theatre company; scenic artist, advance agent and stage manager for a marionette showman; itinerant showman; dock labourer; enlisted in the army (3 years); Volunteer; contributed articles and stories to the Bradford Observer; joint-editor of the Keighley Spectator; ran a grocer’s shop (pre 1872); pattern-dresser (1 year); warp-sizing inspector; ‘bum’ bailiff to an auctioneer; inventor.
affiliations_raw: Poet; author of plays and comic stories; member of Amateur Dramatic Society; active in local politics; Secularist; pamphlet-writer (supporting ironwork strikers, 1871); member of the Royal Order of Ante diluvian Buffaloes. Published verse sheets, with his writing appearing in Random Rhymes and Rambles (1876) and Revised Edition of Poems (1891).
content_tone: A lively account of the colourful and varied life of a local celebrity and character. Among the accounts of his many adventures can be found references to plug-drawing; Chartism, and skirmishes with the military; ‘breeching’; poaching and the Keighley Riot of 1852; School Board elections (1875); the ‘ticket-of-leave’ strike in the Keighley iron trade (1871); fortune-telling; and profiles of scsome of his acquaintances. The narrative contains many examples of his poetry.
title: ‘Adventures and Recollections of Bill o’th Hoylus End. Told by Himself’, Keighley Herald, 2 June - 8 Dec 1893
